Deliver an unsynchronized biphasic shock immediately

questions.rationale: This patient is in ventricular fibrillation, a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm. The priority is immediate unsynchronized defibrillation while CPR continues. Early defibrillation is the definitive treatment for VF and offers the best chance of return of spontaneous circulation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable tachyarrhythmias with an organized rhythm and a pulse; it is not appropriate for pulseless ventricular fibrillation.
Amiodarone can be used for refractory VF/pulseless VT after defibrillation and CPR, but it should not delay the initial shock.
A 12-lead ECG is helpful in patients with a perfusing rhythm, but this patient is in cardiac arrest and requires immediate defibrillation without delaying resuscitation.
Magnesium sulfate is mainly indicated for torsades de pointes or suspected hypomagnesemia, not as the initial treatment for ventricular fibrillation.

questions.teaching_point: Pulseless ventricular fibrillation is treated with immediate unsynchronized defibrillation and ongoing high-quality CPR; do not delay for diagnostics or medications.

questions.topic: Avascular necrosis of the proximal femur
questions.vignette: A 71-year-old man comes to clinic for 4 months of gradually worsening left groin pain and stiffness. He has difficulty putting on socks and getting out of his car. The pain is worse with weight-bearing and occasionally wakes him at night. He has a history of polymyalgia rheumatica treated with repeated courses of prednisone over the past year. He denies fever, recent trauma, or low back pain. Examination shows an antalgic gait, decreased internal rotation of the left hip, and pain with passive range of motion. There is no overlying erythema or warmth.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this patient’s presentation?

answer_choices.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

questions.rationale: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is suggested by progressive groin pain, pain with weight-bearing, restricted hip range of motion, and an important risk factor for impaired bone blood supply: repeated glucocorticoid use. In older adults, symptoms can mimic degenerative joint disease, but the steroid exposure and pattern of pain and motion limitation make avascular necrosis the best fit.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hip osteoarthritis can also cause groin pain and limited internal rotation, but the chronic corticosteroid exposure and relatively rapid progression with night pain raise stronger concern for avascular necrosis.
Trochanteric bursitis usually causes lateral hip pain and tenderness over the greater trochanter rather than groin pain and painful restriction of passive hip motion.
Septic arthritis typically presents more acutely with marked pain, inability to bear weight, warmth, swelling, and often systemic symptoms such as fever, which are absent here.

Lumbar radiculopathy can cause radiating leg pain or neurologic symptoms, but this patient’s pain is localized to the groin and is reproduced with hip motion, which points to an intra-articular hip process.

questions.teaching_point: Progressive groin pain with decreased hip internal rotation in a patient with glucocorticoid exposure should raise concern for avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman presents to clinic with new mid-back pain that began after she bent over to lift a laundry basket 4 days ago. She describes sudden, sharp pain that is worse with standing and getting out of a chair and somewhat better when she lies flat. She denies numbness, weakness, fever, weight loss, or bowel/bladder changes. She has a history of postmenopausal osteoporosis and takes calcium, vitamin D, and alendronate inconsistently. Exam shows focal tenderness over the lower thoracic spine without bruising, step-off, or neurologic deficit. Plain radiographs reveal anterior wedging of a thoracic vertebral body with loss of height.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: This patient most likely has a vertebral compression fracture. The key clues are an older adult with osteoporosis, acute focal back pain after minimal trauma, point tenderness over the spine, pain worsened by axial loading or movement, and radiographic anterior vertebral wedging with loss of height. The absence of neurologic deficits and systemic symptoms also supports an uncomplicated compression fracture rather than infection or nerve root compression.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis usually presents with inflammatory back pain in a younger patient, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, and reduced spinal mobility rather than an acute focal injury in an older adult with osteoporosis.

Spinal epidural abscess usually presents with fever, severe pain, and progressive neurologic findings or risk factors such as bacteremia or injection drug use; this patient lacks systemic illness and imaging shows a compression deformity instead.
Lumbar disc herniation typically causes radicular pain radiating into the leg, often with sensory changes, weakness, or positive straight-leg raise, none of which are present here.

Degenerative spondylolisthesis more often causes chronic low back pain with neurogenic claudication or radicular symptoms, and it is diagnosed by vertebral slippage on imaging rather than anterior wedging from a fragility injury.

questions.teaching_point: In an older adult with osteoporosis, sudden focal back pain after minor stress and vertebral body wedging on x-ray strongly suggests a vertebral compression fracture.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 46-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 5 days of mouth soreness and a burning sensation when eating spicy foods. He recently completed a 10-day course of oral antibiotics for cellulitis. He has no fever, throat swelling, or dental pain. On examination, there are multiple white, creamy plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that scrape off easily, leaving a red base underneath.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: This patient has oral candidiasis, which classically presents with white, curd-like plaques on the oral mucosa that can be removed by scraping, often after recent antibiotic use or other factors that disrupt normal oral flora.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Herpetic gingivostomatitis typically causes painful vesicles or ulcers with gingival inflammation, not removable white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa.
Oral lichen planus often causes lacy white reticular streaks or chronic erosive lesions, not the removable creamy plaques seen here.
Aphthous stomatitis causes shallow, painful ulcers with erythematous halos, usually on nonkeratinized mucosa, rather than scrapable white plaques.
Oral leukoplakia presents as a persistent white oral plaque that does not scrape off; it is associated with premalignant change rather than an acute removable coating.

questions.teaching_point: Scrapable white oral plaques, especially after antibiotic use, are classic for oral candidiasis.

questions.vignette: A 16-year-old girl is admitted for same-day outpatient repair of a fractured radius after a skateboard injury. She appears anxious and asks repeated questions about fasting before anesthesia. Her mother reports that over the past year the patient has had episodes of eating large amounts of food in secret and then immediately going to the bathroom. She has been increasingly preoccupied with weight, has worn loose clothing despite normal body habitus, and recently complained of intermittent dizziness. On preoperative evaluation, her pulse is 54/min and blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg. She has normal mental status and no focal neurologic deficits. The anesthesiologist is concerned about a potentially occult complication that could increase perioperative risk.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step before proceeding with anesthesia?

answer_choices.text: Obtain a serum electrolyte panel including potassium, bicarbonate, and magnesium

questions.rationale: This adolescent has features strongly suggestive of bulimia nervosa, including binge eating, compensatory bathroom trips, weight preoccupation, and bradycardia with hypotension. In the perioperative setting, the most important immediate diagnostic assessment is serum electrolytes, particularly potassium, bicarbonate, and magnesium, because purging can cause hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and hypomagnesemia. These abnormalities increase the risk of peri-anesthetic arrhythmias and hemodynamic instability.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A urine toxicology screen could be considered if substance misuse were suspected, but the history already points to bulimic behavior. It would not be the most appropriate pre-anesthesia test compared with checking for purging-related electrolyte disturbances.

An electrocardiogram may be useful if an electrolyte abnormality is found or if arrhythmia is suspected, but it does not identify the likely underlying perioperative risk in this patient. Serum electrolytes are the priority because purging commonly causes clinically important abnormalities.

A pregnancy test is a standard preoperative study in patients who could be pregnant, but it does not address the anesthesiologist's concern about occult complications from purging behavior. The more immediate concern is an electrolyte disturbance that could precipitate arrhythmia during anesthesia.

Serum amylase can be elevated in patients with recurrent vomiting and may support an eating disorder, but it does not address the most urgent perioperative safety concern. Electrolyte abnormalities are more clinically important before anesthesia.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected bulimia nervosa before anesthesia, check electrolytes first because purging commonly causes hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis that can make sedation and surgery unsafe.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old man comes to an urgent care clinic because of 2 days of blurred vision, drooping eyelids, dry mouth, and increasing difficulty swallowing. He says he has felt weak and “heavy” since eating a home-canned green bean dish at a family gathering 18 hours before his symptoms began. His wife notes that his speech has become muffled, and he now has trouble holding his head up. He is afebrile, alert, and breathing comfortably, but his pupils are sluggishly reactive and he has symmetric descending weakness on exam.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

answer_choices.text: Arrange routine outpatient neurology follow-up and start pyridostigmine for presumed myasthenia gravis
Call poison control and public health, but delay antitoxin until toxin studies confirm the diagnosis
Perform bedside spirometry, prescribe oral antibiotics for possible food poisoning, and schedule next-day follow-up
Send him to the emergency department for urgent evaluation, airway monitoring, and administration of botulinum antitoxin
Observe him in urgent care for several hours, obtain stool cultures, and discharge him if his breathing remains comfortable

questions.rationale: This patient has classic foodborne botulism: blurred vision, ptosis, dysphagia, dry mouth, muffled speech, and symmetric descending weakness after eating home-canned food. The immediate priority is emergency transfer for airway and respiratory monitoring because paralysis can progress to respiratory failure. Botulinum antitoxin should be given as soon as botulism is suspected because it neutralizes circulating toxin and limits progression; treatment should not be delayed for confirmatory testing.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Myasthenia gravis can cause ptosis and bulbar weakness, but it does not fit the history of home-canned food exposure or the prominent dry mouth and descending paralysis. Pyridostigmine and routine outpatient follow-up are inappropriate for a suspected toxin-mediated emergency.

Public health notification is appropriate, but antitoxin should not be delayed while waiting for toxin confirmation. Botulism is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment is most effective when started promptly after suspicion arises.

Foodborne botulism is not treated with antibiotics, and bedside spirometry alone is insufficient management in a patient with cranial nerve and bulbar symptoms. Next-day follow-up would dangerously delay definitive emergency care.

Brief observation and stool cultures do not adequately address the risk of rapid respiratory deterioration in suspected botulism. Diagnostic testing should not delay immediate hospital evaluation and antitoxin when the clinical picture is strongly suggestive.

questions.teaching_point: Suspected botulism is a medical emergency: send the patient for immediate hospital evaluation, monitor airway and respiratory status, and give botulinum antitoxin without waiting for confirmatory testing.

questions.vignette: A 48-year-old man comes to clinic for fatigue and decreased libido that have gradually worsened over the past year. He reports mild aching in both hands and right upper quadrant discomfort. He drinks alcohol only on weekends and takes no medications. Exam shows mild hepatomegaly, bronze hyperpigmentation of the skin, and tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. Laboratory studies reveal ferritin 980 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 68%, AST 62 U/L, and ALT 58 U/L. Hepatitis B and C testing are negative. Genetic testing confirms HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis, and liver ultrasound shows no focal mass or cirrhosis. He is hemodynamically stable and has no anemia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Refer for urgent liver transplantation evaluation

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis with markedly elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation, but no contraindication to blood removal. The appropriate first-line management in a stable, nonanemic adult is scheduled therapeutic phlebotomy to reduce iron stores and prevent end-organ damage. Chelation is generally reserved for patients who cannot undergo phlebotomy, and he does not have evidence of acute liver failure or another inflammatory condition requiring steroids.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Liver transplantation is considered for end-stage liver disease or acute liver failure, neither of which is present here. Although he needs monitoring for hepatic complications, the immediate treatment is iron removal with phlebotomy.

Prednisone is not indicated for hereditary hemochromatosis. Corticosteroids would not reduce iron burden and would expose the patient to unnecessary adverse effects without treating the underlying problem.

Vitamin B12 replacement treats cobalamin deficiency and would not address iron overload. This patient's constellation of hyperferritinemia, high transferrin saturation, skin hyperpigmentation, arthropathy, and liver enzyme elevation is more consistent with iron excess.

Oral iron chelation with deferasirox is not first-line for hereditary hemochromatosis and is typically used when phlebotomy cannot be performed, such as in severe anemia or certain transfusion-related iron overload states.

questions.teaching_point: In stable adults with hereditary hemochromatosis and no major anemia, first-line treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy to lower iron stores.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man collapses while waiting in the emergency department. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally. A monitor is attached and shows a chaotic, irregular waveform with no identifiable QRS complexes. A pulse is not palpable. A nurse has already called for help and is beginning chest compressions. The defibrillator is being charged while oxygen is being delivered by bag-mask ventilation.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

answer_choices.text: Obtain a 12-lead ECG before further treatment
Give intravenous amiodarone before any shock

questions.rationale: This patient is in ventricular fibrillation, a pulseless shockable rhythm. After immediate high-quality CPR, the next step is unsynchronized defibrillation as soon as the defibrillator is ready. Synchronized cardioversion requires an organized rhythm with a pulse, adenosine is for certain supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, amiodarone is an adjunct after defibrillation attempts in refractory VF/pulseless VT, and waiting for a 12-lead ECG would inappropriately delay lifesaving therapy.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A 12-lead ECG is helpful in patients with a perfusing rhythm, but it should not delay immediate defibrillation and resuscitation in pulseless ventricular fibrillation.
Amiodarone can be given during refractory ventricular fibrillation, but it does not replace immediate defibrillation. Shock and CPR come first.
Adenosine is used for selected regular narrow-complex tachycardias and some stable wide-complex tachycardias, not for pulseless ventricular fibrillation.
Synchronized cardioversion is used for unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse. In ventricular fibrillation there is no organized QRS complex to synchronize with, so defibrillation is required.

questions.teaching_point: Pulseless ventricular fibrillation requires immediate unsynchronized defibrillation plus high-quality CPR; do not delay shock for diagnostic testing or medications.

questions.vignette: A 38-year-old man with HIV presents to clinic with 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and low-grade fevers. He stopped taking antiretroviral therapy 1 year ago. He is afebrile in the office, with respiratory rate 22/min and oxygen saturation 94% on room air at rest, decreasing to 88% after walking down the hall. Lung examination is unremarkable. Chest radiograph shows diffuse, bilateral interstitial infiltrates. A recent CD4 count is 96 cells/mm3. The clinician suspects Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and wants the most appropriate study to detect the organism.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage with fungal staining and PCR for Pneumocystis jirovecii
Sputum Gram stain and routine bacterial culture

questions.rationale: This patient has classic Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: subacute dyspnea, dry cough, exertional hypoxemia, diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, and advanced HIV immunosuppression. Confirmation is made by detecting the organism in a respiratory specimen, usually with induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage. Organism-specific staining and/or PCR on these specimens are appropriate diagnostic tests; bronchoalveolar lavage is generally more sensitive than induced sputum. Serum beta-D-glucan can support the diagnosis but is not specific enough to confirm it.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Serum beta-D-glucan is a nonspecific fungal marker that can support Pneumocystis infection, but it does not directly confirm the diagnosis.
QuantiFERON-TB Gold assesses immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and does not detect Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Routine sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture evaluate typical bacterial pneumonia, which does not fit this subacute hypoxemic interstitial presentation as well as Pneumocystis pneumonia.
Serum galactomannan supports invasive Aspergillus infection, not Pneumocystis pneumonia.

questions.teaching_point: In patients with advanced HIV and a classic interstitial pneumonia pattern, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is confirmed by detecting the organism in induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage, usually with special staining and/or PCR.

questions.vignette: A 38-year-old man is admitted for recurrent severe right-sided headaches that began abruptly 2 days ago. Each attack lasts 45 to 90 minutes and is associated with marked restlessness, tearing of the right eye, nasal congestion, and right eyelid droop. During attacks he paces the room and says he cannot lie still. He has had 3 similar attacks each day since admission. Acetaminophen and IV ketorolac have provided no relief. He has a 15-pack-year smoking history and drinks alcohol on weekends, but he denies trauma, fever, focal weakness, or visual loss. Neuroimaging from the emergency department was unrevealing.
questions.lead_in: Which inpatient treatment is most appropriate to abort his acute headache attacks?
questions.rationale: High-flow oxygen delivered by nonrebreather mask is a first-line abortive treatment for cluster headache and is especially appropriate in the inpatient setting when the patient is having recurrent attacks. The short, severe unilateral headaches with cranial autonomic symptoms and agitation are characteristic of cluster headache, and oxygen can rapidly reduce or terminate an attack. Compared with triptans, oxygen avoids medication adverse effects and is often the simplest immediate therapy to administer in the hospital.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Intravenous methylprednisolone may be used as short-term transitional therapy to suppress attacks while preventive treatment is started, but it is not the most appropriate immediate abortive therapy for an active cluster headache attack.

Intranasal lidocaine has been used in some patients as an adjunctive option, but its efficacy is less consistent than high-flow oxygen or a rapid-onset triptan and it is not the best choice for aborting these attacks.

Subcutaneous sumatriptan is an effective acute treatment for cluster headache, but high-flow oxygen is the preferred inpatient abortive therapy here because it works rapidly, can be repeated, and avoids triptan-related contraindications and adverse effects.
Oral prednisone can help as bridge therapy to reduce attack frequency, but it does not rapidly abort an individual cluster headache attack and is therefore not the best immediate treatment.

questions.teaching_point: Cluster headache attacks are best aborted with high-flow oxygen or a rapid-onset triptan; oral analgesics and opioids are usually ineffective, and steroids are used mainly as transitional therapy.

questions.vignette: A 38-year-old man presents to clinic with 3 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough, low-grade fevers, fatigue, and shortness of breath with exertion. He reports that his symptoms are worse when walking up stairs. He has a history of HIV but has not taken antiretroviral therapy for several years. His oxygen saturation is 93% on room air at rest and drops to 88% with ambulation. Lung examination reveals scattered fine inspiratory crackles without focal wheezes or egophony. Chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates without focal consolidation or pleural effusion. A diagnosis of opportunistic pulmonary infection is suspected.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate to help confirm the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and nucleic acid amplification testing
Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage for Pneumocystis jirovecii staining and PCR

questions.rationale: This patient has the classic subacute presentation of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: progressive dry cough, exertional dyspnea, mild hypoxemia, advanced untreated HIV, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. The best test to help confirm the diagnosis is induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage with Pneumocystis-directed testing such as staining and PCR, which directly identifies the organism from lower respiratory tract samples. In practice, bronchoscopy with BAL is often used when induced sputum is nondiagnostic or the pretest probability is high.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A respiratory viral multiplex PCR panel may identify viral causes of pneumonia, but this presentation is more consistent with an opportunistic fungal infection in advanced HIV rather than a viral respiratory illness.

Serum β-D-glucan can support the diagnosis of Pneumocystis pneumonia because it is often elevated, but it is nonspecific and does not confirm the organism. A direct respiratory sample with staining or PCR is more appropriate for confirmation.

Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear and nucleic acid amplification testing are appropriate when pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected, but this patient's presentation is more typical of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia than active TB.

High-resolution chest CT can further characterize diffuse lung disease and may show findings suggestive of Pneumocystis pneumonia, but it does not confirm the diagnosis and is less definitive than organism-directed testing of respiratory secretions.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia, confirm the diagnosis with induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage and organism-directed testing; serum β-D-glucan or imaging may support suspicion but are not definitive.

questions.vignette: A 54-year-old man is evaluated during preoperative testing before an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. He feels well and denies abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, or prior liver disease. He was born in Vietnam and moved to the United States as a teenager. Laboratory studies show AST 48 U/L, ALT 61 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and INR 1.0. Because of his country of birth and mildly elevated transaminases, the surgeon requests hepatitis B assessment before surgery.
questions.lead_in: Which additional diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for chronic hepatitis B infection?

answer_choices.text: Hepatitis B e antigen and anti-hepatitis B e antibody only
Hepatitis C antibody with reflex RNA testing
Hepatitis B virus DNA polymerase chain reaction only
Hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis B surface antibody, and total hepatitis B core antibody

questions.rationale: The most appropriate next step is a complete hepatitis B serologic panel with HBsAg, anti-HBs, and total anti-HBc. In an asymptomatic adult with epidemiologic risk factors for hepatitis B and mild transaminitis, this initial serologic evaluation best identifies active infection, prior resolved infection, or vaccine-induced immunity and determines whether chronic hepatitis B is present. HBeAg and HBV DNA are used later to assess infectivity and viral replication after infection is established, not as the initial screening study.

distractor_rationales.explanation: HBeAg and anti-HBe help assess viral replication and infectivity in someone already known to have hepatitis B, but they are not the initial diagnostic studies to establish infection status.

Hepatitis C testing may be appropriate in some patients with elevated liver enzymes, but this vignette includes a specific epidemiologic risk for hepatitis B, so HBV serologies are the more appropriate initial study.
HBV DNA PCR is useful for quantifying viral load and guiding management once hepatitis B is suspected or confirmed, but it is not the best first-line test for initial evaluation.
Ultrasonography can assess structural liver or biliary disease, but it does not evaluate hepatitis B infection status and would not be the first diagnostic study for this question.

questions.teaching_point: Initial hepatitis B evaluation is done with HBsAg, anti-HBs, and total anti-HBc; more specialized tests such as HBeAg and HBV DNA come later if infection is confirmed.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man presents to an outpatient clinic with 1 day of rapidly worsening redness and pain on his left lower leg. He has fever, malaise, and a history of chronic tinea pedis. He takes no immunosuppressive medications and has no diabetes. On exam, his temperature is 38.7°C (101.7°F), and the anterior lower leg has a bright red, warm, tender plaque with a sharply demarcated raised border. No fluctuance, crepitus, or purulent drainage is present. He is able to bear weight, and distal pulses are intact.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

answer_choices.text: Immediate incision and drainage of the lesion
Oral penicillin or amoxicillin with leg elevation and close outpatient follow-up
Topical mupirocin applied to the affected area three times daily

questions.rationale: This patient has erysipelas, a superficial skin infection most often caused by streptococci, suggested by the acute onset, fever, bright erythema, warmth, tenderness, and sharply demarcated raised borders without purulence or abscess. In an otherwise stable outpatient, first-line therapy is an oral beta-lactam such as penicillin or amoxicillin, along with supportive measures such as leg elevation and management of portals of entry like tinea pedis. Close follow-up is appropriate to ensure improvement.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Incision and drainage is indicated for an abscess or purulent collection, which is not present here.

IV vancomycin and admission are generally reserved for severe infection, systemic toxicity, failed outpatient therapy, or concern for MRSA/complicated cellulitis; this stable patient can be treated as an outpatient.
Topical mupirocin is insufficient for a deeper nonpurulent bacterial skin infection and is used for limited superficial infections, not erysipelas.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone is not preferred for classic nonpurulent erysipelas because streptococcal coverage may be inadequate.

questions.teaching_point: Nonpurulent erysipelas is usually streptococcal and is treated first-line with an oral beta-lactam plus supportive care when the patient is clinically stable.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman is seen in clinic for intermittent fatigue and "bone aches." She has had two low-impact wrist fractures over the past 4 years and reports worsening constipation and increased urination. Her medications include hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and vitamin D. She has already stopped hydrochlorothiazide for 6 weeks, but repeat testing still shows persistent mild hypercalcemia, low-normal phosphate, and an elevated parathyroid hormone level. Examination shows mild proximal muscle weakness but is otherwise unremarkable. Bone mineral density demonstrates osteoporosis at the femoral neck.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Begin cinacalcet therapy and continue observation
Start oral bisphosphonate therapy as definitive treatment
Reassure the patient and repeat calcium testing in 1 year

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism with end-organ complications, including osteoporosis and fragility fractures. She also has persistent hypercalcemia with inappropriately elevated parathyroid hormone after stopping hydrochlorothiazide, confirming that the thiazide was not the sole cause. In a patient who is an acceptable operative candidate, parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and is recommended for symptomatic disease or for asymptomatic disease with osteoporosis or fragility fractures.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cinacalcet can lower calcium in patients who are not surgical candidates or who need temporary control, but it is not preferred over surgery in a patient with symptomatic disease and skeletal complications.

Bisphosphonates may improve bone density in patients who cannot undergo surgery, but they do not correct the excess parathyroid hormone secretion and are not definitive treatment when surgical criteria are met.
Calcitonin is used mainly for short-term treatment of acute severe hypercalcemia, not for chronic outpatient management of primary hyperparathyroidism with osteoporosis and fractures.

Observation with periodic monitoring is reserved for selected patients without symptoms or end-organ complications. This patient has symptoms, fragility fractures, and osteoporosis, so surveillance alone is not appropriate.

questions.teaching_point: Primary hyperparathyroidism with symptoms, osteoporosis, or fragility fractures is an indication for parathyroidectomy in an operative candidate, after reversible contributors to hypercalcemia such as thiazides have been addressed.

questions.vignette: A 9-year-old girl is seen for a pre-travel visit with her mother 2 weeks before leaving for 3 weeks to visit relatives in rural Peru. She is healthy, up to date on routine childhood immunizations, and has no history of hepatitis A vaccination. Her mother asks what vaccine is most appropriate to reduce the child’s risk of acquiring hepatitis A during the trip. The child has no contraindications to vaccination.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive recommendation?

answer_choices.text: Delay hepatitis A vaccination until the child turns 10 years old
Begin the hepatitis A vaccine series now and give the second dose at least 6 months later
Administer hepatitis A immune globulin only before departure
No hepatitis A prevention is needed because the destination is not in the United States
Give a single booster dose of hepatitis A vaccine only after she returns from travel

questions.rationale: Hepatitis A vaccination is recommended for children older than 1 year who are traveling to countries with intermediate or high hepatitis A endemicity, including many areas outside the United States. She should receive the 2-dose vaccine series, with the second dose given at least 6 months after the first. Because she is healthy and has enough time before departure, vaccination is the appropriate preventive measure.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hepatitis A vaccine is recommended beginning at age 1 year for children who have indications such as international travel. Waiting until age 10 would leave her unprotected for this trip.

Immune globulin is reserved for specific situations such as certain infants, older travelers with limited time before departure, or people for whom vaccine is contraindicated. This healthy 9-year-old can receive vaccine instead.
Travel outside the United States can increase exposure risk to hepatitis A, especially in areas with higher endemicity. Prevention is still indicated based on travel destination and age.
A single dose given only after return does not provide pre-exposure protection for the upcoming trip. Hepatitis A prevention should be started before travel when possible.

questions.teaching_point: Children older than 1 year traveling to areas with higher hepatitis A risk should receive hepatitis A vaccine before departure, with a second dose at least 6 months later.

questions.vignette: A 24-year-old woman is admitted the day before an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She reports long-standing restriction of food intake and intense fear of weight gain after a remote sports injury led to weight-focused criticism. Over the past 6 months, she has lost 11 kg, has missed several menstrual periods, and exercises compulsively. On exam, she appears cachectic with cool extremities and bradycardia. Preoperative labs show potassium 3.1 mEq/L, bicarbonate 31 mEq/L, and magnesium at the low end of normal. The surgeon asks which additional study is most important before proceeding with anesthesia.
questions.lead_in: Which additional diagnostic study is most appropriate before surgery?
questions.rationale: This patient has anorexia nervosa with significant malnutrition and electrolyte abnormalities before anesthesia. A 12-lead ECG is the most appropriate additional study because bradycardia and hypokalemia increase the risk of conduction abnormalities and malignant arrhythmias during the perioperative period. ECG results help assess immediate anesthesia risk and guide correction of electrolyte disturbances before surgery.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Serum cortisol testing is not the most appropriate study in this setting. Although endocrine disorders can contribute to weight loss, her chronic restrictive behaviors, amenorrhea, and compulsive exercise point to anorexia nervosa, and the urgent perioperative issue is cardiac evaluation.
DEXA scanning can assess bone loss in patients with chronic anorexia nervosa, but it does not address the acute anesthesia-related risk from bradycardia and hypokalemia before an elective procedure.

Brain MRI is not the most appropriate preoperative study here because the presentation is already consistent with anorexia nervosa and the urgent perioperative concern is cardiac risk from malnutrition and electrolyte abnormalities, not a structural neurologic cause of weight loss.

Upper endoscopy may be useful if there were alarm symptoms suggesting a gastrointestinal lesion or obstruction, but this patient’s history strongly suggests a restrictive eating disorder and the immediate preoperative priority is evaluating cardiac stability.

questions.teaching_point: In an underweight patient with anorexia nervosa before anesthesia, obtain an ECG to assess for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia risk, especially when bradycardia or electrolyte abnormalities are present.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old woman is scheduled for elective total knee arthroplasty in 3 months because of severe medial compartment osteoarthritis. She has daily knee pain with walking and stands much of the day as a cashier. Her medications include lisinopril and acetaminophen as needed. She asks what medication would be most appropriate to help control her knee pain before surgery. She has no history of peptic ulcer disease, chronic kidney disease, or anticoagulant use. Examination shows crepitus and bony enlargement of the right knee without warmth or effusion.
questions.lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic therapy for her knee osteoarthritis pain?
questions.rationale: Topical diclofenac gel is an evidence-based first-line pharmacologic option for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, especially when pain is localized to one or a few joints. It provides analgesia with lower systemic exposure than oral NSAIDs, which helps reduce the risk of gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular adverse effects. In a patient awaiting elective surgery, using a topical NSAID is a reasonable way to control pain while minimizing systemic medication burden.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Duloxetine can be used for chronic osteoarthritis pain in selected patients, but it is not the preferred first-line therapy for localized knee osteoarthritis.
Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug used for inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, not for degenerative osteoarthritis.

Naproxen can reduce osteoarthritis pain, but oral NSAIDs have greater systemic adverse-effect risk than topical NSAIDs, making them a less preferred first choice for isolated knee symptoms when a topical option is available.
Oral prednisone is not recommended for routine osteoarthritis pain control and carries unnecessary risks such as hyperglycemia, hypertension, and impaired wound healing.

questions.teaching_point: For localized knee osteoarthritis, topical NSAIDs are preferred first-line pharmacologic therapy because they relieve pain while limiting systemic adverse effects compared with oral NSAIDs.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old woman comes to clinic for worsening right knee pain that has gradually progressed over 4 years. The pain is worse after gardening and climbing stairs and improves with rest. She has no morning stiffness lasting more than 15 minutes. She has tried acetaminophen with minimal relief and has a history of hypertension treated with lisinopril. Examination shows bony enlargement of the knee with mild crepitus and no warmth, erythema, or effusion. Body mass index is 31 kg/m2. She asks for a treatment that will improve her function and allow her to stay active.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment to improve her symptoms and function?

answer_choices.text: Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy and an exercise/weight-loss program
Oral ibuprofen therapy with consideration of gastroprotection
Oral prednisone for 10 days followed by taper

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, suggested by chronic activity-related pain, minimal morning stiffness, crepitus, and bony enlargement without inflammatory findings. After inadequate relief with acetaminophen, the next appropriate management is conservative therapy aimed at improving pain and function. Exercise and weight loss are key interventions that improve symptoms and mobility, and a topical NSAID is a reasonable medication choice in an older adult because it provides local pain relief with less systemic exposure than oral NSAIDs. Her hypertension also makes minimizing systemic NSAID exposure preferable when possible.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are used for inflammatory arthritides such as rheumatoid arthritis, not for osteoarthritis.

Oral NSAIDs can help osteoarthritis pain, but in this older patient with hypertension, a topical NSAID is generally preferred first to reduce systemic adverse effects. Gastroprotection does not make oral NSAIDs the best next step here.
Oral prednisone is not recommended for routine osteoarthritis management because osteoarthritis is a degenerative, not inflammatory, joint disease, and corticosteroids add avoidable adverse effects.

Intra-articular corticosteroid injection can provide short-term relief for persistent osteoarthritis symptoms, but it is usually considered after initial conservative therapy such as exercise, weight loss, and NSAIDs.

questions.teaching_point: For knee osteoarthritis, initial outpatient management should emphasize exercise, weight loss, and topical NSAIDs; oral NSAIDs, injections, and surgery are reserved for patients whose symptoms persist despite conservative therapy.

questions.vignette: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated for easy bruising and recurrent nosebleeds for 3 weeks. She had a viral upper respiratory illness about a month ago. She takes only a multivitamin and denies aspirin, NSAID, alcohol, or illicit drug use. Her exam shows scattered petechiae and bruises on her arms and legs without lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Vital signs are normal. Platelet count is 18,000/µL, hemoglobin and white blood cell count are normal, and peripheral smear shows isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets. She is otherwise well and has no active bleeding.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial outpatient treatment?
questions.rationale: This patient has newly recognized immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) with a platelet count well below 30,000/µL and mucocutaneous bleeding, but no hemodynamic instability or life-threatening hemorrhage. In symptomatic adults with severe thrombocytopenia, initial outpatient treatment is corticosteroids to rapidly reduce immune-mediated platelet destruction and raise the platelet count.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Observation alone is reasonable for asymptomatic adults with higher platelet counts, but this patient has clinically significant bleeding and a markedly low platelet count, warranting treatment.
Rituximab can be used for persistent or refractory ITP, but it is not the preferred initial outpatient therapy for a newly diagnosed symptomatic patient.
Platelet transfusion is generally reserved for life-threatening bleeding, urgent procedures, or severe hemorrhage because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed in ITP.
Splenectomy is a second-line option for chronic or refractory ITP, not an immediate first-line intervention in a newly diagnosed outpatient.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic adult ITP with platelets <30,000/µL is usually treated first with corticosteroids; reserve platelet transfusion and definitive therapies for severe bleeding or refractory disease.

questions.vignette: A 3-month-old boy is brought to clinic because of poor weight gain and increasing fatigue during feeds. His mother reports that he tires after several ounces, sweats with feeding, and has looked "blue" around the lips when crying. He was born at term without complications. On examination, his oxygen saturation is 82% on room air. He has mild central cyanosis, a single second heart sound, and a systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border. The liver edge is not enlarged, and there are no signs of respiratory distress. Chest radiograph shows a normal-sized heart with decreased pulmonary vascular markings.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Patent ductus arteriosus with Eisenmenger physiology
Ventricular septal defect with pulmonary overcirculation

questions.rationale: Tricuspid atresia causes cyanosis in infancy due to absent direct communication between the right atrium and right ventricle, requiring blood to cross an atrial septal defect for systemic output. Common clues include early cyanosis, poor feeding and growth, a single S2, a systolic murmur from associated shunts, and decreased pulmonary blood flow on chest radiograph.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Patent ductus arteriosus with Eisenmenger physiology can cause cyanosis, but this typically develops later after longstanding left-to-right shunting and pulmonary vascular disease, not as an early-infant presentation with a normal-sized heart and decreased pulmonary vascular markings.

A ventricular septal defect with pulmonary overcirculation usually produces signs of heart failure such as tachypnea, hepatomegaly, and increased pulmonary vascularity on imaging, rather than cyanosis with decreased pulmonary blood flow.

Transposition of the great arteries causes severe cyanosis in the newborn period, often within the first days of life, and is usually associated with a striking discrepancy between severe hypoxemia and minimal murmur; the later onset and exam findings here are less consistent.

Tetralogy of Fallot also causes cyanosis and a systolic murmur, but it more often presents with hypercyanotic spells, a harsh systolic ejection murmur, and decreased pulmonary flow with classic boot-shaped cardiac silhouette rather than a single second heart sound as the key finding.

questions.teaching_point: Tricuspid atresia typically presents with early cyanosis, poor feeding, a single S2, and decreased pulmonary blood flow because right ventricular inflow is absent.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 78-year-old woman comes to clinic because of a sore mouth and decreased appetite for 1 week. She has type 2 diabetes and uses inhaled fluticasone-salmeterol for COPD. She reports a burning sensation on her tongue and says food tastes “different.” On examination, she has several creamy white plaques on the buccal mucosa and tongue that can be partially scraped off, leaving a mildly erythematous surface. Her vital signs are normal, and she has no facial swelling or trismus.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: This patient most likely has oral candidiasis (thrush). The combination of removable white oral plaques, burning mouth symptoms, altered taste, and risk factors such as inhaled corticosteroid use and diabetes is classic for Candida overgrowth in the oral cavity.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Aphthous ulcers are discrete, painful shallow ulcers with an erythematous halo, not diffuse removable white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa.
Oral lichen planus often causes lacy white reticular streaks on the buccal mucosa and is not characterized by easily removed creamy plaques.
Herpetic gingivostomatitis typically causes painful vesicles or shallow ulcers with gingival inflammation rather than scrapable white plaques.
Leukoplakia presents as a white oral patch that cannot be scraped off and is more concerning for premalignant change, unlike the removable plaques seen here.

questions.teaching_point: Scrapable white oral plaques in an older patient using inhaled steroids strongly suggest oral candidiasis.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man is brought to an outpatient psychiatry visit by his sister because of progressively worsening odd behavior over the past year. He has become socially withdrawn, has stopped working, and his speech during the interview is difficult to follow because his answers are loosely connected and frequently shift to unrelated topics. He laughs inappropriately, appears disheveled, and needs prompting to maintain basic hygiene and other day-to-day self-care, but he is still eating, sleeping, and able to remain safely at home with his sister. He denies hearing voices or having a fixed false belief system. His sister reports that symptoms have been present continuously for more than 6 months and are causing major impairment at home and at work. He is calm, denies suicidal or homicidal thoughts, and has no signs of intoxication or medical instability.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Order urine toxicology testing and observe without treatment until symptoms resolve
Begin an SSRI for presumed depression-related withdrawal and disorganization
Start an antipsychotic medication and arrange close outpatient follow-up
Reassure the patient that this is a personality disorder and recommend psychotherapy alone
Refer for inpatient admission for immediate electroconvulsive therapy

questions.rationale: This patient has schizophrenia with prominent disorganized speech and behavior, functional decline, and symptoms persisting for more than 6 months. He is not suicidal, homicidal, intoxicated, medically unstable, or unable to be kept safe at home, so the appropriate next step is outpatient antipsychotic treatment with close follow-up. Ongoing care should also include monitoring for side effects, adherence, and psychosocial support. Although he needs prompting for hygiene, the vignette clarifies that he is still eating, sleeping, and can remain safely at home, so inpatient admission is not required at this time.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Substance use should be considered in psychosis, but the history here supports a chronic primary psychotic disorder. Observation without treatment would delay appropriate care and does not address the symptoms.
An SSRI may be used for comorbid depression, but it does not treat schizophrenia or disorganized psychotic symptoms. Withdrawal and speech disorganization are not explained well by depression alone.
A personality disorder does not explain this level of thought disorganization, inappropriate affect, and sustained functional decline. Psychotherapy alone is not adequate treatment for schizophrenia.
ECT is not first-line treatment for a stable outpatient with schizophrenia. It is generally reserved for catatonia, severe mood episodes, or refractory psychosis with specific indications.

questions.teaching_point: Stable outpatient schizophrenia with disorganized speech and behavior is treated with antipsychotic medication and close follow-up; hospitalization is reserved for danger to self or others, grave disability/inability to care for self, or severe decompensation.

questions.vignette: A 52-year-old man comes to clinic for evaluation of increasing thirst and blurry vision over the past 3 months. He has gained 8 kg (18 lb) over the past 2 years and exercises rarely because of a desk job. He has hypertension and hypertriglyceridemia and takes lisinopril and atorvastatin. BMI is 33 kg/m2. On examination, blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg, and foot exam shows decreased vibratory sensation over both great toes with intact skin and normal pedal pulses. Random fingerstick glucose in the office is 246 mg/dL. He reports that his father developed kidney disease from diabetes.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most characteristic of this patient’s likely condition?

answer_choices.text: Acanthosis nigricans on the posterior neck
Bilateral nonpitting edema of the lower extremities

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has type 2 diabetes mellitus, suggested by hyperglycemic symptoms, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, elevated random glucose, and early peripheral neuropathy. Acanthosis nigricans is a classic physical finding of insulin resistance and is commonly associated with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. It appears as hyperpigmented, velvety plaques, often on the posterior neck or axillae.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pretibial myxedema is associated with Graves disease, not type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Fine tremor with lid lag suggests hyperthyroidism, not insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Palmar erythema with spider angiomas suggests chronic liver disease, not diabetes-related insulin resistance.
Bilateral nonpitting edema may be seen in conditions such as lymphedema or hypothyroidism, but it is not characteristic of type 2 diabetes mellitus.

questions.teaching_point: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is commonly associated with insulin resistance findings such as acanthosis nigricans, along with obesity and neuropathic complications.

questions.vignette: A 2-day-old term newborn is brought to the emergency department for poor feeding, fast breathing, and blue-tinged lips that have worsened since discharge home. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. On examination, the infant is tachypneic with mild retractions, oxygen saturation is 82% on room air, and a single loud second heart sound is heard. A harsh systolic murmur is present along the left sternal border, and the femoral pulses are equal. Chest radiograph shows mild cardiomegaly with increased pulmonary vascular markings.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

questions.rationale: Truncus arteriosus is a cyanotic congenital heart defect in which a single great vessel arises from the heart, leading to early neonatal cyanosis, tachypnea, poor feeding, a systolic murmur, and increased pulmonary blood flow on chest radiograph.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart defect, but it is more often associated with a harsh systolic ejection murmur, decreased pulmonary vascular markings, and episodic hypercyanotic spells rather than increased pulmonary blood flow.

Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn can cause hypoxemia and cyanosis, but it usually occurs with respiratory distress and labile oxygenation without the structural murmur and chest radiograph pattern suggesting a congenital heart defect.

Coarctation of the aorta can present in neonates with poor perfusion and differential pulses, but this infant has equal femoral pulses and prominent cyanosis with increased pulmonary vascular markings, which are not typical findings.

Transposition of the great arteries also causes early cyanosis in a newborn, but it more typically produces minimal murmur and an enlarged mediastinum with decreased pulmonary vascularity unless a mixing lesion is present.

questions.teaching_point: Truncus arteriosus causes early neonatal cyanosis with a systolic murmur and increased pulmonary vascularity from overcirculation.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man comes to clinic for worsening exertional dyspnea and lightheadedness over the past 6 months. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia and takes lisinopril and atorvastatin. He denies chest pain at rest. On exam, the carotid upstroke is delayed and diminished, and a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is loudest at the right upper sternal border and radiates to the carotids. Echocardiography shows a calcified aortic valve with a mean gradient of 46 mm Hg and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction. He remains symptomatic despite optimization of blood pressure and volume status.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

answer_choices.text: Begin metoprolol to reduce exertional symptoms
Refer the patient for aortic valve replacement evaluation
Continue medical management and arrange outpatient follow-up in 6 months
Start low-dose furosemide for chronic symptom control

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, supported by exertional dyspnea and lightheadedness, a delayed carotid upstroke, a classic systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, and a mean aortic valve gradient in the severe range. In a symptomatic patient with severe aortic stenosis and preserved ejection fraction, the next step is referral for aortic valve replacement evaluation, with surgical AVR or transcatheter AVR selected based on anatomy, age, and procedural risk. Medications may provide limited symptom relief in selected patients but do not relieve the fixed outflow obstruction or change the prognosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Beta-blockers are not definitive therapy for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and may worsen exercise intolerance or hypotension in a patient with fixed outflow obstruction.
Observation with routine follow-up is appropriate for asymptomatic or nonsevere disease, not for a patient who is already symptomatic with severe aortic stenosis.
Repeat surveillance echocardiography is appropriate for monitoring asymptomatic disease, but this patient already meets criteria for valve intervention evaluation now.
Diuretics may be used cautiously if there is congestion, but they do not treat the fixed valve obstruction and can worsen preload-dependent symptoms in severe aortic stenosis.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis requires referral for valve replacement; medical therapy may palliate symptoms but does not correct the fixed obstruction.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man comes to clinic because his father was recently found to have a hereditary endocrine tumor syndrome after surgery for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Genetic testing in the family identified a RET pathogenic variant. The patient feels well and has no neck mass, palpitations, flushing, or episodic headaches. He asks what he should do now to reduce his future cancer risk. Physical examination is normal. He has never had endocrine screening.
questions.lead_in: Which preventive action is the most appropriate next step for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Test serum calcitonin only and use that result to determine whether the patient is a carrier of the familial RET pathogenic variant
Obtain serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels now and defer further evaluation unless those results are abnormal
Order plasma free metanephrines now and repeat annually, without genetic testing, to screen for pheochromocytoma
Schedule prophylactic total thyroidectomy now because all first-degree relatives of patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma should undergo thyroid removal
Refer for genetic counseling and RET testing, then perform syndrome-specific surveillance if he is found to carry the familial pathogenic variant

questions.rationale:
This patient is an asymptomatic first-degree relative of someone with a known RET pathogenic variant associated with MEN 2A. The most appropriate preventive step is genetic counseling and targeted RET testing. If he carries the familial variant, he should then undergo syndrome-specific surveillance for medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism, with management guided by the specific RET mutation and age-related recommendations. Cascade testing identifies who truly needs lifelong endocrine surveillance and helps guide family counseling.

Choice C is incorrect because screening for pheochromocytoma is important in MEN 2A, but it does not replace genetic counseling and RET testing in an at-risk relative with a known familial mutation.

Choice D is incorrect because prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated for confirmed RET mutation carriers according to mutation-specific risk and timing, not for all first-degree relatives before genetic evaluation.

Choice B is incorrect because serum calcium and parathyroid hormone testing may be part of surveillance in confirmed carriers, but isolated biochemical screening is incomplete and does not address the need for cascade genetic testing or surveillance for other MEN 2A manifestations.

Choice A is incorrect because calcitonin can help detect medullary thyroid carcinoma, but it cannot determine RET carrier status and should not be used as the sole preventive strategy.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Calcitonin may be used in medullary thyroid carcinoma surveillance, but it cannot establish whether the patient inherited the familial RET pathogenic variant and is not a substitute for genetic testing.

Calcium and parathyroid hormone testing can screen for hyperparathyroidism, but isolated biochemical screening is incomplete and does not substitute for RET testing or comprehensive MEN 2A surveillance.
Plasma free metanephrines are used to screen for pheochromocytoma, a MEN 2A manifestation, but this does not address cascade genetic testing of an at-risk relative with a known familial RET variant.

Prophylactic thyroidectomy is reserved for confirmed RET mutation carriers based on genotype-specific risk and timing; it is not the immediate next step before genetic confirmation in an asymptomatic relative.

questions.teaching_point: In a first-degree relative of a patient with MEN 2A and a known RET pathogenic variant, the key preventive step is genetic counseling with RET testing, followed by mutation-guided surveillance if positive.

questions.vignette: A 6-year-old boy is admitted with 1 day of worsening abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. His mother reports that he has not passed stool or flatus since yesterday morning. He had an appendectomy 2 years ago. On exam, he is uncomfortable and mildly dehydrated. His abdomen is distended with high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds and diffuse, crampy tenderness without rebound or guarding. His vital signs are normal, and his groin exam is unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical exam finding would be most consistent with the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Sudden severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with rigid abdomen
Pain relief after bowel movement with palpable left lower quadrant stool burden
Right lower quadrant tenderness with rebound and involuntary guarding
Painful right groin mass that increases with coughing
Visible, intermittent waves of bowel peristalsis moving across the abdomen

questions.rationale: This child’s presentation is most consistent with small bowel obstruction, likely due to postoperative adhesions after appendectomy. SBO commonly causes crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, abdominal distention, obstipation, and high-pitched bowel sounds. A classic associated physical finding is visible peristaltic waves as the intestine contracts forcefully against the obstruction.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with a rigid abdomen suggests pancreatitis or a perforated viscus, not typical small bowel obstruction.
Relief after stool passage with a palpable stool burden is more consistent with constipation than mechanical small bowel obstruction.
Right lower quadrant rebound and guarding suggest peritoneal irritation, such as appendicitis or perforation, rather than uncomplicated small bowel obstruction.
A painful groin mass that worsens with coughing suggests an inguinal hernia, which may cause obstruction but is not the classic additional physical finding described in this case.

questions.teaching_point: Small bowel obstruction classically presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, obstipation, high-pitched bowel sounds, and sometimes visible peristaltic waves.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his sister because of 5 days of worsening agitation and erratic behavior. He has slept only 2 to 3 hours per night but says he feels "great" and has been working on three business ideas at once. His sister reports he has been spending unusually large amounts of money, talking faster than usual, interrupting others, and becoming irritable when questioned. He has no fever, head trauma, or recent substance use. He has a history of depression treated with an antidepressant, which he stopped taking 2 months ago because he felt it was "slowing him down." On examination, he is distractible, speaks rapidly with frequent topic changes, and insists he does not need to be here. He denies hallucinations and suicidal thoughts.
questions.lead_in: Which additional historical feature would most strongly support bipolar I disorder rather than bipolar II disorder, cyclothymic disorder, borderline personality disorder, or substance-induced mania?

answer_choices.text: A lifelong pattern of unstable relationships, impulsivity, and fear of abandonment beginning in early adulthood
A recurrent pattern of low-grade depressed mood lasting most days for several years without clear episodes of mania or hypomania
A history of auditory hallucinations and fixed delusions that occurred for 6 weeks in the absence of mood symptoms
An episode of excessive energy and decreased sleep that developed only after starting a stimulant medication and resolved when the medication was stopped
A prior discrete episode of elevated or irritable mood with decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, and marked impairment that lasted at least 1 week

questions.rationale:
This patient is currently showing symptoms consistent with a manic episode: decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, distractibility, increased activity, grandiosity/expansiveness, irritability, and risky spending. Bipolar I disorder is defined by at least one manic episode, which is a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood and increased energy or activity lasting at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization is required) and causing marked impairment. A prior discrete episode meeting these criteria would strongly support bipolar I disorder and distinguish it from bipolar II disorder, cyclothymic disorder, borderline personality disorder, and substance-induced mood symptoms.

Choice B is incorrect because chronic low-grade depressive symptoms without discrete hypomanic or manic episodes are more consistent with persistent depressive disorder, not bipolar I disorder.
Choice A is incorrect because a pervasive pattern of unstable relationships, impulsivity, and abandonment fears is characteristic of borderline personality disorder rather than bipolar disorder.
Choice C is incorrect because psychotic symptoms occurring for a sustained period in the absence of mood symptoms suggest a schizophrenia spectrum disorder, not bipolar I disorder.
Choice D is incorrect because manic symptoms that begin only after stimulant exposure and resolve after stopping the medication suggest a substance/medication-induced bipolar and related disorder.

distractor_rationales.explanation: This pattern is characteristic of borderline personality disorder and does not indicate a manic episode.
This describes persistent low-grade depression over time without discrete manic or hypomanic episodes, which does not support bipolar I disorder.
Psychosis for a sustained period without mood symptoms suggests a schizophrenia spectrum disorder rather than bipolar disorder.
Manic symptoms that occur only after starting a stimulant and resolve after stopping it suggest a substance/medication-induced mood disorder.

questions.teaching_point: Bipolar I disorder requires at least one true manic episode: a discrete period of elevated or irritable mood with increased energy, decreased need for sleep, and impaired functioning lasting at least 1 week or requiring hospitalization.

questions.vignette: A 4-month-old boy is in a pediatric rehabilitation clinic for follow-up after prolonged hospitalization for poor weight gain and intermittent oxygen desaturation with feeding. His mother reports that he becomes increasingly fussy and turns dusky around the lips when he cries or is positioned upright for therapy, but he is usually comfortable between episodes. During the visit, he develops acute cyanosis after a period of crying; the episode improves when he is held in a knee-chest position and calmed. On exam, he is small for age, mildly tachypneic, has a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border, and has mild clubbing of the fingertips.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most consistent with this child’s underlying cardiac condition?

answer_choices.text: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound
Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border
Bounding peripheral pulses with widened pulse pressure
Continuous machinery-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area
Single second heart sound with diminished intensity

questions.rationale: This child has Tetralogy of Fallot, a cyanotic congenital heart defect that causes episodic hypoxemia (“tet spells”) often triggered by crying or exertion and improved by knee-chest positioning. The harsh systolic ejection murmur reflects right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Because pulmonic valve flow is reduced, the pulmonary component of the second heart sound is soft or absent, producing a single second heart sound with diminished intensity.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Fixed splitting of the second heart sound is characteristic of an atrial septal defect, due to persistently delayed right ventricular emptying, not Tetralogy of Fallot.

A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border suggests a ventricular septal defect or tricuspid regurgitation. Although a ventricular septal defect is part of Tetralogy of Fallot, the expected additional finding in this lesion is a soft or absent pulmonic component of S2.
Bounding peripheral pulses with widened pulse pressure suggest patent ductus arteriosus or aortic regurgitation, not the decreased pulmonary blood flow seen in Tetralogy of Fallot.
A continuous machinery-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area is typical of a patent ductus arteriosus, not Tetralogy of Fallot.

questions.teaching_point: Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanotic spells relieved by knee-chest positioning and is classically associated with a harsh systolic ejection murmur and a single second heart sound.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of easy bruising and gum bleeding for 2 weeks. She recently recovered from an upper respiratory infection and takes no prescription medications. She denies heavy menstrual bleeding, melena, hematuria, fever, weight loss, or joint pain. Examination shows scattered petechiae on the lower legs and ecchymoses on the arms. She is afebrile, and the remainder of the exam is normal. Complete blood count shows hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, white blood cell count 6,200/mcL, and platelet count 18,000/mcL. Peripheral smear shows isolated thrombocytopenia without schistocytes or blasts.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

answer_choices.text: Observation only and repeat platelet count in 1 month

questions.rationale: This patient has presumed immune thrombocytopenia (ITP): isolated thrombocytopenia, mucocutaneous bleeding, normal hemoglobin and white blood cell count, and no evidence of hemolysis or bone marrow failure. In an adult with symptomatic ITP and a platelet count well below 30,000/mcL, initial outpatient treatment is a corticosteroid such as prednisone to reduce immune-mediated platelet destruction and raise the platelet count. IV immune globulin is also used in ITP, but it is typically reserved for patients with severe bleeding, need for a rapid platelet increase, or when corticosteroids are contraindicated; prednisone is the most appropriate initial treatment here.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Rituximab can be used for persistent or refractory ITP, but it is not the usual first-line initial treatment for a newly diagnosed symptomatic adult with isolated thrombocytopenia.

IV immune globulin can rapidly raise the platelet count in ITP, but it is usually reserved for severe bleeding, urgent procedures, or patients who need a quick response. In this stable outpatient with new symptomatic ITP, corticosteroids are the preferred initial therapy.

Observation is reasonable only when thrombocytopenia is mild and bleeding is absent or minimal, typically with higher platelet counts. This patient has active mucocutaneous bleeding and a platelet count of 18,000/mcL, so treatment is indicated.

Platelet transfusion is generally reserved for life-threatening bleeding or urgent invasive procedures because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed in ITP and are not the preferred initial therapy for a stable outpatient.

questions.teaching_point: Adults with symptomatic immune thrombocytopenia and platelets <30,000/mcL are usually treated first with corticosteroids; IV immune globulin is reserved for situations requiring a rapid platelet rise, and platelet transfusion is reserved for major bleeding or urgent procedures.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic dyspnea presents to the clinic with sudden left-sided pleuritic chest pain and increased shortness of breath that began 2 hours ago while resting. He is speaking in short phrases. Temperature is 36.8 C (98.2 F), blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, pulse is 108/min, respirations are 28/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on his usual home oxygen. Exam shows diminished breath sounds and hyperresonance over the left hemithorax. Trachea is midline. He is alert but uncomfortable, and no signs of shock are present.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Administer supplemental oxygen and discharge with close outpatient follow-up
Perform needle decompression of the left chest
Start nebulized albuterol and oral prednisone
Insert a chest tube into the left pleural space
Obtain an upright chest radiograph before any intervention

questions.rationale: This patient likely has a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to underlying COPD. He is symptomatic with tachypnea, hypoxemia, and unilateral decreased breath sounds/hyperresonance, which makes observation or discharge inappropriate. In a secondary pneumothorax, especially in a clinically significant or symptomatic case, the preferred management is tube thoracostomy to evacuate air and allow lung re-expansion. He is not in extremis with hypotension or tracheal deviation, so emergent needle decompression for tension physiology is not the best next step.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Supplemental oxygen alone and outpatient follow-up would be inadequate for a symptomatic secondary pneumothorax, which carries higher risk of respiratory decompensation than a small primary pneumothorax.
Needle decompression is reserved for suspected tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic compromise or severe instability; this patient is symptomatic but does not show shock or tracheal deviation.
Bronchodilator and steroid therapy may help COPD exacerbation, but they do not treat a pneumothorax and would miss the immediate cause of his acute symptoms.

Although chest radiography can confirm the diagnosis in a stable patient, the presentation is already highly suggestive of a clinically significant secondary pneumothorax that requires urgent treatment rather than delay for additional imaging.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease generally requires chest tube drainage rather than observation.

questions.vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents to establish care for exertional fatigue and lifelong mild cyanosis. She reports that she was “born with a heart problem” and had several childhood procedures, but she has not seen a cardiologist in years. On exam, her oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, she has clubbing of the fingers, a single second heart sound, and a systolic murmur best heard along the left sternal border. There is no jugular venous distention or peripheral edema.
questions.lead_in: Which congenital heart defect is most consistent with this patient’s findings?
questions.rationale: Tricuspid atresia is the congenital absence of the tricuspid valve. Because blood cannot pass directly from the right atrium to the right ventricle, systemic venous return must cross an interatrial communication and mix with oxygenated blood, producing chronic cyanosis. Adults who survive after childhood palliation may have lifelong hypoxemia, clubbing, a systolic murmur from associated shunting or outflow obstruction, and a single S2.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A ventricular septal defect usually produces a holosystolic murmur and, if large, can lead to heart failure or pulmonary hypertension, but isolated VSD does not usually cause lifelong cyanosis and clubbing in an adult.

Ebstein anomaly can cause cyanosis and a murmur, but it is classically associated with apical displacement of the tricuspid valve, tricuspid regurgitation, and right atrial enlargement rather than the obligatory mixing physiology and single second heart sound seen here.

Atrial septal defect usually causes a fixed split S2 and a systolic ejection murmur, but it does not typically cause lifelong marked cyanosis or clubbing unless severe pulmonary hypertension leads to shunt reversal.

Tetralogy of Fallot can present with cyanosis and a systolic murmur, but it is characterized by ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy rather than absence of the tricuspid valve.

questions.teaching_point: Tricuspid atresia causes chronic cyanosis from obligatory right-to-left mixing through an atrial communication and is suggested by lifelong hypoxemia, clubbing, and a single S2.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man is admitted after 2 days of sharp central chest pain that is worse when lying flat and improved when he sits up and leans forward. He recently recovered from a viral upper respiratory illness. On exam, he is afebrile, his blood pressure is normal, and a scratchy, high-pitched sound is heard best at the left lower sternal border with the patient leaning forward during end-expiration. An ECG shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression.
questions.lead_in: Which underlying pathophysiologic process best explains this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the endocardial valves causing regurgitant lesions
Acute occlusion of a coronary artery causing transmural myocardial necrosis
Inflammation of the pericardial layers causing friction between the parietal and visceral pericardium
Pulmonary embolic obstruction of the pulmonary arterial circulation causing right heart strain
Infection of the myocardium leading to reduced contractility and arrhythmia

questions.rationale: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, which produces pleuritic, positional chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. The ECG classically shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression. The underlying process is inflammation of the pericardial layers, leading to friction between the parietal and visceral pericardium.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Autoimmune valvular disease can cause chronic regurgitant murmurs, but it does not explain the acute pleuritic chest pain, friction rub, or ECG findings seen here.
