Acute coronary artery occlusion causes myocardial infarction, which typically presents with ischemic chest pain and localized ECG changes rather than a pericardial rub and diffuse ST elevation.
Pulmonary embolism can cause acute dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and right heart strain, but it does not typically cause a pericardial friction rub or diffuse ST-segment elevation.

Myocarditis involves inflammation of the myocardium and can cause heart failure or arrhythmias, but it does not classically produce a pericardial friction rub with positional pain and diffuse PR depression.

questions.teaching_point: Acute pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium and is classically associated with positional chest pain, a friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man with no known lung disease is in the post-anesthesia care unit 30 minutes after laparoscopic appendectomy. He reports sudden right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath that began while he was recovering from extubation. He is anxious and tachypneic. Blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg, heart rate is 108/min, respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 92% on 2 L/min nasal cannula. On exam, the right hemithorax has decreased chest expansion and diminished breath sounds compared with the left, with hyperresonance to percussion. The trachea is midline, and there is no jugular venous distention. His surgery was uncomplicated, and he has no fever, wheezing, or productive cough.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's postoperative symptoms and exam findings?
questions.rationale: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax best fits the abrupt onset of unilateral pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea with decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on the affected side in a young adult without known underlying lung disease. The perioperative context can precipitate an air leak, and the lack of hypotension, tracheal deviation, or jugular venous distention argues against tension physiology.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Aspiration pneumonitis may follow anesthesia and cause hypoxemia and respiratory symptoms, but it more often produces cough, wheeze, crackles, or infiltrates rather than unilateral hyperresonance with absent breath sounds.
Atelectasis is common after surgery and can cause hypoxemia and decreased breath sounds, but it usually presents more gradually and does not cause hyperresonance or sudden pleuritic chest pain.
Tension pneumothorax would be more likely to cause hemodynamic instability, tracheal deviation, and jugular venous distention; this patient is stable and has a midline trachea.
Pulmonary embolism can cause postoperative dyspnea and tachycardia, but it does not typically produce unilateral hyperresonance and markedly decreased breath sounds on one side.

questions.teaching_point: Sudden postoperative unilateral pleuritic pain with decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance strongly suggests pneumothorax; tension physiology is suggested by instability and mediastinal shift.

questions.vignette: A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction returns for follow-up. His current medications include metformin, lisinopril, and furosemide. He checks fasting glucose most mornings; recent readings are 160-190 mg/dL. His A1c is 8.4%. He reports mild urinary frequency but no dysuria, dizziness, or weight loss. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg, heart rate is 72/min, and BMI is 29 kg/m2. Serum creatinine and potassium are stable compared with prior values. He has had no hypoglycemic episodes and prefers to avoid injections.
questions.lead_in: Which change in diabetes management is most appropriate at this time?

answer_choices.text: Increase metformin to the maximum dose
Stop metformin and switch to acarbose

questions.rationale: An SGLT2 inhibitor is the best addition because this older adult has type 2 diabetes with suboptimal glycemic control plus chronic kidney disease and heart failure, both of which are conditions for which SGLT2 inhibitors provide important cardiorenal benefit. His renal function is stable, he is not having symptomatic hyperglycemia, and he prefers to avoid injections, making an oral agent with low hypoglycemia risk especially appropriate. Mild urinary frequency is a relevant adverse effect to discuss, but it is not a contraindication in this context.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Increasing metformin may modestly improve A1c, but he is already on metformin and has CKD, so further dose escalation may be limited by renal function and would not provide the added heart failure and kidney benefit of an SGLT2 inhibitor.

Acarbose is not an optimal switch for this patient because it is less effective for A1c reduction, often causes gastrointestinal adverse effects, and does not offer the same cardiorenal benefits as an SGLT2 inhibitor. Stopping metformin is unnecessary given stable renal function.

Basal insulin can lower A1c, but it is not the preferred next step here because he is not severely symptomatic, has no catabolic features, and wants to avoid injections. It also increases hypoglycemia risk in a geriatric patient.
Glyburide is a poor choice in an older adult because sulfonylureas increase the risk of prolonged hypoglycemia, especially in patients with chronic kidney disease. Safer alternatives are preferred.

questions.teaching_point: In older adults with type 2 diabetes plus heart failure or CKD, an SGLT2 inhibitor is often the preferred next medication because it improves cardiorenal outcomes with low hypoglycemia risk.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man comes to clinic after an abdominal ultrasound obtained for vague flank discomfort showed a 5.2-cm solid mass in the upper pole of the left kidney. He has no fever, dysuria, or weight loss. His blood pressure is 148/92 mm Hg, and serum creatinine is normal. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirms an enhancing renal mass confined to the kidney without renal vein invasion or distant disease. He is otherwise healthy and takes no anticoagulants. He asks what the next step in treatment should be.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Begin active surveillance with repeat imaging in 6 months
Perform percutaneous renal mass biopsy before any treatment
Treat with external beam radiation therapy

questions.rationale: An enhancing 5.2-cm renal mass confined to the kidney is most consistent with localized renal cell carcinoma. In an otherwise healthy adult, nephron-sparing surgery is preferred when technically feasible for localized tumors, including many tumors up to 7 cm, because it provides definitive treatment while preserving renal function. Partial nephrectomy is therefore the best next step.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Active surveillance is generally reserved for very small renal masses, patients with limited life expectancy, or those who are poor surgical candidates. A healthy patient with a 5.2-cm enhancing mass should undergo definitive treatment.

Percutaneous biopsy can be considered when the diagnosis is uncertain or when pathology would change management, but an enhancing solid renal mass in a surgical candidate is typically treated definitively without requiring biopsy first.
External beam radiation therapy is not standard primary treatment for localized renal cell carcinoma and is not the preferred definitive therapy when the lesion is resectable.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are used for selected cases of advanced or metastatic renal cell carcinoma, not for a localized kidney-confined mass amenable to surgery.

questions.teaching_point: Localized renal cell carcinoma in a surgical candidate is treated with nephron-sparing surgery when feasible, especially for tumors confined to the kidney.

questions.vignette: A 78-year-old man presents to a clinic with 1 day of crampy, intermittent abdominal pain and progressive abdominal distention. He has had nausea and has not passed flatus since yesterday. He had an open colectomy several years ago. On examination, his abdomen is tympanitic with diffuse mild tenderness without guarding. He is afebrile and his blood pressure and heart rate are normal.
questions.lead_in: Which physical examination finding is most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Murphy sign in the right upper quadrant
Absent bowel sounds with rigid abdomen

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has a small bowel obstruction, which classically presents with crampy intermittent abdominal pain, progressive distention, nausea/vomiting, obstipation, and early high-pitched, hyperactive, or "tinkling" bowel sounds due to increased peristalsis against an obstruction. Prior abdominal surgery is a common risk factor because postoperative adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A Murphy sign suggests acute cholecystitis, which typically causes right upper quadrant pain and tenderness rather than obstipation and progressive abdominal distention.
Costovertebral angle tenderness is more consistent with renal pathology such as pyelonephritis or nephrolithiasis, not bowel obstruction.
Absent bowel sounds with a rigid abdomen suggests peritonitis or advanced bowel compromise, not the usual early finding in uncomplicated small bowel obstruction.
Left lower quadrant rebound tenderness suggests localized peritoneal irritation such as diverticulitis, not the diffuse obstructive pattern seen in small bowel obstruction.

questions.teaching_point: Early small bowel obstruction commonly presents with intermittent crampy abdominal pain, distention, obstipation, and high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds, especially in patients with prior abdominal surgery.

questions.vignette: A 46-year-old woman comes to clinic with 2 days of pleuritic right-sided chest discomfort and mild shortness of breath that began while she was recovering from a 6-hour car ride. She has a history of uterine fibroids and started an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive 3 weeks ago. Vital signs show temperature 36.8 C (98.2 F), heart rate 104/min, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Lung examination is clear. There is mild tenderness and swelling of the left calf without erythema. She has no wheezing, fever, or reproducible chest wall tenderness.
questions.lead_in: Which pathophysiologic mechanism best explains the most likely cause of her symptoms?

answer_choices.text: Thrombus formation in the deep veins with embolization to the pulmonary arterial circulation
Inflammation and spasm of the bronchi causing transient airflow obstruction
Rupture of an apical bleb causing collapse of the affected lung
Inflammation of the pleural lining causing sharp pain with breathing
Obstruction of a coronary artery causing myocardial ischemia

questions.rationale: This patient has a pulmonary embolism. Her pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, recent prolonged immobility, estrogen use, and unilateral calf swelling are most consistent with venous thromboembolism originating in the deep veins of the leg. The key pathophysiologic mechanism is formation of a thrombus in the deep venous system with embolization to the pulmonary arterial circulation, which produces acute ventilation-perfusion mismatch and pleuritic symptoms.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Bronchospasm describes asthma or reactive airway disease, which typically causes wheezing and episodic airflow obstruction rather than calf swelling and thromboembolic risk factors.

A ruptured apical bleb causes spontaneous pneumothorax, which typically presents with sudden unilateral pleuritic pain and decreased breath sounds, not signs of deep venous thrombosis or estrogen-related thromboembolic risk.
Pleuritis can cause sharp pain with breathing, but isolated pleural inflammation does not explain the unilateral calf swelling or the major risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
Coronary artery obstruction causes acute coronary syndrome, which usually presents with pressure-like chest pain rather than pleuritic pain and does not explain the calf findings.

questions.teaching_point: Pulmonary embolism is usually caused by a deep venous thrombus that embolizes to the pulmonary arteries, especially in patients with recent immobility and estrogen exposure.

questions.vignette: A 3-year-old boy is admitted for poor oral intake and dehydration after 2 days of fever, drooling, and irritability. His parents report that he has been refusing solid foods and cries when he tries to drink. He attends day care, where several children recently had a febrile illness. On examination, he has a temperature of 38.4°C, multiple shallow gray ulcers on the soft palate and buccal mucosa, and a scattered vesicular rash on the palms, soles, and buttocks. He is alert, has no neck stiffness, and his lungs are clear.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is most likely because this child has a typical combination of fever, painful oral ulcers causing decreased intake, and a vesicular rash involving the palms and soles, with exposure to other ill children in day care. The buttock involvement also supports this enteroviral exanthem.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Impetigo causes superficial bacterial skin infection with honey-colored crusts, not oral ulcers and a palm/sole vesicular eruption.
Herpangina can cause fever and posterior oropharyngeal ulcers, but it does not typically produce the characteristic vesicular rash on the palms and soles.

Kawasaki disease can present with fever and mucous membrane changes, but it is a vasculitis with conjunctivitis, extremity edema or erythema, and a polymorphous rash rather than discrete oral ulcers with palm and sole vesicles.
Varicella usually causes a generalized pruritic vesicular rash in different stages of healing, rather than a distribution centered on the hands, feet, and mouth.

questions.teaching_point: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease classically causes fever, painful oral ulcers, and vesicular lesions on the hands, feet, and sometimes buttocks in young children.

questions.vignette: A 3-month-old infant is brought to clinic because of poor weight gain and increasing fatigue during feeds. The parents report that the baby becomes sweaty and breathless after a few minutes of feeding and has looked "bluish" around the lips since birth, especially when crying. Pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated. On examination, the infant has central cyanosis, a systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border, and a single second heart sound. The oxygen saturation is 82% on room air. The chest is not markedly distressed, and pulses are equal in all extremities.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.rationale: Tricuspid atresia is a cyanotic congenital heart defect caused by absence of the tricuspid valve, leading to obligatory right-to-left shunting through an atrial septal defect and often a ventricular septal defect/patent ductus arteriosus for pulmonary blood flow. Infants commonly present with early cyanosis, poor feeding, diaphoresis with exertion, failure to thrive, a systolic murmur, and a single second heart sound.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A patent ductus arteriosus more often causes a continuous machinery murmur and, when significant, findings of left-to-right shunting and heart failure rather than persistent cyanosis from birth. It does not explain the single second heart sound and chronic desaturation as well as tricuspid atresia.

Tetralogy of Fallot can cause cyanosis and a systolic murmur, but the classic harsh systolic ejection murmur and episodic hypercyanotic spells are not the best fit here. The single second heart sound and progressive cyanosis since birth are more suggestive of tricuspid atresia.

A ventricular septal defect usually causes a holosystolic murmur and signs of pulmonary overcirculation rather than central cyanosis in a young infant. Cyanosis and a single second heart sound point to a more complex cyanotic lesion.

Transposition of the great arteries typically presents with profound neonatal cyanosis soon after birth and may have minimal murmur unless there is an associated defect. This infant’s presentation is more consistent with a mixing lesion that produces chronic cyanosis and a single S2.

questions.teaching_point: Tricuspid atresia classically presents in infancy with cyanosis, poor feeding, failure to thrive, a systolic murmur, and a single second heart sound due to absent right ventricular inflow and obligatory interatrial shunting.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man is evaluated for 2 days of sharp anterior chest pain that is worse when he lies flat and improves when he leans forward. He had a low-grade fever and a viral upper respiratory infection last week. He has no exertional component to the pain, and his troponin level is normal. On examination, his blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal. Cardiac auscultation reveals a scratchy, high-pitched sound that is heard best at the left lower sternal border when the patient sits upright and leans forward. There is no radiation of pain to the arm or jaw.
questions.lead_in: Which underlying pathophysiologic mechanism best explains this patient’s chest pain and physical examination finding?

answer_choices.text: Inflammation of the myocardium causing impaired ventricular contractility
Obstruction of a coronary artery causing transmural myocardial ischemia
Inflammation of the pericardial layers causing friction between the parietal and visceral pericardium
Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with distal coronary embolization
Inflammation of the pleura causing pleural friction during breathing

questions.rationale: This patient has acute pericarditis, suggested by pleuritic, positional chest pain after a recent viral illness and a pericardial friction rub. The pain and the scratchy auscultatory sound are caused by inflammation of the pericardium, which makes the parietal and visceral pericardial layers rub against each other during cardiac motion. The normal troponin level and the absence of exertional ischemic symptoms also argue against myocardial ischemia or myocarditis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Myocarditis involves inflammation of the myocardium and may follow a viral illness, but it more often causes elevated troponin, arrhythmias, or heart failure symptoms rather than a pericardial friction rub.

Coronary artery obstruction causes acute myocardial infarction, which typically produces pressure-like chest pain, may radiate to the arm or jaw, and is often associated with troponin elevation rather than a positional pain syndrome with a friction rub.

Plaque rupture with distal coronary embolization is a mechanism of acute coronary syndrome, which presents with ischemic chest pain and biomarker or ECG changes rather than pleuritic positional pain and a pericardial rub.

Pleuritis can cause sharp pleuritic chest pain that worsens with breathing, but it does not produce a pericardial friction rub heard best at the left lower sternal border or the classic positional improvement seen with pericarditis.

questions.teaching_point: Acute pericarditis causes pleuritic, positional chest pain and a pericardial friction rub due to inflamed pericardial layers rubbing together.

questions.vignette: An 82-year-old man is admitted after slipping on ice and sustaining a deep laceration to his lower leg while gardening. The wound was contaminated with soil and required irrigation and repair. He is recovering on the surgical floor. His daughter is unsure when he last received a tetanus-containing vaccine, and there is no immunization record available in the chart. He has no history of severe vaccine reactions.
questions.lead_in: Which prophylactic intervention is most appropriate now to reduce this patient’s risk of tetanus?

answer_choices.text: No tetanus prophylaxis is needed if the wound has been irrigated
Administer both tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine and tetanus immune globulin
Obtain a tetanus antibody titer before deciding on prophylaxis

questions.rationale: This patient has a contaminated wound and an unknown tetanus immunization history. In that setting, he should receive both a tetanus toxoid–containing vaccine and tetanus immune globulin for immediate and long-term protection.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Wound irrigation is important, but contaminated wounds with unknown vaccination status still require tetanus prophylaxis.
Immune globulin alone provides temporary passive protection but does not establish active immunity for future protection.
Vaccine alone is insufficient for a contaminated wound when the immunization history is unknown because it does not provide immediate passive immunity.
Antibody titers are not used to guide urgent postexposure tetanus prophylaxis in this setting.

questions.teaching_point: Contaminated wounds with unknown or incomplete tetanus immunization history require both tetanus toxoid vaccine and tetanus immune globulin.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: An 81-year-old man is admitted for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. He has a history of type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and recent inhaled corticosteroid use. On hospital day 4, he reports a painful burning sensation in his mouth and difficulty swallowing pills. He has been eating poorly since admission. Examination shows several adherent, creamy white plaques on his tongue and buccal mucosa; when one plaque is gently scraped, a red, irritated base is seen. He is afebrile and his neck exam is unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this patient’s oral findings?
questions.rationale: This patient most likely has oral candidiasis (thrush). He has several strong risk factors, including advanced age, hospitalization, diabetes, poor oral intake, and recent inhaled corticosteroid exposure. The key exam finding is removable white plaques with an erythematous base after scraping, which is characteristic of Candida infection of the oral mucosa.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Oral lichen planus usually produces bilateral, lacy white reticular lines or erosive mucosal lesions, not easily scraped-off plaques with an erythematous base.
Aphthous ulcer disease causes discrete, painful shallow ulcers with a yellow-gray base and erythematous halo, not diffuse adherent white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa.
Leukoplakia causes a persistent white oral plaque that cannot be scraped off and is more concerning for premalignant change, rather than the removable plaques described here.
Herpetic gingivostomatitis typically presents with painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on the oral mucosa and gingiva, often with systemic symptoms, rather than removable white plaques.

questions.teaching_point: In older hospitalized patients, removable white oral plaques with an erythematous base strongly suggest oral candidiasis, especially with diabetes or corticosteroid exposure.

questions.vignette: A 47-year-old man is admitted for evaluation of worsening headaches and exertional dyspnea. Over the past 3 years, he has needed larger shoe and ring sizes and says his wife noticed his face looks different. He snores loudly, has new daytime somnolence, and reports intermittent numbness in both hands. Vital signs are stable. Examination shows coarse facial features, frontal bossing, prognathism, widened spacing between teeth, enlarged hands with thickened soft tissue, and a blood pressure of 156/94 mm Hg. Cardiac exam reveals a forceful apical impulse and a soft systolic murmur. Which additional physical finding would be most consistent with this patient’s condition?
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding would be most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Brown hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa and palmar creases
Thin extremities with proximal muscle weakness and violaceous abdominal striae
Exophthalmos with lid lag and pretibial myxedema
Bitemporal visual field loss with decreased libido and sparse facial hair

questions.rationale: This patient has acromegaly due to excess growth hormone, usually from a pituitary somatotroph adenoma. The condition causes progressive enlargement of the hands, feet, and facial bones, along with coarse facial features, prognathism, widened tooth spacing, headache, carpal tunnel symptoms, sleep apnea, hypertension, and cardiomyopathy. Macroglossia and oily skin are classic associated findings. Enlarged tongue with oily skin is therefore the best additional finding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa and palmar creases suggests primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), which does not explain progressive acral enlargement and coarse facial features.
Thin extremities, proximal muscle weakness, and violaceous striae are more consistent with Cushing syndrome from cortisol excess, not acromegaly.
Exophthalmos, lid lag, and pretibial myxedema are classic findings of Graves disease, an autoimmune hyperthyroid disorder rather than acromegaly.

Bitemporal visual field loss can occur from pituitary tumors, and decreased libido with sparse facial hair suggests hypogonadism, but these findings do not specifically identify acromegaly as well as macroglossia and oily skin do.

questions.teaching_point: Acromegaly causes progressive enlargement of acral and facial features; common associated findings include macroglossia, oily skin, headaches, sleep apnea, and signs of pituitary mass effect or cardiomyopathy.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of progressively worsening hoarseness and a feeling of fullness in the front of her neck for 3 months. She reports mild trouble swallowing solid foods and says her shirt collars have become tighter. She has no fever, sore throat, or recent upper respiratory infection. She has a 2-cm firm, fixed nodule in the right thyroid region and several hard cervical lymph nodes. Laryngoscopy shows unilateral vocal cord paralysis. Thyroid function tests are normal. She does not smoke and has no history of radiation exposure.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.rationale: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is most likely. This patient has a firm thyroid nodule with hard cervical lymph nodes and hoarseness from unilateral vocal cord paralysis, which suggests an invasive thyroid malignancy with regional lymph node involvement and recurrent laryngeal nerve impairment. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer and classically spreads to cervical lymph nodes. It can present with a painless thyroid nodule and compressive symptoms when locally advanced.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma usually presents in older adults as a rapidly enlarging, very aggressive neck mass with severe compressive symptoms and a much more fulminant course than described here.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma can present as a thyroid nodule and may metastasize to cervical lymph nodes, but it is more strongly associated with MEN2, diarrhea, and flushing. Those associated findings are absent here, making papillary thyroid carcinoma more likely.

Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis typically causes a tender thyroid after a viral prodrome and often transient hyperthyroid symptoms, not a fixed nodule with hard lymph nodes and vocal cord paralysis.

Follicular carcinoma typically spreads hematogenously to bone or lung rather than to cervical lymph nodes. It is less likely to cause hard cervical lymphadenopathy and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy at presentation.

questions.teaching_point: Papillary thyroid carcinoma commonly presents as a firm thyroid nodule with cervical lymph node metastasis and hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.

questions.vignette: A 32-year-old woman presents to clinic for worsening migraine headaches. She reports unilateral throbbing headaches 6 to 8 days per month for the past year, often with photophobia and nausea. She has tried ibuprofen at the onset of attacks with only partial relief. Her history includes a remote deep vein thrombosis while taking an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive, and she now uses a progestin-only implant. Blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Neurologic examination is normal. She asks for a medication to take at the start of an attack because she wants something stronger than ibuprofen.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate acute migraine therapy for this patient?
questions.rationale:
Sumatriptan is the most appropriate acute therapy for this patient. She has recurrent migraine attacks with inadequate relief from ibuprofen, and she has no clear contraindication to triptan use such as coronary artery disease, prior stroke or TIA, uncontrolled hypertension, or migraine with brainstem aura. A remote estrogen-associated deep vein thrombosis is a venous thromboembolic event and is not, by itself, the same contraindication as an arterial ischemic disorder. Triptans are standard first-line migraine-specific abortive therapy for outpatient treatment when NSAIDs are insufficient.

Metoclopramide can be helpful for acute migraine, especially when nausea is prominent, but it is usually an adjunct or alternative when triptans cannot be used. Ergotamine-caffeine is also used for acute migraine but has more adverse effects and vasoconstrictive risk than triptans. Butalbital-acetaminophen-caffeine is not preferred because of medication-overuse headache and dependence risk. Topiramate is used for migraine prevention, not for aborting an attack.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Metoclopramide may relieve migraine symptoms and is particularly useful when nausea is prominent, but it is not the preferred first-line migraine-specific abortive therapy for this outpatient scenario.
Ergotamine-caffeine can treat acute migraine, but it is less favored than triptans because of more adverse effects and vasoconstrictive toxicity. It is not the best initial acute option here.
Topiramate is a preventive medication used to reduce migraine frequency over time. It does not provide acute relief at the start of a headache attack.
Butalbital-acetaminophen-caffeine is discouraged for migraine because it is less effective than migraine-specific agents and increases the risk of medication-overuse headache and dependence.

questions.teaching_point: For outpatient acute migraine treatment after NSAID failure, a triptan is generally first-line unless the patient has a true arterial vascular contraindication or other triptan-specific restriction.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old woman is seen for follow-up after an incidental finding of mild hypercalcemia on routine chemistry panel. She reports fatigue, constipation, and intermittent “bone aches,” but denies kidney stones, abdominal pain, confusion, or dehydration. Repeat testing over the last 3 months shows serum calcium persistently 10.9–11.2 mg/dL with an inappropriately elevated intact parathyroid hormone level. Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D level is normal, and her creatinine clearance is preserved. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry shows a T-score of -2.7 at the femoral neck. She asks what the best next step is to reduce her risk of future complications.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism with an indication for definitive treatment. Even though her hypercalcemia is mild, she has osteoporosis on DEXA (T-score ≤ -2.5), which is a guideline-supported indication for parathyroidectomy in otherwise appropriate surgical candidates. Surgery is the only curative treatment and reduces the risk of ongoing bone loss and other complications.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cinacalcet can lower calcium in primary hyperparathyroidism, but it is generally used when surgery is not feasible or as a bridge; it does not address the underlying disease as definitively as parathyroidectomy, and it is not the best first choice in a surgical candidate with osteoporosis.
Loop diuretics are not used chronically to manage stable outpatient primary hyperparathyroidism; they can increase calciuresis only in specific acute settings and do not provide definitive treatment.

Observation is reasonable only for truly asymptomatic patients without surgical criteria. This patient has skeletal involvement with osteoporosis and therefore meets criteria for operative management rather than simple surveillance.

High-dose calcium supplementation would worsen the hypercalcemia and is not appropriate management for primary hyperparathyroidism unless treating a separate, proven deficiency under close supervision.

questions.teaching_point: Primary hyperparathyroidism is treated definitively with parathyroidectomy when patients have symptoms or complications such as osteoporosis, nephrolithiasis, reduced kidney function, or significant hypercalcemia.

questions.vignette: A 26-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of migratory joint pain and swelling. Two weeks ago, he had a febrile sore throat that resolved without antibiotics. He now reports low-grade fevers, fatigue, and painful swelling of his left knee that improved and was followed by pain in his right ankle. On examination, he has a new blowing holosystolic murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla, a nonpruritic serpiginous erythematous rash over his trunk and proximal extremities, and small, tender subcutaneous nodules over the extensor surfaces of both forearms. ECG shows a prolonged PR interval. CBC shows a mild leukocytosis, and inflammatory markers are elevated.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
questions.rationale: This patient has acute rheumatic fever, a post–group A streptococcal inflammatory syndrome. The key features are recent untreated pharyngitis followed by migratory large-joint arthritis, carditis manifested by a new mitral regurgitation murmur, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, and first-degree atrioventricular block (prolonged PR interval). Multiple Jones criteria after streptococcal infection make acute rheumatic fever the best diagnosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Disseminated gonococcal infection may cause migratory arthralgias, but it is not associated with the classic delayed sequelae of streptococcal pharyngitis, carditis, erythema marginatum, or subcutaneous nodules.

Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause inflammatory arthritis and cardiac manifestations, but the recent untreated streptococcal pharyngitis and the specific constellation of Jones criteria point to acute rheumatic fever instead.

Poststreptococcal reactive arthritis can occur after streptococcal infection and cause arthritis, but it usually does not produce the full Jones-criteria pattern of carditis, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, and PR prolongation.

Infective endocarditis can cause fever and a new murmur, but it does not explain the classic post-pharyngitis timing, migratory arthritis, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules, and prolonged PR interval as well as acute rheumatic fever does.

questions.teaching_point: Acute rheumatic fever is diagnosed clinically using Jones criteria after group A streptococcal pharyngitis; migratory polyarthritis plus carditis and characteristic skin or conduction findings are highly suggestive.

questions.vignette: A 7-month-old boy is brought to clinic for intermittent episodes of becoming abruptly blue and irritable, usually when crying or feeding. His parents report that he squats down during play less often than before and seems to get tired with exertion compared with other children. Pregnancy and newborn course were unremarkable, but a cardiac murmur was noted shortly after birth. On exam, he has a harsh systolic murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border and a mildly enlarged right ventricular impulse. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Between episodes, he appears comfortable but remains mildly cyanotic around the lips.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding is most likely in this child?

answer_choices.text: Harsh holosystolic murmur at the apex with radiation to the axilla
Delayed femoral pulses compared with radial pulses and upper-extremity hypertension
Bounding peripheral pulses with a continuous machinery-like murmur at the left infraclavicular area
Loud, fixed split second heart sound with a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border
Single second heart sound with a systolic ejection murmur that increases when he squats

questions.rationale: This child has tetralogy of Fallot, suggested by episodic cyanosis with crying/feeding, chronic hypoxemia, a murmur at the left upper sternal border from right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and the tendency to squat. Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance, which decreases right-to-left shunting and can improve oxygenation. A single second heart sound from a diminished pulmonic component is a classic associated physical finding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla is typical of mitral regurgitation and is not the expected auscultatory finding in tetralogy of Fallot.
Delayed femoral pulses with upper-extremity hypertension point to coarctation of the aorta, a different congenital lesion with another exam pattern.
Bounding pulses with a continuous machinery murmur suggest patent ductus arteriosus, which does not explain the episodic cyanosis and squatting described here.
A loud, fixed split S2 with a systolic ejection murmur is most characteristic of atrial septal defect, not tetralogy of Fallot.

questions.teaching_point: Tetralogy of Fallot causes cyanotic spells and classically features a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, a single S2, and improvement with squatting due to increased systemic vascular resistance.

questions.vignette: A 13-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation after her school nurse noticed that one shoulder appears higher than the other. Her parents report no back pain, weakness, or gait problems. She had menarche 8 months ago and has otherwise been healthy. On examination, she stands with the right shoulder and right scapula slightly elevated. When asked to bend forward at the waist with her arms hanging, there is a subtle prominence of the right thoracic rib cage. Neurologic examination is normal, and her leg lengths are equal.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding is most consistent with the suspected condition?

answer_choices.text: Hyperreflexia with clonus and a positive Babinski sign
Severe midline spinal tenderness with fever and refusal to move the back
Fixed limitation of hip abduction with asymmetric knee height
A right thoracic rib hump that becomes more apparent on forward flexion
Lumbar spine tenderness with pain reproduced on straight-leg raise

questions.rationale: This adolescent has findings consistent with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, which is often first noticed as shoulder or scapular asymmetry. On forward flexion, vertebral rotation produces a thoracic rib hump on the convex side of the curve, making this the most characteristic additional physical finding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Upper motor neuron signs such as hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski indicate possible spinal cord involvement or neurologic disease, which would prompt evaluation for secondary causes of curvature rather than a typical idiopathic scoliosis finding.
Midline spinal tenderness with fever and reluctance to move the back is more concerning for spinal infection or another acute inflammatory process, not uncomplicated adolescent scoliosis.

Fixed hip abduction limitation with asymmetric knee height points to pelvic obliquity or hip pathology/leg-length discrepancy, which can mimic scoliosis but is not the classic finding of structural scoliosis.
Lumbar tenderness and a positive straight-leg raise suggest a radicular process such as lumbar strain or disk herniation, not scoliosis.

questions.teaching_point: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis commonly presents with shoulder or scapular asymmetry and a rib hump that is most visible on forward bend testing.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the clinic for follow-up. He takes metformin, glipizide, and basal insulin at bedtime. Over the past month, he has had three early-morning episodes of sweating, tremor, and confusion that improve after he drinks orange juice. His wife reports one episode in which he was difficult to awaken. He checks his glucose only when symptomatic; readings during episodes have been 48 to 62 mg/dL. His HbA1c is 6.4%. He reports he often skips dinner because of a poor appetite and has recently lost 8 lb. Vital signs are normal, and the rest of the exam is unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Decrease the glipizide dose and review hypoglycemia recognition and treatment
Add a bedtime snack without changing the diabetes medications
Increase the bedtime basal insulin dose to improve fasting control
Stop metformin and start a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor
Continue the current regimen because the HbA1c is at goal

questions.rationale: This patient has recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia, likely driven by a sulfonylurea plus basal insulin in the setting of reduced oral intake and weight loss. In outpatient management, the priority is to reduce the hypoglycemia risk by deintensifying therapy most likely to cause low glucose, especially the sulfonylurea, and to counsel him on recognition and treatment of hypoglycemia. His HbA1c is already low enough that continuing the same regimen would be unsafe.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A bedtime snack may help if hypoglycemia is due to missed meals alone, but it does not address medication-related hypoglycemia from glipizide and insulin, especially with repeated episodes.
Increasing basal insulin would worsen fasting and nocturnal hypoglycemia in a patient already having recurrent low glucose episodes.

Metformin is not the likely cause of hypoglycemia, and switching to a DPP-4 inhibitor alone does not directly address the more likely drivers of his recurrent low glucose and would be a less appropriate first adjustment than deintensifying glipizide.
Although the HbA1c is below 7%, recurrent symptomatic hypoglycemia makes the current regimen inappropriate; safety takes priority over maintaining a tight A1c.

questions.teaching_point: Recurrent outpatient hypoglycemia should prompt deintensification of hypoglycemia-causing therapy, especially sulfonylureas and insulin, rather than pursuing tighter glycemic control.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man comes to an urgent care clinic 18 hours after cutting his left hand on a rusty metal fence while working in his yard. He washed the wound at home but did not seek care until the next day because of increasing soreness. He has a 3-cm superficial laceration on the palm with mild contamination from dirt, but no foreign body is seen and there is no tendon, nerve, or vascular injury. He reports that his last tetanus-containing vaccine was more than 10 years ago. He does not remember completing the childhood series.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive management today?

answer_choices.text: Administer tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis vaccine and tetanus immune globulin
Administer tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis vaccine now and repeat in 6 months
Clean and dress the wound without tetanus prophylaxis
Administer tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis vaccine only

questions.rationale: This patient has a contaminated wound and an unknown/incomplete tetanus immunization history. For a dirty or major wound, tetanus prophylaxis includes both tetanus vaccination and tetanus immune globulin when the primary series is unknown or incomplete, because passive immunity is needed for immediate protection and the vaccine starts active immunity for future protection.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A second dose in 6 months is not the appropriate acute prophylaxis strategy. He needs immediate wound management with vaccination now, and tetanus immune globulin because his immunization history is incomplete/unknown.
Wound cleansing is important, but it does not replace indicated tetanus prophylaxis in a patient with a contaminated wound and unknown/incomplete immunization history.
Vaccination alone is insufficient for a contaminated wound when the tetanus primary series is unknown or incomplete, because protection from the vaccine is not immediate.
Tetanus immune globulin alone provides temporary passive protection but does not establish active immunity; this patient also needs tetanus vaccination.

questions.teaching_point: For dirty wounds, give tetanus vaccine plus tetanus immune globulin when the patient’s tetanus immunization is unknown or incomplete.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man is brought to the inpatient psychiatric unit by his family after 4 days of markedly increased energy, decreased need for sleep, and irritability. He has been pacing the halls, speaking rapidly, and interrupting staff. He says he has started three business ventures, spent most of his savings on equipment, and can “finally see how everything connects.” His chart shows two prior admissions for depression, and his sister reports that over the past month he stopped taking all medications because he felt they were “slowing him down.” On exam, he is alert but distractible, has pressured speech, flight of ideas, grandiose thinking, and limited insight. He has not slept more than 2 hours per night since admission and has become verbally threatening toward other patients.
questions.lead_in: Which additional history or physical finding would most strongly support the diagnosis of bipolar I disorder in this patient?

answer_choices.text: A prior episode of at least 1 week of elevated or irritable mood with increased activity and marked impairment
Chronic low mood most days for at least 2 years with no symptom-free intervals longer than 2 months
Auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions that occur only during times of depressed mood
A history of intermittent panic attacks triggered by crowded places and leaving home
Persistent social communication difficulties and restricted interests beginning in early childhood

questions.rationale: Bipolar I disorder is defined by at least one manic episode, which is a distinct period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood and increased energy/activity lasting at least 1 week, or any duration if hospitalization is required, and causing marked functional impairment. In this patient, the current presentation is strongly consistent with mania; a prior similar episode would best support bipolar I disorder rather than another mood or psychotic disorder.

distractor_rationales.explanation: This describes persistent depressive disorder, which involves chronic depressed mood rather than episodic mania.
Psychotic symptoms limited to depressive episodes suggest major depressive disorder with psychotic features, not bipolar I disorder unless there is also a history of mania.
This describes panic disorder/agoraphobia, which can cause anxiety and avoidance but does not establish a manic episode.
This describes autism spectrum disorder, a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by lifelong social-communication deficits and restricted behaviors rather than episodic mood elevation.

questions.teaching_point: Bipolar I disorder requires at least one manic episode; collateral history of a prior week or more of elevated/irritable mood with increased energy and impairment is highly supportive.

questions.vignette: A 24-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic for recurrent sore throat and dental sensitivity. She reports episodes over the past year in which she eats large amounts of food in secret, feels out of control during the episodes, and then induces vomiting several times per week because of intense fear of weight gain. Her BMI is 23 kg/m2. She denies laxative use, diuretic use, or self-harm. On exam, she has mild parotid enlargement and erosions on the lingual surfaces of her teeth. Her vital signs are stable.
questions.lead_in: Which laboratory abnormality is most likely to be present in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Elevated serum calcium with low phosphate

questions.rationale: This patient’s recurrent binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting is consistent with bulimia nervosa. Repeated emesis causes loss of gastric acid and volume depletion, leading to metabolic alkalosis. Renal compensation and secondary hyperaldosteronism promote urinary potassium wasting, so hypokalemia is a common associated laboratory abnormality.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis is more consistent with renal failure, hypoaldosteronism, or certain toxin exposures, not purging by vomiting.
Elevated calcium with low phosphate is not expected in bulimia nervosa; this pattern suggests other endocrine or metabolic disorders.
Vomiting can contribute to hyponatremia in some cases, but the characteristic acid-base pattern is metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia rather than hyponatremic alkalosis.
Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis is more typical of diarrhea or renal tubular acidosis, not recurrent vomiting.

questions.teaching_point: Self-induced vomiting in bulimia nervosa classically causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis due to gastric acid loss and renal potassium wasting.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old woman is admitted 1 day after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma. She is alert and reports mild neck discomfort. Her vital signs are stable, and the surgical dressing is clean and dry. On exam, the incision is intact without expanding hematoma, but she says her hands feel "tight" and she has tingling around her mouth. A nurse reports the patient has been increasingly anxious and is requesting discharge because she feels "fine overall." Her current medications include levothyroxine and calcium carbonate started this morning. The surgeon has not yet rounded.
questions.lead_in: What is the nurse's first action?

answer_choices.text: Administer an additional dose of oral calcium carbonate and reassess in several hours
Encourage ambulation and reassure the patient that these symptoms are expected after thyroid surgery
Assess for signs of hypocalcemia and immediately notify the surgical team of the new symptoms
Hold levothyroxine until outpatient endocrine follow-up confirms thyroid function
Give acetaminophen for pain and discharge the patient with routine follow-up instructions

questions.rationale: This patient has symptoms concerning for postoperative hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy, likely from transient hypoparathyroidism. Perioral tingling and hand tightness are early manifestations that require prompt nursing assessment and immediate communication to the surgical team so treatment can be ordered and the calcium level can be checked. Because the stem asks for the nurse's first action, the safest immediate response is to recognize the complication and escalate care right away rather than simply giving oral calcium or waiting. Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia can worsen quickly and progress to tetany, laryngospasm, or arrhythmias.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Oral calcium may be part of treatment, but giving more calcium before promptly escalating the new neurologic symptoms is not the best first nursing action. The patient needs immediate assessment and provider notification because symptomatic hypocalcemia may require more urgent intervention than routine oral dosing.
These symptoms are not expected routine postoperative discomfort. Perioral tingling and hand tightness suggest hypocalcemia and require urgent assessment and escalation, not reassurance alone.

Levothyroxine replacement is important after thyroidectomy, but withholding it does not address the acute postoperative symptoms. The immediate concern is symptomatic hypocalcemia, not thyroid hormone titration.

Acetaminophen may help mild incisional discomfort, but discharge is unsafe when the patient has symptoms suggestive of hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy. The priority is recognition of the complication and immediate notification of the surgical team.

questions.teaching_point: After thyroidectomy, perioral paresthesias and hand tightness should prompt immediate nursing assessment and rapid notification of the surgical team for suspected hypocalcemia.

questions.vignette: A 7-year-old boy is brought to an outpatient clinic in late winter for fever and headache that began this morning. Over the past 6 hours, he has become progressively more irritable and has vomited twice. His mother reports that he complained of neck pain when trying to look down and wanted to stay in a dark room because light bothered his eyes. On exam, he is febrile, tachycardic, and listless. He resists passive neck flexion and has no focal weakness.
questions.lead_in: Which pathophysiologic process best explains this child’s illness?

answer_choices.text: Localized suppuration within brain parenchyma following hematogenous spread of infection
Inflammation of the meninges caused by viral infection of the central nervous system
Inflammatory cerebral edema causing increased intracranial pressure and meningeal irritation
Inflammation of the subarachnoid space caused by bacterial invasion and multiplication in the cerebrospinal fluid
Viral replication within cortical neurons leading to diffuse encephalitis

questions.rationale: This child has acute meningitis, suggested by fever, headache, vomiting, photophobia, irritability, and nuchal rigidity. Acute bacterial meningitis occurs when bacteria invade the subarachnoid space and multiply in the cerebrospinal fluid, triggering a brisk inflammatory response in the meninges. This inflammation produces the classic syndrome of fever, headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and altered behavior or mental status.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A brain abscess usually presents with a more focal neurologic syndrome and signs of localized mass effect rather than the acute diffuse meningeal symptoms seen here.
This describes viral meningitis. Viral infection can cause meningeal inflammation, but it is not the best explanation for the classic bacterial meningitis mechanism asked for here.
Increased intracranial pressure can occur secondary to meningitis, but cerebral edema is a consequence rather than the primary pathophysiologic process explaining this presentation.

Encephalitis involves infection of the brain parenchyma, often causing altered mental status, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits, rather than isolated meningeal irritation with photophobia and neck stiffness.

questions.teaching_point: Acute bacterial meningitis results from bacterial invasion of the subarachnoid space and cerebrospinal fluid, producing meningeal inflammation with fever, headache, photophobia, and nuchal rigidity.

questions.vignette: A 74-year-old woman is seen in clinic for evaluation of recurrent kidney stones and increasing fatigue. Over the past year, she has had two episodes of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and several fractures after minor falls. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and denies calcium supplement use. Exam is notable for mild proximal muscle weakness and a normal mental status. Laboratory studies show serum calcium 11.6 mg/dL, albumin 4.1 g/dL, phosphorus 2.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and intact parathyroid hormone elevated above the reference range. Her bone density testing shows a T-score of -2.7 at the femoral neck. She asks what the best next step is to reduce her future complications.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management at this time?

answer_choices.text: Begin cinacalcet as first-line long-term therapy
Reassure her and repeat calcium and parathyroid hormone levels in 12 months
Discontinue hydrochlorothiazide and no further treatment is needed

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism with clear indications for surgery: recurrent nephrolithiasis, osteoporosis with fragility fractures/low T-score, and elevated calcium with inappropriately high PTH. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and is the best intervention to reduce future stone formation, skeletal loss, and hypercalcemia-related complications.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cinacalcet may lower calcium in patients who are not surgical candidates, but it is not the preferred first-line definitive therapy for an otherwise operative patient with symptomatic disease and end-organ involvement.
Bisphosphonates can improve bone density but do not treat the underlying excess PTH or reliably address hypercalcemia, kidney stones, or the full complication burden in a surgical candidate.

Observation is reserved for selected asymptomatic patients without guideline-based indications for surgery. This patient already has renal stones and osteoporosis, so deferring treatment would miss the opportunity to prevent further complications.

Stopping hydrochlorothiazide is reasonable because thiazides can increase calcium levels, but medication adjustment alone is insufficient here. Her recurrent stones and osteoporosis indicate established primary hyperparathyroidism requiring definitive management.

questions.teaching_point: Primary hyperparathyroidism with stones, osteoporosis, or fragility fractures is treated definitively with parathyroidectomy when the patient is an acceptable surgical candidate.

questions.vignette: A 78-year-old man is admitted after 18 hours of worsening blurred vision, drooping eyelids, dry mouth, and progressive difficulty swallowing. He reports that earlier in the day he ate home-canned green beans at a family gathering. In the emergency department he is afebrile, alert, and oriented. Examination shows symmetric bilateral ptosis, dilated pupils that react sluggishly, hoarse voice, and descending weakness in the neck and upper extremities. Sensation is intact, and he has no altered mental status. His oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, but bedside spirometry shows declining forced vital capacity over the last hour.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

answer_choices.text: Obtain a head CT scan before starting treatment
Begin high-dose intravenous acyclovir and maintain airborne isolation
Administer naloxone and observe for recurrent sedation
Start pyridostigmine and arrange outpatient neurology follow-up
Administer botulinum antitoxin and closely monitor respiratory function

questions.rationale: This patient has classic foodborne botulism with cranial nerve involvement, descending symmetric weakness, preserved sensation, and autonomic symptoms after ingestion of home-canned food. The most important immediate treatment is botulinum antitoxin, which should be given as soon as botulism is suspected because it neutralizes circulating toxin and can stop further progression, although it does not reverse weakness that has already developed. Because respiratory failure is the major cause of morbidity and mortality, close inpatient respiratory monitoring is also essential.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Neuroimaging is not the immediate management for a patient with a classic toxic neuromuscular syndrome and signs of bulbar/respiratory involvement. Delaying treatment for a head CT could allow further progression to respiratory failure.

Acyclovir and airborne isolation are not appropriate for this presentation. Botulism is a toxin-mediated neuromuscular disorder, not a viral encephalitic illness, and there is no indication of a contagious airborne infection.

Naloxone treats opioid toxicity, which can cause CNS depression and respiratory compromise, but this patient is alert and has a pattern of cranial nerve palsies with descending paralysis after canned food exposure, which is much more consistent with botulism.

Pyridostigmine is used for myasthenia gravis, which can cause fatigable weakness and ptosis, but this presentation is more consistent with botulism after a high-risk food exposure and with prominent autonomic findings. Outpatient follow-up would be unsafe given the risk of rapid respiratory decline.

questions.teaching_point: Suspected botulism requires immediate botulinum antitoxin and close respiratory monitoring; do not wait for confirmatory testing before treating.

questions.vignette: A 24-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic with her partner because of 10 months of progressive weight loss, fatigue, and missed menstrual periods. She reports increasing calorie restriction, avoiding meals with others, and exercising for 2 hours daily. She denies bingeing, purging, laxative use, or substance use. Her BMI is 16.8 kg/m2. Vital signs show BP 88/54 mm Hg and HR 48/min. Physical examination shows dry skin, lanugo on the forearms, and cool extremities. She is alert and oriented but appears anxious when discussing her weight. The clinician is concerned about complications of restrictive eating and wants to assess for cardiac risk before initiating treatment.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to evaluate this patient’s current medical risk?
questions.rationale: A 12-lead electrocardiogram is the most appropriate study because this patient has anorexia nervosa with marked bradycardia, hypotension, and significant weight loss, which raises concern for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias related to malnutrition and possible electrolyte disturbances. ECG screening helps evaluate immediate cardiac risk before treatment is initiated and can identify sinus bradycardia, QT prolongation, or other abnormalities that may require closer monitoring or higher level of care.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Serum troponin is used to evaluate myocardial injury or acute coronary syndromes. This patient’s presentation is most consistent with restrictive eating disorder–related malnutrition, not acute cardiac ischemia.

Serum prolactin is not an appropriate test for evaluating medical risk in anorexia nervosa. Amenorrhea in this setting is more likely due to hypothalamic suppression from low energy availability than to hyperprolactinemia.

Upper endoscopy may be indicated if there are symptoms suggesting structural gastrointestinal disease, dysphagia, or GI bleeding, but it does not assess the immediate cardiovascular complications of anorexia nervosa.

Bone mineral density testing can be useful in patients with prolonged amenorrhea or chronic anorexia nervosa to assess for osteopenia or osteoporosis, but it does not address the immediate cardiac instability suggested by bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.teaching_point: In anorexia nervosa with bradycardia, hypotension, or marked weight loss, a 12-lead ECG is an important initial study to assess for cardiac complications before treatment begins.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman presents to clinic with sudden midback pain that began after she lifted a heavy box 5 days ago. She has a history of postmenopausal osteoporosis and takes only calcium supplements. The pain is localized to the lower thoracic region, worsens with standing and bending, and improves when she lies down. She denies leg weakness, numbness, bowel or bladder incontinence, fever, weight loss, or recent major trauma. On exam, she is afebrile, has point tenderness over the lower thoracic spine, and has limited range of motion due to pain. Neurologic examination of the lower extremities is normal.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Thoracic radiculopathy from intervertebral disc herniation

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has an acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture. Clues include advanced age, known osteoporosis, sudden focal thoracic pain after minimal strain, point tenderness over the spine, pain worsened by movement or axial loading, and a normal neurologic examination. Lack of fever, weight loss, major trauma, cancer history, and neurologic deficits makes infection, malignancy with cord compression, and other neurologic causes less likely, though those diagnoses are still considered when red flags are present.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Discitis/vertebral osteomyelitis usually causes progressive back pain with systemic symptoms such as fever, elevated inflammatory markers, or risk factors such as bacteremia, spinal procedures, or immunosuppression. Those features are not described here.

Thoracic paraspinal muscle strain can follow lifting and cause back pain, but it more often produces diffuse paraspinal tenderness rather than focal midline vertebral point tenderness in an older patient with osteoporosis.

Metastatic spinal cord compression is more likely with a known malignancy, progressive pain often worse at night, and neurologic findings such as weakness, sensory loss, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Those findings are absent in this patient.

Thoracic radiculopathy from disc herniation would more typically cause band-like pain radiating around the chest or abdomen in a dermatomal pattern, sometimes with sensory symptoms. This patient has focal midline lower thoracic pain without radicular features.

questions.teaching_point: In an older patient with osteoporosis, sudden focal back pain after minor strain with localized vertebral tenderness and a normal neurologic exam strongly suggests an acute vertebral compression fracture.

questions.vignette: A 13-year-old girl is brought to clinic for 3 months of fatigue, intermittent low-grade fevers, and painful swelling of both wrists and knees. Her mother reports that she also develops a red rash across her cheeks after being outdoors and has had two episodes of painless mouth ulcers. Today her blood pressure is normal, urinalysis shows mild proteinuria, and serum creatinine is normal. Serologic testing is positive for antinuclear antibody and anti–double-stranded DNA antibody. The family asks what medication is typically started to help control her disease activity and reduce flares.
questions.lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate first-line treatment to start now?
questions.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine is a standard first-line medication for systemic lupus erythematosus, including in pediatric patients, because it helps control skin, joint, and constitutional symptoms and reduces disease flares. It is commonly used as baseline therapy unless contraindicated.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Methotrexate can be used for inflammatory arthritis in selected cases, but it is not the usual first-line baseline therapy for systemic lupus erythematosus overall.
Ibuprofen may help with pain from mild arthralgias, but it does not control lupus disease activity or prevent flares.

Prednisone may be used for acute symptom control or organ-threatening disease, but long-term management is ideally steroid-sparing rather than starting chronic systemic corticosteroids as first-line therapy.

Azathioprine is used as an immunosuppressive agent for more significant disease or as a steroid-sparing medication, but it is not the typical initial baseline therapy for uncomplicated systemic lupus erythematosus.

questions.teaching_point: Hydroxychloroquine is foundational therapy for most patients with systemic lupus erythematosus and helps reduce flares and control mucocutaneous and joint symptoms.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C is admitted for worsening abdominal distention and fatigue. Over the past 3 months, he has unintentionally lost 8 kg and has had increasing early satiety. He denies fever, melena, or recent alcohol use. Exam shows jaundice, shifting dullness, and mild right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound. Laboratory studies show albumin 2.6 g/dL, total bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL, AST 96 U/L, ALT 61 U/L, and an AFP level of 980 ng/mL. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen shows a 5.2-cm arterial phase hyperenhancing lesion in the right hepatic lobe with washout on delayed images.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Metastatic colorectal cancer to the liver

questions.rationale: This patient with cirrhosis has a markedly elevated AFP and a liver lesion showing arterial phase hyperenhancement with venous/delayed washout on contrast CT, which is highly characteristic of hepatocellular carcinoma. His weight loss, early satiety, and worsening ascites further support a malignancy arising in the setting of chronic liver disease.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma can present with jaundice and a hepatic mass, but it is less associated with very high AFP and typically does not show the classic arterial enhancement with delayed washout pattern seen here.
Metastatic colorectal cancer can involve the liver, but the imaging pattern and markedly elevated AFP in a patient with cirrhosis are much more consistent with a primary hepatocellular malignancy.
A hemangioma is usually an incidental benign lesion and has a different contrast pattern, often peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in, rather than arterial enhancement with washout.

A hepatic abscess would more likely cause fever, leukocytosis, and a systemic infectious presentation rather than progressive weight loss with a tumor marker elevation and classic multiphase CT findings.

questions.teaching_point: In a patient with cirrhosis, a hypervascular liver lesion that washes out on delayed imaging is classic for hepatocellular carcinoma, especially when AFP is elevated.

questions.vignette: A 48-year-old woman comes to the clinic for evaluation of a neck mass she first noticed 2 months ago. She reports mild hoarseness and a sense of pressure when swallowing, but no fever, sore throat, or recent upper respiratory infection. She has no history of thyroid disease. On exam, she has a firm, non-tender 2.2-cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe that moves with swallowing. Cervical lymph nodes are not enlarged. TSH is normal. Thyroid ultrasound shows a solid hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins and tiny punctate echogenic foci.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis. It commonly presents as a painless thyroid nodule in an adult, and ultrasound features such as a solid hypoechoic lesion with irregular margins and punctate echogenic foci (microcalcifications) are highly suspicious. Mild hoarseness can occur from local mass effect. A normal TSH does not exclude thyroid cancer.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Follicular thyroid carcinoma can present as a thyroid nodule, but it is less associated with microcalcifications and irregular hypoechoic ultrasound findings; diagnosis requires evidence of capsular or vascular invasion on histology.
Subacute thyroiditis usually causes a painful, tender thyroid after a viral prodrome and is often associated with transient thyrotoxicosis, which is not suggested by this presentation.
Thyroid lymphoma usually occurs in older adults and is strongly associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis, often presenting as a rapidly enlarging goiter rather than a solitary suspicious nodule.
Multinodular goiter typically causes an enlarged thyroid with multiple nodules and lacks the highly suspicious ultrasound features described here.

questions.teaching_point: A painless thyroid nodule with suspicious ultrasound findings—especially a solid hypoechoic lesion with irregular margins and microcalcifications—strongly suggests papillary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.vignette: A 5-week-old boy is admitted for evaluation of worsening feeding intolerance. He has been increasingly hungry after feeds but then vomits forcefully shortly after nearly every feeding. The emesis is nonbilious and has become more frequent over the past several days. His parents report fewer wet diapers and poor weight gain. On exam, he appears hungry, mildly dehydrated, and has a small palpable mass in the right upper abdomen after feeding. Abdomen is otherwise soft and nondistended.
questions.lead_in: Which additional finding is most likely in this infant?

answer_choices.text: Visible peristaltic waves moving from left to right across the upper abdomen
Intermittent severe crampy abdominal pain with currant jelly stools
Bilious vomiting with abdominal distension and shock in the first day of life
Small-volume effortless spit-ups with normal weight gain

questions.rationale: This infant has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which classically presents at 2 to 8 weeks of age with progressive, forceful nonbilious vomiting after feeds, persistent hunger, dehydration, poor weight gain, and a palpable "olive" in the right upper abdomen or epigastrium. Recurrent loss of gastric contents leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, making this the most likely additional finding. Visible peristaltic waves can also be seen in pyloric stenosis, but the electrolyte abnormality is the most characteristic associated finding in this presentation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Visible peristaltic waves can occur with pyloric stenosis, but they are not as characteristic as the metabolic alkalosis caused by repeated vomiting.
Intermittent severe crampy abdominal pain with currant jelly stools suggests intussusception, not pyloric stenosis.

Bilious vomiting with abdominal distension and shock in the first day of life suggests a neonatal intestinal obstruction such as malrotation with volvulus, not pyloric stenosis, which causes nonbilious vomiting in a 2- to 8-week-old infant.
Small-volume effortless spit-ups with normal weight gain describe physiologic infant reflux, not the progressive obstruction seen in pyloric stenosis.

questions.teaching_point: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting in a hungry infant and commonly leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis from gastric fluid loss.

questions.vignette: A 16-year-old girl is brought to an outpatient mental health clinic by her mother because of repeated intense arguments, unstable friendships, and frequent mood changes over the past year. Her mother reports that after perceived criticism from a friend, the patient became very upset, sent dozens of texts threatening to hurt herself if the friend stopped talking to her, and later acted as if nothing had happened. The patient says she “always feels empty” and has a history of cutting her forearm when distressed. She denies hallucinations, substance use, or episodes of decreased need for sleep with increased energy. Mental status examination shows an anxious affect and marked fear of abandonment.
questions.lead_in: Which additional clinical feature is most characteristic of borderline personality disorder?

answer_choices.text: Repetitive handwashing and intrusive contamination fears
Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment
Sudden onset of auditory hallucinations and disorganized speech
Persistent social withdrawal with flat affect
Grandiose delusions with decreased need for sleep

questions.rationale: Borderline personality disorder is characterized by unstable interpersonal relationships, affective instability, impulsivity, recurrent self-harm, chronic feelings of emptiness, and frantic efforts to avoid abandonment. In adolescents, these features can be recognized clinically when the pattern is persistent and impairing.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Repetitive handwashing and contamination fears are characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder, not borderline personality disorder.
Auditory hallucinations and disorganized speech are psychotic symptoms that point toward a psychotic disorder, not the core features of borderline personality disorder.
Persistent social withdrawal and flat affect suggest a negative-symptom pattern such as schizophrenia spectrum illness or depression, rather than borderline personality disorder.
Grandiosity and decreased need for sleep are more consistent with mania or bipolar disorder, not borderline personality disorder.

questions.teaching_point: Borderline personality disorder commonly presents with unstable relationships, self-harm, emotional lability, and intense fear of abandonment.

questions.vignette: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department for intermittent severe abdominal pain and repeated vomiting for 12 hours. His parents report that he has been drawing his knees to his chest in waves and seems briefly well between episodes. He has not passed stool or flatus since yesterday. Two months ago, he underwent surgery for intussusception. On examination, he is uncomfortable and mildly dehydrated. His abdomen is distended with high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness without guarding or rebound.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would most strongly support small bowel obstruction in this child?

answer_choices.text: A minimally distended abdomen with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant
Visible abdominal peristaltic waves with a tympanitic, distended abdomen
Localized right lower quadrant rebound tenderness with a positive psoas sign
Diffuse abdominal distension with quiet bowel sounds and mild, generalized tenderness
Absent bowel sounds with a rigid, board-like abdomen and diffuse involuntary guarding

questions.rationale: Small bowel obstruction classically causes crampy, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, obstipation, and high-pitched bowel sounds. A tympanitic, distended abdomen with visible peristaltic waves is a classic physical finding in mechanical obstruction because the bowel is contracting against a blockage. In a child with prior abdominal surgery, adhesions are a common cause of small bowel obstruction.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant is classic for intussusception, which can cause intermittent colicky pain but is a different physical finding from adhesive small bowel obstruction.
Right lower quadrant rebound tenderness with a positive psoas sign suggests appendicitis rather than small bowel obstruction.

Diffuse distension with quiet bowel sounds and mild generalized tenderness is more consistent with ileus than with mechanical small bowel obstruction, which often has high-pitched bowel sounds early on.
A rigid, board-like abdomen with diffuse involuntary guarding and absent bowel sounds is more concerning for peritonitis or perforation than uncomplicated small bowel obstruction.

questions.teaching_point: In pediatric small bowel obstruction, prior abdominal surgery, intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, obstipation, distension, high-pitched bowel sounds, and visible peristalsis are key clues to a mechanical obstruction.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man presents to a primary care clinic with 4 days of watery diarrhea, crampy lower abdominal pain, and low-grade fever.
