Emergency evaluation for ischemia is more appropriate when there is severe pain out of proportion to the exam, peritonitis, lactic acidosis, or unstable vital signs. Those features are not present here.

questions.teaching_point: Postoperative ileus is usually managed supportively with bowel rest, hydration, and reduction of opioids unless features suggest obstruction or a surgical emergency.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man is admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation facility after an ischemic stroke. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and difficulty with self-care because of right-sided weakness. His home medications include metformin and glipizide. Over the past 24 hours, multiple capillary glucose checks have ranged from 220 to 310 mg/dL despite a consistent carbohydrate diet. He is eating reliably, but his therapy sessions are being interrupted by fatigue and polydipsia. His serum creatinine is stable, and there are no signs of infection or dehydration.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate adjustment to his diabetes management at this time?

answer_choices.text: Continue his current oral regimen and add correctional insulin for premeal glucose elevations
Reduce the dose of glipizide and continue metformin without additional therapy
Hold all diabetes medications until his rehabilitation course is complete
Start a basal-bolus insulin regimen with correction-scale insulin
Start basal insulin alone and stop all oral diabetes medications

questions.rationale: This patient has persistent inpatient hyperglycemia despite oral therapy, with glucose values consistently above target and symptoms interfering with rehabilitation. In a hospitalized adult who is eating reliably, the most effective and predictable approach is scheduled insulin therapy. A basal-bolus regimen with correctional insulin addresses both basal needs and prandial elevations and can be titrated to his carbohydrate intake and glucose trends. Oral agents alone are generally insufficient for this degree of inpatient hyperglycemia.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Adding only correctional insulin to the current oral regimen may help transient elevations, but persistent glucose values in the 220-310 mg/dL range usually require scheduled insulin rather than reactive treatment alone.
Reducing glipizide would not address the current marked hyperglycemia, and continuing metformin alone is unlikely to provide adequate control in the inpatient setting.
Stopping all diabetes medications would worsen hyperglycemia and is inappropriate in a patient already demonstrating poor inpatient glycemic control.

Basal insulin alone may be used in selected patients with limited or unpredictable oral intake, but this patient is eating reliably and has significant postprandial hyperglycemia, so basal-bolus therapy is more appropriate.

questions.teaching_point: Persistent inpatient hyperglycemia in a stable adult who is eating reliably is best managed with scheduled insulin, often a basal-bolus regimen with correctional doses, rather than oral therapy alone.

questions.vignette: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle collision. He was restrained in the back seat and has a small abrasion on his chest. Over the last hour, he has become increasingly anxious and short of breath. On exam, he is tachycardic, hypotensive for age, and has distended neck veins. Heart sounds are muffled, and his extremities are cool. Lung exam is clear bilaterally. Bedside pulse oximetry shows 96% on room air. The team is concerned that his hemodynamics are deteriorating.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate next step to confirm the suspected cause of his instability?

answer_choices.text: Computed tomography angiography of the chest

questions.rationale: Focused bedside transthoracic echocardiography is the best next diagnostic study because this child has a high-risk blunt chest trauma presentation with obstructive shock findings concerning for cardiac tamponade. In an unstable patient, bedside echo rapidly evaluates for pericardial effusion and signs of impaired cardiac filling and can be performed immediately without delaying definitive treatment.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A 12-lead ECG may show nonspecific abnormalities such as tachycardia or low voltage, but it does not confirm tamponade and is less useful than bedside echocardiography in this emergency.
CT angiography can identify thoracic injuries, but it requires transport out of the resuscitation area and is inappropriate in a hemodynamically unstable patient when tamponade is suspected.

A portable chest radiograph may show an enlarged cardiac silhouette or associated thoracic injury, but it is not the most appropriate study to confirm tamponade in an unstable child and should not delay bedside ultrasound or intervention.

Right heart catheterization can demonstrate equalization of diastolic pressures, but it is invasive, not a first-line diagnostic test in the ED, and would delay urgent management in an unstable pediatric trauma patient.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic instability, bedside echocardiography is the fastest and most appropriate diagnostic study.

questions.vignette: A 5-week-old male is brought to a pediatric rehabilitation follow-up visit after a NICU stay for prematurity. Over the past 10 days, his mother reports progressively forceful vomiting shortly after feeds. The emesis is nonbilious and he is hungry again soon after vomiting. She also notes fewer wet diapers and that his weight gain has stalled. On exam, the infant appears mildly dehydrated.
questions.lead_in: Which additional finding is most consistent with this infant’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Frothy vomiting, choking, and coughing during feeds from birth
Loose stools and fever preceding the vomiting episodes
Bilious vomiting with abdominal distention and bloody stool
Visible peristaltic waves moving from left to right across the upper abdomen
Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with currant jelly stools

questions.rationale: This infant has hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which typically presents at 2 to 8 weeks of age with progressively forceful nonbilious vomiting after feeds, persistent hunger, poor weight gain, and dehydration. A characteristic associated finding is visible gastric peristaltic waves moving from left to right across the upper abdomen as the stomach contracts against the narrowed pylorus. An olive-shaped pyloric mass may also be palpable, but visible peristalsis is the best answer here because it is a classic additional physical finding.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Frothy vomiting with choking and coughing during feeds from birth suggests esophageal atresia with tracheoesophageal fistula, not pyloric stenosis. That condition presents much earlier and does not cause the classic age-dependent progression described here.

Loose stools and fever preceding vomiting episodes are more consistent with infectious gastroenteritis. Gastroenteritis can cause vomiting, but it does not produce the classic nonbilious postprandial projectile vomiting, hunger after emesis, and dehydration pattern of pyloric stenosis.

Bilious vomiting with abdominal distention and bloody stool suggests an intestinal obstruction such as malrotation with volvulus or a severe distal obstruction, not pyloric stenosis. Pyloric stenosis causes nonbilious vomiting because the blockage is proximal to the duodenum.

Intermittent colicky abdominal pain with currant jelly stools is characteristic of intussusception, which is a different diagnosis and does not typically cause the progressive post-feed nonbilious projectile vomiting seen in pyloric stenosis.

questions.teaching_point: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting in young infants and may be associated with visible peristaltic waves and a palpable pyloric olive.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after developing sudden mid-back pain while reaching into a high kitchen cabinet. She has a history of postmenopausal osteoporosis and has taken alendronate inconsistently. She denies fever, weight loss, leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, and bowel or bladder dysfunction. On exam, she is uncomfortable but afebrile. There is focal tenderness over the lower thoracic spine without step-off, and neurologic examination of the lower extremities is normal. Plain radiographs show loss of anterior vertebral body height at T12 with a wedge-shaped deformity; the posterior vertebral border is preserved.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: This patient has the classic presentation of an acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture: an older adult with known osteoporosis, sudden onset pain after minimal trauma, focal midline spinal tenderness, normal neurologic findings, and a wedge-shaped vertebral body deformity with preserved posterior vertebral border on x-ray. The absence of fever, systemic symptoms, or neurologic deficits makes infection, inflammatory spondyloarthropathy, and cord compression less likely.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Spinal epidural abscess typically presents with back pain plus fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and often neurologic deficits or risk factors such as bacteremia or injection drug use, none of which are present here.

Metastatic spinal cord compression is a concern in patients with known malignancy, progressive pain, and neurologic compromise; this patient lacks cancer history, constitutional symptoms, and exam findings suggesting cord involvement.

Thoracic disc herniation would be more likely to cause radicular pain, sensory changes, or myelopathic findings rather than isolated focal bony tenderness and vertebral body height loss on radiograph.

Ankylosing spondylitis can predispose to spinal fractures, but it usually occurs in younger patients with inflammatory back pain, morning stiffness, and reduced spinal mobility; the vignette instead supports fragility fracture from osteoporosis.

questions.teaching_point: Older adults with osteoporosis and sudden focal back pain after minimal stress plus a wedge-shaped vertebral deformity on x-ray most likely have a vertebral compression fracture.

questions.vignette: An 78-year-old man returns to clinic 5 days after being treated as an outpatient for community-acquired pneumonia. He now reports worsening shortness of breath, marked fatigue, and inability to lie flat without gasping for air. He has become increasingly confused over the past day. His wife notes that he is breathing faster and that his lips look bluish when he walks across the room. On exam, temperature is 37.4 C (99.3 F), blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min, respiratory rate is 34/min, and oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. He is using accessory muscles, and diffuse inspiratory crackles are heard over both lung fields. Chest radiograph from the emergency department shows bilateral patchy opacities without cardiomegaly.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding is most consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Unilateral pleuritic chest pain with absent breath sounds over one hemithorax
Diffuse cyanosis with severe respiratory distress that does not improve with increasing supplemental oxygen
Dullness to percussion and decreased fremitus at the right lung base
Productive cough with focal bronchial breath sounds over one lobe
Audible wheezing that improves after albuterol treatment

questions.rationale: Acute respiratory distress syndrome causes diffuse alveolar damage with noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and intrapulmonary shunting, leading to severe hypoxemia that is often refractory to supplemental oxygen. In this patient with recent pneumonia, bilateral opacities, and worsening respiratory distress, diffuse cyanosis despite increasing oxygen support is most consistent with ARDS.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Unilateral pleuritic chest pain with absent breath sounds over one hemithorax suggests pneumothorax, which typically produces unilateral rather than diffuse bilateral findings.

Dullness to percussion with decreased fremitus suggests pleural effusion, which can cause dyspnea but does not best fit the diffuse bilateral crackles, severe hypoxemia, and bilateral opacities seen here.
Productive cough with focal bronchial breath sounds over one lobe is more consistent with lobar pneumonia or localized consolidation, not the diffuse bilateral process of ARDS.
Wheezing that improves with albuterol suggests bronchospasm from asthma or COPD rather than diffuse alveolar-capillary injury with refractory hypoxemia.

questions.teaching_point: ARDS is suggested by acute severe hypoxemia after an inflammatory lung insult, bilateral infiltrates, and respiratory distress with poor oxygenation despite supplemental oxygen.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old woman with a 4-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus presents to the emergency department with sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath for 1 day. She has been less active for the past month because of a lupus flare and has been taking prednisone daily. Vital signs show T 37.2 C, HR 122/min, RR 26/min, BP 118/74 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 91% on room air. Exam reveals mild unilateral swelling and tenderness of the left calf. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. CT pulmonary angiography demonstrates segmental pulmonary emboli without right heart strain. She has no history of major bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, severe thrombocytopenia, or severe renal impairment, but she is likely to need a procedure later today to remove a large lupus-related pleural effusion.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

answer_choices.text: Place an inferior vena cava filter without anticoagulation

questions.rationale: This patient has an acute pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic stability and no evidence of right ventricular strain, so the immediate priority is anticoagulation. Intravenous unfractionated heparin is the best choice here because she may need a procedure later today; UFH has a short half-life and can be rapidly stopped or reversed if an intervention is needed. In a stable patient without a near-term procedure, low-molecular-weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant would also be appropriate, but the anticipated procedure makes UFH preferable in this case.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Apixaban is an appropriate oral anticoagulant for many stable patients with pulmonary embolism, but it is not the best immediate choice here because a procedure may be needed later today and a rapidly titratable agent is preferred.
An inferior vena cava filter is generally reserved for patients with acute venous thromboembolism who have an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation. This patient can receive anticoagulation.

Low-molecular-weight heparin is an effective treatment for acute pulmonary embolism, but it is less convenient when a procedure may be needed soon because it cannot be titrated or reversed as quickly as unfractionated heparin.
Thrombolytic therapy is reserved for massive pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability, or selected high-risk cases with deterioration. This patient is stable and has no right heart strain.

questions.teaching_point: In hemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism, prompt anticoagulation is the key immediate intervention. Intravenous unfractionated heparin is preferred when rapid interruption or reversal may be needed for an upcoming procedure.

questions.vignette: A 74-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease comes for routine follow-up. He takes metformin and lifestyle measures, but his A1c has remained 8.4% over the past 6 months. He lives independently and reports mild urinary frequency but no dysuria or fever. Home glucose readings are mostly 160-220 mg/dL. He has a BMI of 31 kg/m2 and wants to avoid medications that cause hypoglycemia or significant weight gain. His eGFR is 46 mL/min/1.73 m2, and he has no history of pancreatitis or recurrent genital infections.
questions.lead_in: Which additional medication is the most appropriate next step to improve his glycemic control?
questions.rationale: An SGLT2 inhibitor is an appropriate add-on agent for an older adult with type 2 diabetes who has persistent hyperglycemia on metformin, CKD stage 3, obesity, and a desire to avoid hypoglycemia and weight gain. In addition to lowering glucose, this class has renal and cardiovascular benefits in many patients and remains usable at this level of kidney function, making it a strong next step in outpatient management.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pioglitazone may lower glucose, but it commonly causes weight gain and fluid retention and is not an optimal replacement for metformin in this patient, especially given his CKD and desire to avoid weight gain.
Glyburide is a poor choice in an older adult and in CKD because it has a high risk of prolonged hypoglycemia. It also does not address the patient’s preference to avoid weight gain and hypoglycemia.
Acarbose can modestly improve postprandial glucose, but it is less effective than an SGLT2 inhibitor and is not the best next choice for this patient’s persistent A1c elevation on metformin.

Basal insulin can improve glycemic control, but it is usually not the preferred next step here because the patient is not severely symptomatic or markedly uncontrolled, and insulin increases hypoglycemia risk and often causes weight gain.

questions.teaching_point: For older adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD, an SGLT2 inhibitor is often a preferred add-on because it lowers glucose with low hypoglycemia risk and provides kidney and cardiovascular benefits.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is 3 days into an inpatient rehabilitation stay after surgical repair of a hip fracture. He has fluctuating confusion that is worse in the evening, repeatedly tries to get out of bed, and has difficulty following simple commands during therapy sessions. His wife says he was oriented and conversational earlier today but became disorganized after lunch. He has a Foley catheter for urinary retention, has slept poorly since admission, and recently started oxycodone for pain. On examination, he is inattentive, answers questions inconsistently, and is disoriented to time. He has no focal motor deficits, and his vital signs are stable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer disease

questions.rationale: Delirium is the best diagnosis because the patient has an acute change in attention and cognition with a fluctuating course in the setting of recent hospitalization, sleep disruption, Foley catheter use, and opioid exposure. The inattention, waxing and waning mental status, and evening worsening are classic features, and the absence of focal neurologic deficits makes stroke less likely.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Catatonia involves psychomotor abnormalities such as mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, or stupor. This patient instead has fluctuating confusion and inattention, which are more consistent with delirium.
Depression can cause slowed thinking and poor concentration, but it does not typically produce acute disorientation, fluctuating consciousness, and marked inattention in this setting.

Major neurocognitive disorder usually has a chronic, progressive decline rather than an acute fluctuating change over hours to days. The prominent inattention and waxing/waning course strongly favor delirium.

An ischemic stroke causing aphasia would usually produce a more focal language deficit, often with lateralizing neurologic findings, rather than a global, fluctuating attention deficit and disorientation.

questions.teaching_point: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition, often triggered by medications, infection, sleep deprivation, or hospitalization in older adults.

questions.vignette: A 9-year-old boy is brought to clinic for 4 days of watery diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Two weeks ago, he completed a course of clindamycin for a dental abscess. Since then, he has had 6 to 8 loose stools daily, low-grade fever, decreased appetite, and mild abdominal tenderness. His mother reports that the stools have a foul odor and one episode appeared streaked with mucus. He is able to drink fluids, and his vital signs are stable. There is no recent travel, sick contacts, or history of inflammatory bowel disease.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains this patient’s symptoms?
questions.rationale: Clostridioides difficile colitis is the best diagnosis because the child has new-onset watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, low-grade fever, and recent clindamycin exposure, which is a classic trigger for antibiotic-associated colitis. The foul-smelling stools and mucus can occur with toxin-mediated colonic inflammation. In a stable outpatient with a mild presentation, this history strongly supports pseudomembranous colitis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Ulcerative colitis can cause bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and urgency, but the abrupt onset after clindamycin exposure makes antibiotic-associated colitis more likely than a new chronic inflammatory bowel disease diagnosis.

Intussusception usually presents with episodic severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and sometimes currant jelly stools, often in younger children. The chronic watery diarrhea after antibiotic exposure is not typical.

Rotavirus typically causes acute viral gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea, most often in younger children, and is less likely to present after recent antibiotic use with persistent foul-smelling diarrhea and mucus.

Giardiasis can cause foul-smelling diarrhea and abdominal cramps, but it is more associated with exposure to contaminated water, travel, or daycare outbreaks and does not fit the recent antibiotic trigger as well as C. difficile colitis.

questions.teaching_point: Recent antibiotic use followed by watery diarrhea and abdominal pain in a child should raise concern for C. difficile colitis, a common cause of pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.vignette: A 34-year-old man comes to an urgent care clinic because of 1 day of worsening blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty swallowing. He says he developed constipation several days ago and now feels that his voice is becoming weak and nasal. He denies fever, diarrhea, headache, or sensory loss. He recently ate home-canned green beans shared by a relative at a picnic. On exam, he is alert and afebrile. Pupils are dilated and sluggishly reactive, extraocular movements are limited, and his speech is dysarthric. Strength is mildly decreased symmetrically in the arms.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

answer_choices.text: Administer botulinum antitoxin and arrange urgent hospital transfer for airway monitoring
Give pyridostigmine and schedule neurology referral for suspected myasthenia gravis
Perform emergent lumbar puncture to evaluate for Guillain-Barré syndrome
Treat with activated charcoal and discharge if symptoms do not progress
Start oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and provide outpatient follow-up in 48 hours

questions.rationale: This patient has classic botulism with descending cranial nerve dysfunction, autonomic symptoms, symmetric weakness, and a high-risk food exposure. Botulism is a medical emergency because paralysis can progress to respiratory failure. The immediate priority is administration of botulinum antitoxin as soon as possible and urgent transfer to a hospital for close respiratory and neurologic monitoring; outpatient management is inappropriate.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Myasthenia gravis can cause fatigable weakness and bulbar symptoms, but the autonomic findings, fixed dilated pupils, constipation, and implicated home-canned food exposure are more consistent with botulism. Pyridostigmine would not address toxin-mediated paralysis.

Guillain-Barré syndrome is a competing cause of weakness, but lumbar puncture is not the first action here and would delay urgent antitoxin therapy. The cranial nerve-predominant pattern and pupillary/autonomic findings favor botulism.

Activated charcoal is only useful very early after certain ingestions and does not treat established toxin-mediated neurologic illness. Discharging the patient would be unsafe because respiratory compromise can develop quickly.
Antibiotics do not neutralize botulinum toxin and are not the immediate treatment for foodborne botulism. This presentation also lacks features of a routine bacterial GI infection.

questions.teaching_point: Botulism causes descending paralysis with cranial nerve and autonomic findings; treat immediately with botulinum antitoxin and hospitalize for respiratory monitoring.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old man is admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation unit after surgical repair of a tibial fracture. He has a 6-cm laceration on his left forearm from a fall that occurred 2 hours ago. The wound was irrigated and closed in the emergency department. It is a clean, minor laceration with no devitalized tissue or contamination. He is otherwise stable, but his immunization history is unclear because he recently relocated and does not have prior records. He recalls receiving childhood vaccines but is unsure whether he ever completed the adult tetanus series or had a booster. His medication list is otherwise unremarkable, and he has no history of adverse reactions to vaccines.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate tetanus-related preventive intervention for this patient today?

answer_choices.text: Administer Td only and no further vaccination is needed
Administer Tdap now and complete the tetanus vaccine series according to schedule
Defer tetanus vaccination until the wound has fully healed
No tetanus prophylaxis is indicated because the wound was already sutured

questions.rationale: This patient has a clean, minor wound and an unknown or incomplete tetanus immunization history. For clean, minor wounds, a tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine is indicated when the patient has received fewer than 3 doses or has an unknown history. Because he is an adult and may not have previously received Tdap, giving Tdap now is appropriate, and he should then complete the remaining tetanus series using tetanus-toxoid-containing vaccine at the recommended intervals. Tetanus immune globulin is not needed for a clean, minor wound in this setting.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A tetanus-toxoid vaccine is indicated, but a single dose of Td alone is not sufficient when the patient may have an incomplete primary series. He should also complete the series, and Tdap is preferred if he has not previously received it as an adult.

Tetanus immune globulin is reserved for higher-risk wounds in patients with unknown or incomplete immunization. For a clean, minor wound, TIG is not indicated; active immunization is the needed intervention.
Tetanus prophylaxis should be given immediately when indicated; delaying until the wound heals does not provide protection against tetanus after an exposure.
Wound closure does not eliminate tetanus risk. Prophylaxis is determined by wound type and immunization status, and this patient still needs vaccination because his history is unknown.

questions.teaching_point: For an adult with a clean, minor wound and unknown or incomplete tetanus immunization history, give Tdap now and complete the tetanus vaccine series; TIG is reserved for higher-risk wounds when vaccination is incomplete or unknown.

questions.vignette: A 38-year-old woman comes to the emergency department for 2 days of generalized weakness after a viral upper respiratory infection. She has a history of primary hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine but reports that she stopped taking her medication 4 months ago because she could not afford refills. She has had increasing fatigue, constipation, dry skin, and cold intolerance over several months. Temperature is 35.8 C (96.4 F), blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg, pulse is 58/min, and respirations are 14/min. Examination shows periorbital puffiness, slowed speech, and delayed relaxation of the deep tendon reflexes. She is alert and oriented and has no focal neurologic deficits.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following counseling points is most appropriate to prevent recurrence of hypothyroid symptoms and complications after she is restarted on treatment?

answer_choices.text: Stop levothyroxine once symptoms improve and restart it only if fatigue recurs
Use levothyroxine only on days when she feels cold or constipated
Take levothyroxine daily on an empty stomach and arrange periodic thyroid-stimulating hormone monitoring
Take levothyroxine with calcium supplements to improve absorption
Substitute over-the-counter iodine supplements for prescribed thyroid hormone therapy

questions.rationale: Primary hypothyroidism in adults usually requires lifelong levothyroxine replacement. The most appropriate preventive counseling is to emphasize consistent daily use, taking the medication on an empty stomach to optimize absorption, and periodic thyroid-stimulating hormone monitoring to confirm adequate replacement and adjust the dose as needed. These measures help prevent recurrent symptoms and complications of hypothyroidism.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Levothyroxine should not be stopped when symptoms improve, because primary hypothyroidism generally recurs without ongoing hormone replacement.
Levothyroxine should not be taken intermittently based on symptoms; stable thyroid hormone levels require consistent daily dosing.
Calcium decreases levothyroxine absorption and should not be taken with it. If both are needed, they should be separated by several hours.
Iodine supplements are not an appropriate substitute for levothyroxine in established primary hypothyroidism and may worsen thyroid dysfunction in some patients.

questions.teaching_point: Adults with primary hypothyroidism generally need lifelong levothyroxine with adherence counseling, proper administration, and periodic TSH monitoring to prevent recurrent hypothyroidism and serious complications.

questions.vignette: A 49-year-old man presents to the emergency department because of worsening headaches and intermittent blurry vision over the past 6 months. He says his wedding ring and shoe size have both increased over the last few years, and his family has noticed his face looks “coarser.” He also reports snoring, new jaw discomfort when chewing, and occasional tingling in both hands. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows frontal bossing, prognathism, enlarged hands with thickened soft tissue, widened spacing between the teeth, and bitemporal visual field loss on confrontation.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding is most likely to be present in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Enlarged tongue with deepening of the voice
Heat intolerance with a fine tremor and hyperreflexia
Violaceous abdominal striae with proximal muscle weakness
Pretibial myxedema with lid lag and proptosis
Dry skin, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, and bradycardia

questions.rationale: This patient has acromegaly from excess growth hormone, most often due to a pituitary adenoma. Progressive enlargement of acral and facial features, mandibular overgrowth, soft-tissue swelling, carpal tunnel symptoms, headaches, and visual field defects from pituitary mass effect all support the diagnosis. Macroglossia and a deepened voice are common additional findings from soft-tissue overgrowth.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Heat intolerance, tremor, and hyperreflexia suggest hyperthyroidism, which can cause some overlap in anxiety or weight changes but does not explain the progressive acral enlargement, prognathism, or bitemporal hemianopsia.

Violaceous striae and proximal muscle weakness are classic for Cushing syndrome. Although pituitary tumors can cause Cushing disease, the vignette centers on growth hormone excess with characteristic bony and soft-tissue overgrowth rather than glucocorticoid excess.
Pretibial myxedema, lid lag, and proptosis point to Graves disease. This would not account for the enlarged hands, coarse facial features, jaw changes, and visual field loss from a sellar mass.

Dry skin, delayed reflexes, and bradycardia are findings of hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism can cause fatigue and weight gain, but it does not produce the progressive facial coarsening, enlarged extremities, or pituitary mass-effect symptoms seen here.

questions.teaching_point: Acromegaly causes progressive enlargement of acral and facial features, soft-tissue overgrowth, and symptoms from a pituitary mass such as headaches and bitemporal visual field loss.

questions.vignette: A 71-year-old man is brought to clinic by his daughter because of 3 months of progressive change in behavior and function. He has become apathetic, has difficulty managing his checkbook, and recently left the stove on twice. Over the past 2 weeks, he has developed worsening headaches that are most noticeable in the morning and occasional episodes of nausea. His daughter also reports one brief episode of jerking of the right arm followed by confusion. He has no fever, neck stiffness, or recent head trauma. Examination shows a mildly slowed, inattentive man with intact cranial nerves, normal gait, and mild weakness of the right hand compared with the left. MRI of the brain shows a solitary ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis in the left frontal lobe and surrounding vasogenic edema.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Glioblastoma is the most likely diagnosis. This older adult has a subacute, progressive syndrome with behavioral and cognitive changes, morning headaches with nausea suggesting increased intracranial pressure, a focal seizure, and mild unilateral weakness. The MRI finding of a solitary ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic edema is classic for an aggressive primary brain tumor such as glioblastoma.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Subdural hematoma can cause cognitive change and focal neurologic deficits in older adults, but it is usually associated with trauma or anticoagulant use and would not typically present with a solitary ring-enhancing necrotic mass on MRI.

Brain metastasis can also present as a ring-enhancing lesion with vasogenic edema and neurologic deficits, but the vignette does not provide a known systemic primary malignancy, and the solitary frontal lesion with central necrosis is most consistent with glioblastoma in this context.

Brain abscess can produce a ring-enhancing lesion and seizures, but it is usually associated with fever, infectious symptoms, leukocytosis, endocarditis, sinusitis, otitis, or immunosuppression; those features are absent here.

Meningioma commonly causes a dural-based, extra-axial mass and may lead to seizures or focal deficits, but it does not typically appear as a ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic edema in this pattern.

questions.teaching_point: In an older adult, progressive cognitive or behavioral change plus morning headache, nausea, focal deficit, seizure, and a ring-enhancing lesion with central necrosis should raise strong concern for glioblastoma.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of gradually worsening central vision over the past year. She reports that straight lines on her kitchen tiles now look wavy and that she has trouble recognizing faces and reading small print. She has no eye pain, redness, or flashes of light. She has a 40-pack-year smoking history and takes medication for hypertension. Visual acuity is mildly reduced in both eyes. Dilated ophthalmic examination shows bilateral drusen and pigmentary changes in the macula without retinal hemorrhage or signs of choroidal neovascularization. She asks what she can do to lower her risk of further vision loss.
questions.lead_in: Which recommendation is most appropriate to reduce the risk of progression of her condition?

answer_choices.text: Start oral corticosteroids to reduce retinal inflammation
Start intravitreal anti-VEGF injections in both eyes to prevent future vision loss
Begin daily antioxidant and zinc supplementation formulated for age-related macular degeneration
Recommend routine observation only because vitamin supplementation has no benefit before severe vision loss
Advise smoking cessation alone because no other intervention reduces progression of this condition

questions.rationale: This patient has intermediate nonexudative age-related macular degeneration, suggested by gradual central vision loss, metamorphopsia, bilateral drusen, and pigmentary changes without evidence of choroidal neovascularization. In patients with intermediate AMD, or advanced AMD in one eye, AREDS/AREDS2 antioxidant plus zinc supplementation reduces the risk of progression to advanced vision loss. Smoking cessation is also important, but it is not the best single recommendation among the options because vitamin-mineral supplementation has demonstrated benefit in slowing progression for appropriate patients.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Oral corticosteroids are not used to prevent progression of age-related macular degeneration and would expose the patient to unnecessary adverse effects.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy is used for neovascular (wet) AMD with choroidal neovascularization, which is not present in this patient.
Observation alone misses a proven preventive strategy in patients with intermediate AMD; AREDS/AREDS2 supplementation can reduce progression to advanced disease.

Smoking cessation is important risk reduction, but it is not the only intervention that can reduce progression in intermediate AMD; AREDS/AREDS2 supplementation also helps slow progression in appropriate patients.

questions.teaching_point: For intermediate age-related macular degeneration, AREDS/AREDS2 vitamin-zinc supplementation and smoking cessation can help slow progression; anti-VEGF therapy is reserved for neovascular disease.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man comes to clinic for recurrent episodes of severe right-sided pain around his eye. The attacks began 2 weeks ago and occur once or twice daily, often in the late evening, lasting about 45 minutes. During attacks, he paces the room and cannot lie still. His eye becomes red and teary on the painful side, and his right nostril runs. He has a history of hypertension and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. Neurologic examination between attacks is normal. He has been taking over-the-counter ibuprofen without relief.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate acute treatment for this patient’s headache attacks?
questions.rationale: High-flow oxygen delivered by nonrebreather mask is a first-line acute treatment for cluster headache and can rapidly abort an attack. The patient’s short-lasting, unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms and restlessness is characteristic of cluster headache. Although rapid-acting triptans can also treat cluster headache, oxygen is an appropriate first choice and avoids potential cardiovascular concerns associated with triptan use in patients with significant vascular disease.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Triptans can be effective for cluster headache, but oral sumatriptan is too slow for acute attacks and is less effective than subcutaneous or intranasal formulations. Triptans also require caution in patients with significant cardiovascular disease.

Daily propranolol is used for migraine prophylaxis, not for aborting acute cluster headache attacks. The presentation is not typical of migraine because the attacks are brief, strictly unilateral, and associated with autonomic symptoms and agitation.

Intravenous metoclopramide and ketorolac are commonly used for migraine in the emergency department, but they are not first-line therapy for cluster headache. Ketorolac also has potential renal adverse effects, which is a concern in a patient with chronic kidney disease.

Oral amitriptyline is a preventive agent sometimes used for chronic headache syndromes, but it does not provide rapid relief of cluster headache attacks. It is not appropriate acute therapy for this patient’s current episodes.

questions.teaching_point: Cluster headache attacks are best aborted with high-flow oxygen or a rapid-acting triptan; oral preventives are used for prophylaxis, not acute relief.

questions.vignette: A 13-year-old girl is admitted for evaluation of a rapidly enlarging anterior neck mass. Her parents report that over the past 2 months she has developed intermittent hoarseness and a sensation of fullness when swallowing solids. She has no fever or sore throat. On exam, there is a firm, nontender nodule in the right thyroid lobe with several small, mobile cervical lymph nodes on the same side. Her history is notable for treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 4 with head and neck radiation. Thyroid function tests are normal.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.rationale: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most likely diagnosis. In children and adolescents, a painless thyroid nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy is concerning for thyroid malignancy, and prior head and neck radiation is a major risk factor. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer in pediatrics and often presents with regional lymph node involvement while thyroid function remains normal.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is an aggressive cancer seen almost exclusively in older adults and would be very unlikely in a pediatric patient.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma can present as a thyroid nodule, but it is less common in children and is more strongly associated with MEN2 and elevated calcitonin rather than prior radiation exposure and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Multinodular goiter usually causes diffuse thyroid enlargement rather than a firm solitary nodule with suspicious cervical lymph nodes, and it is not classically associated with radiation exposure or hoarseness.
Subacute thyroiditis typically causes a painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness and is often associated with thyrotoxic symptoms, which are not present here.

questions.teaching_point: In a child, a painless thyroid nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy—especially after neck radiation—strongly suggests papillary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD and chronic home oxygen use presents to the emergency department with sudden worsening shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain that began while he was resting. He is tachypneic and speaking in short phrases. Blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg, heart rate is 118/min, respiratory rate is 30/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on his usual 2 L/min nasal cannula. Exam shows decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance over the right hemithorax with mild tracheal deviation to the left. Bedside ultrasound shows absent lung sliding on the right. He remains anxious but is awake and mentating appropriately.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

answer_choices.text: Obtain an emergent chest CT to confirm the diagnosis before intervening
Administer high-flow oxygen and repeat a chest radiograph in 1 hour
Perform incentive spirometry and bronchodilator therapy
Perform needle decompression of the right chest followed by tube thoracostomy
Arrange urgent outpatient pulmonology follow-up for elective management

questions.rationale: This patient has a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax with signs concerning for tension physiology: severe COPD risk factor, acute pleuritic dyspnea, unilateral decreased breath sounds with hyperresonance, mild tracheal deviation, tachycardia, and borderline hypotension. In a clinically unstable patient, the immediate priority is decompression rather than waiting for confirmatory imaging. Needle decompression is the rapid temporizing measure, followed by definitive chest tube placement.

distractor_rationales.explanation: CT can define the extent of pneumothorax, but imaging should not delay treatment when tension pneumothorax is suspected and the patient is hemodynamically tenuous.
Supplemental oxygen may help a stable small pneumothorax resolve faster, but observation is inappropriate here because he has acute instability and exam findings suggesting tension physiology.
Incentive spirometry and bronchodilators do not treat a pneumothorax. This patient needs immediate pleural decompression, not supportive therapy alone.
Outpatient follow-up is unsafe in a patient with an acute secondary pneumothorax and possible tension features; this is an emergency requiring immediate intervention.

questions.teaching_point: Suspected tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis—do not wait for imaging; decompress immediately and then place a chest tube.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 2 days of worsening shortness of breath and pleuritic chest discomfort after a recent pericarditis diagnosis treated as an outpatient. He is now lightheaded when sitting up, and his blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg, heart rate 122/min, and respiratory rate 24/min. On examination, his neck veins are distended, heart sounds are muffled, and there is a narrow pulse pressure. Bedside assessment suggests an accumulated pericardial effusion, and tamponade physiology is suspected.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the most appropriate to confirm the suspected condition and guide immediate management?

answer_choices.text: Computed tomography angiography of the chest

questions.rationale: Transthoracic echocardiography is the best diagnostic study for suspected cardiac tamponade because it rapidly identifies a pericardial effusion and can demonstrate hemodynamic compromise such as right atrial or right ventricular diastolic collapse, respiratory variation in filling, and impaired cardiac output. It is the most useful bedside test to confirm tamponade physiology and guide urgent pericardiocentesis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Electrocardiography may show low voltage or electrical alternans in tamponade, but it cannot confirm the diagnosis or define the degree of hemodynamic compromise.
Serial troponin measurements may help evaluate myocardial injury, but they do not assess pericardial fluid or hemodynamic compromise and would delay the correct diagnostic approach.
Chest radiography may show an enlarged cardiac silhouette with a large effusion, but it cannot confirm tamponade physiology or reliably guide urgent intervention.
CT angiography is not the preferred initial study in an unstable patient with suspected tamponade; it is slower and does not provide the immediate hemodynamic information that echocardiography does.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected cardiac tamponade, transthoracic echocardiography is the key diagnostic study because it confirms effusion and shows hemodynamic effects that require urgent drainage.

questions.vignette: A 49-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a progressively worsening headache and blurred peripheral vision over the past 8 months. He also reports that his wedding ring no longer fits, his shoe size has increased, and his wife says his voice has become deeper and he snores loudly. He has had increased sweating and joint stiffness but no fever or weight loss. Examination shows coarse facial features, widened spacing between the teeth, enlarged hands and feet, and bitemporal visual field loss on confrontation testing.
questions.lead_in: Which finding on history and physical examination is most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Enlargement of the jaw, hands, and feet with soft tissue swelling
Violaceous abdominal striae, proximal muscle weakness, and easy bruising
Goiter with exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema
Periorbital edema, slowed reflexes, and dry coarse skin
Heat intolerance, tremor, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland

questions.rationale: Acromegaly results from excess growth hormone in adulthood, usually from a pituitary adenoma, and causes gradual enlargement of acral and facial structures. Classic history and physical findings include enlarged hands and feet, prognathism/coarse facial features, soft tissue swelling, deepened voice, sweating, and visual field defects from pituitary mass effect.

distractor_rationales.explanation: This pattern suggests Cushing syndrome. While cortisol excess can cause proximal weakness and bruising, it does not produce the characteristic enlargement of the hands, feet, and jaw or the mass-effect visual symptoms described.

This is most consistent with Graves disease. Exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema are thyroid-related findings and do not fit the chronic somatic enlargement, coarse facial features, and pituitary mass effect of acromegaly.

These are typical features of hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism can cause fatigue, dry skin, and delayed reflexes, but it does not cause the progressive acral enlargement and facial coarsening seen here.

These findings are more consistent with hyperthyroidism, not acromegaly. Although thyroid disease can cause goiter and tremor, it does not explain progressive enlargement of the hands, feet, and jaw or bitemporal visual field loss.

questions.teaching_point: Acromegaly is suggested by progressive enlargement of the hands, feet, and facial bones plus symptoms from pituitary mass effect such as headaches and bitemporal hemianopsia.

questions.vignette: A 61-year-old postmenopausal woman comes to the emergency department for worsening abdominal bloating and early satiety for 3 months. She reports intermittent pelvic discomfort, decreased appetite, and needing to urinate more often. Over the past 2 weeks, she has had increasing shortness of breath when lying flat. She has no fever, vomiting, or vaginal bleeding. She had menopause at age 52 and has no history of hormone therapy. Examination shows a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a nontender, irregular pelvic mass on bimanual examination. Chest radiograph shows a moderate right-sided pleural effusion.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: This patient has a classic constellation concerning for advanced epithelial ovarian carcinoma: postmenopausal status, progressive bloating/early satiety, urinary frequency, adnexal/pelvic mass, ascites, and pleural effusion. Ovarian cancer often presents with vague, progressive abdominal and pelvic symptoms and may be discovered late because early disease is nonspecific.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Uterine leiomyomas can cause bulk symptoms and abnormal bleeding, but they are less likely to present for the first time after menopause with ascites, pleural effusion, and a progressive pelvic mass suspicious for malignancy.

Pelvic inflammatory disease usually causes acute pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, fever, and vaginal discharge in sexually active patients; it does not fit this chronic, progressive, postmenopausal presentation with ascites and pleural effusion.

Ovarian torsion causes sudden, severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea and vomiting, often in the setting of an ovarian cyst or mass. The gradual onset of symptoms over months argues against torsion.

Endometrial hyperplasia typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, especially in perimenopausal or postmenopausal patients, rather than abdominal distention, early satiety, and an adnexal mass.

questions.teaching_point: In a postmenopausal patient, progressive bloating, early satiety, ascites, and an adnexal mass should strongly raise concern for epithelial ovarian cancer.

questions.vignette: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother after collapsing during soccer practice. She reports several months of recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food followed by self-induced vomiting, but she has been avoiding discussing it. Over the past week she has had worsening weakness and intermittent palpitations. She appears thin but is not cachectic. Vitals: T 36.8 C, HR 118/min, BP 96/62 mm Hg, RR 18/min. Exam shows dry mucous membranes and mild parotid enlargement. An initial ECG shows flattened T waves and a prolonged QT interval. Serum studies are ordered.
questions.lead_in: Which additional laboratory abnormality is most likely to be present in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has bulimia nervosa with recurrent self-induced vomiting. Repeated vomiting causes loss of gastric hydrogen and chloride, producing metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion and renal potassium losses commonly lead to hypokalemia, which explains the flattened T waves, prolonged QT interval, weakness, palpitations, and syncope/collapse. Parotid enlargement is a classic physical finding in chronic purging.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hyponatremia with elevated creatine kinase can occur with water intoxication or rhabdomyolysis, but it is not the characteristic acid-base and electrolyte pattern caused by recurrent self-induced vomiting.

Hypocalcemia with prolonged PT/INR is not the expected pattern in bulimia nervosa with vomiting. Prolonged PT/INR suggests vitamin K deficiency, liver dysfunction, or anticoagulant use, which do not fit this presentation.

A normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia is more typical of diarrhea or laxative abuse, not vomiting. Vomiting causes loss of acid and therefore leads to metabolic alkalosis, not acidosis.
Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis is more consistent with renal failure, diabetic ketoacidosis, or type 4 renal tubular acidosis, not purging behavior from bulimia nervosa.

questions.teaching_point: Bulimia nervosa with self-induced vomiting commonly causes hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and may produce ECG changes and dangerous arrhythmias.

questions.vignette: A 14-year-old girl with a 6-month history of systemic lupus erythematosus presents for follow-up after starting hydroxychloroquine and a low-dose prednisone taper 3 months ago. She continues to have morning hand stiffness, fatigue, and recurrent painless swelling of both knees. She has no fever, pleuritic pain, oral ulcers, rash flare, or neuropsychiatric symptoms. Exam shows tender swelling of the wrists and knees without deformity. Vital signs are normal, and urine dipstick remains negative for protein and blood. Her mother asks what treatment is most appropriate to better control the ongoing joint inflammation while trying to minimize long-term steroid exposure.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate next therapeutic step?

answer_choices.text: Begin daily NSAID monotherapy and stop hydroxychloroquine
Increase the prednisone dose and continue it long term
Add methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent

questions.rationale: This patient has persistent inflammatory arthritis from systemic lupus erythematosus despite hydroxychloroquine and a tapering course of prednisone, but she has no evidence of organ-threatening disease. For ongoing musculoskeletal lupus activity, a steroid-sparing immunosuppressive agent such as methotrexate is an appropriate next step to improve control and reduce the need for chronic glucocorticoids. Hydroxychloroquine is usually continued as baseline therapy unless there is a contraindication or toxicity.

distractor_rationales.explanation: NSAIDs can help mild joint pain, but monotherapy would be inadequate for persistent inflammatory lupus arthritis in a patient who has already needed disease-modifying treatment, and hydroxychloroquine should generally be continued.

Increasing prednisone may temporarily improve symptoms, but long-term glucocorticoid therapy is avoided when possible because of substantial toxicity; a steroid-sparing agent is preferred for persistent arthritis.
Mycophenolate mofetil is more commonly used for lupus nephritis or other significant organ involvement rather than isolated persistent arthritis.
High-dose cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe organ-threatening lupus, such as nephritis or serious central nervous system disease, which is not present here.

questions.teaching_point: Persistent non–organ-threatening lupus arthritis despite hydroxychloroquine and a steroid taper is often managed by adding a steroid-sparing agent such as methotrexate while minimizing chronic glucocorticoid exposure.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old man is admitted for treatment of community-acquired pneumonia. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus managed at home with metformin and glipizide. He has been eating poorly since admission, and his bedside glucose values over the past 12 hours have ranged from 210 to 286 mg/dL. He is hemodynamically stable, alert, and able to take oral medications. There is no history of diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.
questions.lead_in: Which inpatient glucose-lowering strategy is most appropriate for this patient?

answer_choices.text: Begin an insulin infusion with hourly glucose monitoring
Continue his outpatient oral diabetes medications only
Hold all glucose-lowering treatment until he resumes a regular diet
Start basal insulin plus correctional subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
Start a correctional insulin scale with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin

questions.rationale: For a noncritically ill hospitalized adult with type 2 diabetes, persistent hyperglycemia, and poor oral intake, the preferred inpatient regimen is scheduled insulin that includes basal insulin plus correctional rapid-acting insulin. This approach provides background insulin coverage while allowing additional insulin for stress-related hyperglycemia and avoids relying on oral agents during acute illness. Correction-only insulin is less effective when hyperglycemia is persistent, whereas an insulin infusion is reserved for critically ill patients or those with diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state.

distractor_rationales.explanation: An insulin infusion is generally reserved for critically ill patients or for diabetic ketoacidosis/hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, neither of which is present here.

Oral agents alone are generally not the preferred inpatient approach in acutely ill patients because insulin is easier to titrate and safer with variable intake; sulfonylureas also increase hypoglycemia risk when meals are inconsistent.
Hyperglycemia should not be left untreated while the patient is hospitalized, even if oral intake is poor.

Correctional insulin alone may be used temporarily in selected patients with mild, transient hyperglycemia, but this patient has persistent glucose elevations >180 mg/dL, so a basal-containing regimen is preferred.

questions.teaching_point: In stable non-ICU inpatients with type 2 diabetes and persistent hyperglycemia, use a basal-containing insulin regimen rather than correction-only insulin, especially when oral intake is poor.

questions.content_area: Eyes, ears, nose, oral cavity, and throat (EENOT)
questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman comes to clinic for a routine follow-up. She has noticed that newspaper print seems more difficult to read over the past several months, especially in dim light, and she sometimes sees a blurry spot in the center of her vision when looking directly at faces. She has a 40-pack-year smoking history and takes no eye medications. Visual acuity is 20/30 in both eyes with correction. Funduscopic examination shows multiple small yellow deposits beneath the retina.
questions.lead_in: Which counseling point is most appropriate to help reduce this patient’s risk of progression?

answer_choices.text: Recommend smoking cessation and daily self-monitoring of vision with an Amsler grid
Recommend referral for cataract surgery to improve her central vision
Reassure her that no lifestyle changes affect the course of this condition
Start topical timolol to lower intraocular pressure and prevent central vision loss
Advise that daily oral vitamin A supplementation will prevent further retinal damage

questions.rationale: This patient has age-related macular degeneration, likely the dry form, given gradual central vision loss and drusen (small yellow subretinal deposits). The most appropriate counseling to reduce risk of progression is smoking cessation, which is a major modifiable risk factor, along with home monitoring of central vision using an Amsler grid to detect new distortion or scotomas early and prompt ophthalmology follow-up.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cataract surgery treats lens opacity, not age-related macular degeneration or drusen. Although cataracts can also cause blurred vision, the funduscopic findings here point to macular degeneration.
Lifestyle changes do affect the course of age-related macular degeneration; smoking cessation and vision self-monitoring are important counseling measures.
Topical timolol is used for glaucoma-related elevated intraocular pressure; it does not prevent progression of age-related macular degeneration.
Vitamin A supplementation does not prevent progression of age-related macular degeneration and is not recommended for this purpose.

questions.teaching_point: For age-related macular degeneration, smoking cessation and self-monitoring with an Amsler grid are key counseling measures to help limit progression and detect worsening early.

questions.vignette: A 39-year-old man is admitted after waking from sleep with a severe, unilateral pain centered behind his right eye. He is pacing the room and cannot lie still. He has had 4 similar attacks over the past week, each lasting about 45 minutes and occurring at roughly the same time each night. During the attacks, his right eye becomes red and tears, and his right nostril runs. Neurologic examination between episodes is normal. Brain MRI performed before admission was unrevealing. He has a history of heavy tobacco use and says acetaminophen and oral ibuprofen have not helped his current pain.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate treatment to abort his current headache attack?
questions.rationale: This patient has classic cluster headache with unilateral periorbital pain, autonomic symptoms, short recurrent attacks, and agitation during episodes. In the inpatient setting, the best immediate abortive therapy is high-flow oxygen via nonrebreather mask, which can rapidly terminate an acute cluster headache attack and is safe to use while other therapies are considered.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Verapamil is a first-line preventive medication for cluster headache, but it requires ongoing use and dose titration; it is not useful for immediate relief of an active attack.

Subcutaneous sumatriptan is also an effective abortive treatment for cluster headache, but high-flow oxygen is a preferred immediate option in a hospitalized patient because it acts quickly and avoids triptan-related cardiovascular concerns.

Oral prednisone may be used as a short transitional therapy to reduce attack frequency while preventive treatment is initiated, but it is not the most appropriate immediate abortive therapy for the current episode.
Topiramate is used for prevention in some patients with recurrent headaches, but it does not abort an acute cluster headache attack and would not relieve his current pain promptly.

questions.teaching_point: Acute cluster headache is best aborted with high-flow oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan; preventive agents such as verapamil do not relieve an ongoing attack.

questions.vignette: A 7-year-old boy is brought to clinic for several days of easy bruising and a few scattered nosebleeds. He recently recovered from an upper respiratory infection. He is afebrile, playful, and has no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Exam shows multiple petechiae on the lower extremities and ecchymoses on the arms. CBC shows hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, WBC 7,400/µL, and platelets 18,000/µL; peripheral smear otherwise appears normal. The child’s bleeding is limited to skin findings and brief epistaxis that stops with pressure.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

answer_choices.text: Observe closely with outpatient follow-up and bleeding precautions

questions.rationale: This child has typical newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia with isolated thrombocytopenia, recent viral illness, normal hemoglobin and WBC count, and only minor mucocutaneous bleeding. In an otherwise well child with no significant bleeding, first-line management is observation with counseling on bleeding precautions and close follow-up rather than immediate medication or invasive testing.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Bone marrow aspiration is not routinely needed in a child with classic isolated thrombocytopenia and a normal exam; it is considered when findings are atypical or there are signs suggesting an alternative marrow disorder.

Platelet transfusion is reserved for life-threatening hemorrhage or urgent procedures because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed in immune thrombocytopenia and are not indicated for mild outpatient bleeding.

Corticosteroids can be used for children with more significant mucosal bleeding or when treatment is needed, but they are not necessary as the initial step for a stable child with minor bleeding only.
IVIG is appropriate when a rapid platelet rise is needed due to significant bleeding or high-risk circumstances, but this child’s presentation is mild enough that observation is preferred.

questions.teaching_point: In pediatric immune thrombocytopenia with isolated thrombocytopenia and only minor bleeding, observation with bleeding precautions is often the best initial management.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman presents to the clinic for recurrent headaches. She reports 2 to 3 attacks per month over the past year. The headaches are unilateral, throbbing, and associated with nausea and sensitivity to light. They usually last 8 to 24 hours and improve only after she lies down in a dark room. She has no focal neurologic deficits and a normal neurologic examination. She has tried acetaminophen and ibuprofen at the onset of symptoms with only partial relief. Her medical history includes mild intermittent asthma and seasonal allergies. She is not pregnant and uses a levonorgestrel IUD.
questions.lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate next step for abortive treatment of her headaches?
questions.rationale: Oral sumatriptan is an appropriate migraine abortive therapy for a patient with recurrent moderate-to-severe migraine attacks that are not adequately relieved by NSAIDs. Triptans are first-line options for acute treatment when taken early in an attack and are effective for associated nausea and photophobia. Her normal neurologic examination and typical migraine features support outpatient abortive therapy rather than further urgent evaluation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Propranolol is used for migraine prevention, not abortive treatment. It would not provide rapid relief during an active headache and is also less desirable in a patient with asthma because it can provoke bronchospasm.
Topiramate is another preventive medication for migraine. It may reduce future attack frequency but is not used to treat an established acute headache episode.

Ergotamine/caffeine can be used for acute migraine in selected patients, but it is generally not preferred over triptans because of greater adverse effects and drug interaction concerns. Sumatriptan is a better first-line abortive option here.

Prednisone is not standard abortive therapy for uncomplicated migraine. Corticosteroids may occasionally be used in refractory prolonged attacks or status migrainosus, but they are not the best next step for a typical outpatient migraine attack.

questions.teaching_point: Triptans are first-line abortive therapy for moderate migraine attacks when NSAIDs are insufficient; preventive agents such as propranolol and topiramate are used to reduce attack frequency, not to stop an active headache.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man is admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. He has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for 10 years and takes metformin and glipizide at home. Over the past 2 days, he has had poor oral intake because of nausea and fever. This morning, he is noted to be diaphoretic and shaky. He is alert and oriented but appears anxious. Vital signs are temperature 38.1 C, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, pulse 108/min, and respirations 18/min. A bedside glucose measurement is 54 mg/dL.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding is most consistent with symptomatic hypoglycemia in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Dry mucous membranes and sunken eyes

questions.rationale: Symptomatic hypoglycemia activates the sympathetic nervous system and commonly causes tremor, diaphoresis, anxiety, palpitations, and cool, clammy skin. In this patient, poor oral intake while taking glipizide increases the risk of hypoglycemia, and the low bedside glucose confirms the diagnosis. Tremor and cool, clammy skin are therefore the best additional physical findings supporting symptomatic hypoglycemia.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Asterixis and fetor hepaticus are findings associated with hepatic encephalopathy, not the adrenergic response to low blood glucose.
Dry mucous membranes and sunken eyes suggest dehydration or hypovolemia rather than symptomatic hypoglycemia.
Orthostatic hypotension and tachypnea are more suggestive of volume depletion, sepsis, or other systemic illness and are not classic findings of hypoglycemia.
Bounding pulses and flushed skin are more consistent with fever, vasodilation, or hyperthyroidism than with hypoglycemia.

questions.teaching_point: In hospitalized adults with type 2 diabetes, poor oral intake plus sulfonylurea use can precipitate hypoglycemia, which typically produces adrenergic signs such as tremor, diaphoresis, anxiety, and cool clammy skin.

questions.vignette: A 9-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes is brought to a primary care clinic by his mother because he was "acting strange" at school. He skipped breakfast after taking his usual morning insulin dose and then developed sweating, tremor, and difficulty concentrating during math class. A school nurse checked his capillary glucose and it was 54 mg/dL. He is awake, able to swallow, and has no vomiting. His mother asks what the school should do first if this happens again.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action for the school to take as the first step in its diabetes care plan when this occurs and the child is awake and able to swallow?

answer_choices.text: Give 15 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck blood glucose in 15 minutes
Send the child to the nurse’s office to rest and drink water before deciding whether to treat
Give a high-protein snack such as cheese or peanut butter crackers only
Delay treatment until a repeat fingerstick confirms the low glucose

questions.rationale: This child has symptomatic hypoglycemia and is awake with an intact ability to swallow, so the appropriate immediate management is a rapid source of carbohydrate, commonly the 15-15 rule: give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the blood glucose in 15 minutes. Fast-acting carbohydrate can include glucose tablets, juice, or regular soda. This quickly raises blood glucose and helps prevent progression to neuroglycopenic symptoms. In a school setting, this is the first step for a conscious child who can safely take oral treatment.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Glucagon is reserved for severe hypoglycemia when the patient cannot safely take oral carbohydrate or is unconscious or unresponsive.
Rest and water do not correct low glucose. The child needs immediate carbohydrate treatment, not observation alone.
Protein or fat alone is too slow to correct acute hypoglycemia; a fast-acting carbohydrate is needed first.
Treatment should not be delayed for repeat testing when hypoglycemia is already documented and the child is symptomatic.

questions.teaching_point: Awake children with symptomatic hypoglycemia should receive 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and have glucose rechecked in 15 minutes; glucagon is for severe cases when oral intake is not possible.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic for chronic low back discomfort that is worse after standing for long periods. She has noticed that her clothes hang unevenly and that she “leans to one side” when she is tired. On physical examination, one shoulder sits higher than the other, the right scapula is more prominent than the left, and there is a visible lateral curvature of the spine when viewed from behind. She has no fever, leg weakness, or bowel or bladder symptoms.
questions.lead_in: Which physical examination finding is most consistent with scoliosis?

answer_choices.text: Inability to stand upright due to hip flexion contracture
Midline spinal tenderness with pain on vertebral percussion
Lateral curvature of the spine with asymmetric shoulder height
Loss of lumbar lordosis with bilateral paraspinal spasm
Kyphotic thoracic curvature with a fixed forward stoop

questions.rationale: Scoliosis is characterized by a lateral curvature of the spine, often accompanied by asymmetric shoulder or scapular height on inspection. In older adults, it may be noticed incidentally because of uneven posture or clothing asymmetry during an outpatient exam.

distractor_rationales.explanation: An inability to stand upright due to hip flexion contracture is more consistent with a hip or flexor contracture problem, not a spinal curvature deformity.
Midline spinal tenderness with percussion pain suggests vertebral compression fracture, osteomyelitis, or malignancy rather than scoliosis.
Loss of lumbar lordosis with paraspinal spasm is more typical of acute lumbar strain or muscle spasm and does not specifically indicate scoliosis.
A fixed forward thoracic stoop describes kyphosis, which is a different spinal curvature abnormality than scoliosis.

questions.teaching_point: Scoliosis is recognized on exam by lateral spinal curvature and asymmetric shoulder, scapular, or waistline height.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is admitted for worsening fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort, and new-onset hyperglycemia. He has a bronze-gray skin tone and mild hepatomegaly on examination. Laboratory studies show ferritin 1,480 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 78%, and elevated AST/ALT. HFE gene testing later confirms hereditary hemochromatosis. He is hemodynamically stable and has no evidence of active bleeding or severe anemia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention to reduce this patient’s risk of end-organ damage?

answer_choices.text: Administer packed red blood cell transfusion

questions.rationale: Therapeutic phlebotomy is first-line treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis in a stable patient with iron overload. Regular removal of blood decreases total body iron stores and helps prevent progression to cirrhosis, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, and arthropathy. This patient has confirmed iron overload and is stable enough for phlebotomy.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Packed red blood cell transfusion would worsen iron overload and is inappropriate in a stable patient without symptomatic anemia or active hemorrhage.
Epoetin alfa stimulates erythropoiesis and can increase iron utilization, but it does not remove excess iron and is not a treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis.

Deferoxamine is an iron chelator used mainly for secondary iron overload or when phlebotomy is not feasible, such as in patients with severe anemia. It is not first-line for uncomplicated hereditary hemochromatosis.
Oral iron supplementation would increase iron burden and aggravate tissue deposition, making end-organ injury more likely.

questions.teaching_point: Stable hereditary hemochromatosis is treated with therapeutic phlebotomy to lower iron stores and prevent organ damage.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old woman comes to an outpatient psychiatry visit after being referred by her primary care clinician for repeated relationship conflicts and "mood swings." She reports feeling empty and lonely since adolescence and says her emotions can shift from "fine" to "devastated" within minutes after she perceives criticism. Over the past year, she has had several intense but short-lived romantic relationships that ended after she became convinced her partners would abandon her. She has a history of cutting her forearms during arguments and says she has threatened self-harm when she felt ignored. During the interview, she alternates between idealizing the clinician as the only person who "finally understands" her and angrily insisting that she is being judged. She denies sustained periods of elevated energy, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity, hallucinations, or fixed paranoid beliefs.
questions.lead_in: Which additional history finding would most strongly support the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Persistent anhedonia, early morning awakening, and psychomotor slowing for 2 months
Recurrent intrusive memories and nightmares beginning after a motor vehicle accident
Distinct episodes of elevated mood, pressured speech, and increased goal-directed activity lasting 1 week
Sustained periods of elevated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, and talkativeness recurring every few months
A long-standing pattern of unstable self-image and impulsive spending when distressed

questions.rationale:
Borderline personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in relationships, self-image, and affect, along with marked impulsivity, fear of abandonment, and recurrent self-harm or suicidal behaviors. A long-standing pattern of unstable self-image with impulsive spending when distressed is a classic additional feature that strongly supports this diagnosis.

Why the other choices are incorrect:
- Persistent anhedonia, early morning awakening, and psychomotor slowing for 2 months point to major depressive disorder.
- Distinct episodes of elevated mood, pressured speech, and increased goal-directed activity lasting 1 week are characteristic of mania, supporting bipolar I disorder.
- Recurrent intrusive memories and nightmares after a traumatic event are more consistent with posttraumatic stress disorder.
- Sustained periods of elevated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, and talkativeness recurring every few months are more consistent with bipolar spectrum illness than borderline personality disorder, which typically causes rapid, stress-reactive mood shifts rather than discrete recurrent hypomanic/manic episodes.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Persistent anhedonia, early morning awakening, and psychomotor slowing for 2 months point toward major depressive disorder. Depressive symptoms can coexist with borderline personality disorder, but this pattern does not best support the diagnosis asked here.
