questions.rationale: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head classically causes progressive groin or hip pain, pain with weight-bearing, and decreased hip range of motion, especially internal rotation. Important risk factors include chronic corticosteroid use and heavy alcohol intake. This patient's presentation is most consistent with avascular necrosis of the proximal femur.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Hip osteoarthritis can cause groin pain and stiffness, but the pain pattern usually improves with rest and is associated with degenerative changes rather than the classic risk factors and exam findings of avascular necrosis.
Lumbar radiculopathy can cause low back pain that radiates below the knee and a positive straight-leg raise, which points to nerve root irritation rather than primary hip joint disease.

Femoroacetabular impingement or a labral tear can cause groin pain and pain with hip flexion and internal rotation, often with clicking, but it is less associated with the key risk factors of corticosteroid use and heavy alcohol intake.
Greater trochanteric pain syndrome typically causes lateral hip pain with focal tenderness over the greater trochanter, not progressive groin pain and loss of internal rotation.

questions.teaching_point: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head should be suspected in adults with groin pain, limited hip internal rotation, and risk factors such as corticosteroid use or heavy alcohol consumption.

questions.vignette: A 46-year-old woman is referred to an outpatient clinic after a thyroid nodule was found incidentally on carotid ultrasound. She has no compressive symptoms. Fine-needle aspiration of the 1.8-cm left thyroid nodule shows papillary thyroid carcinoma. Her TSH is normal, and neck ultrasound shows no suspicious cervical lymph nodes. She is anxious and asks whether there are any “special tests” or treatments she should receive before surgery. She has no family history of thyroid cancer and no history of radiation exposure.
questions.lead_in: Which preoperative counseling point is most appropriate?

answer_choices.text: Cross-sectional imaging of the neck and chest is required in all patients before thyroid surgery to rule out metastatic disease
Routine preoperative laryngoscopy is recommended for all patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma to guide the extent of surgery
No additional thyroid-specific routine preoperative testing is usually needed; the next step is surgical referral with counseling about treatment options, prognosis, and postoperative follow-up
Serum calcitonin should be measured in every patient because it determines whether total thyroidectomy is required
Routine radioactive iodine therapy should be given before surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence

questions.rationale: In a patient with biopsy-proven papillary thyroid carcinoma, normal thyroid function, and no clinical or ultrasound evidence of nodal disease or invasive features, no special thyroid-cancer–specific preoperative test is routinely required. Appropriate counseling focuses on referral for surgery, discussion of the likely need for thyroidectomy based on tumor and patient factors, and postoperative surveillance. Additional testing such as laryngoscopy, cross-sectional imaging, calcitonin testing, or radioactive iodine is reserved for selected situations rather than used routinely in all patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma.

distractor_rationales.explanation: CT or other cross-sectional imaging is not routine for every patient with papillary thyroid carcinoma. It is used when there is suspicion for locally invasive disease, bulky nodal disease, or distant spread based on exam or ultrasound findings.

Preoperative laryngoscopy is not required for all patients. It is considered when there is hoarseness, prior neck surgery, known vocal cord dysfunction, invasive disease, or other concerns about recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement.
Calcitonin is a marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma, not papillary thyroid carcinoma. It is not routinely needed in this setting and does not determine the need for total thyroidectomy here.
Radioactive iodine is not given before surgery. It may be used after thyroidectomy in selected patients, depending on postoperative risk stratification and pathology.

questions.teaching_point: For biopsy-proven papillary thyroid carcinoma without high-risk features, routine thyroid-cancer–specific preoperative testing is usually unnecessary; management centers on surgical referral and postoperative risk-based follow-up.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes to clinic because of recurrent headaches for the past year. The headaches occur 3 to 4 times per month, last 8 to 12 hours, and are associated with nausea, photophobia, and unilateral throbbing pain. She has no focal neurologic deficits and her neurologic examination is normal. She has been taking ibuprofen at the onset of symptoms with only partial relief. Her medical history is notable for asthma and depression, and she uses an albuterol inhaler as needed and sertraline daily. She asks for a medication that can better control her acute migraine attacks.
questions.lead_in: Which medication is the best choice for acute treatment of her migraine attacks?
questions.rationale: Sumatriptan is an appropriate first-line abortive therapy for moderate to severe migraine attacks in an adult without contraindications. It is specifically useful when NSAIDs provide inadequate relief and can reduce headache pain and associated nausea/photophobia when taken early in the attack.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Topiramate is a preventive medication for recurrent migraines. It is not used for rapid relief of an ongoing migraine episode.
Propranolol is used for migraine prophylaxis, not acute abortive treatment. It is also a poor choice in a patient with asthma because it can worsen bronchospasm.

Metoclopramide can be helpful as an adjunct for migraine-associated nausea or in some emergency settings, but it is not the best standalone outpatient abortive therapy compared with a triptan for this presentation.
Amitriptyline can be effective for migraine prevention, especially when comorbid insomnia or tension features are present, but it does not treat an acute migraine attack.

questions.teaching_point: Triptans are preferred abortive agents for moderate to severe migraine attacks when NSAIDs are insufficient and there are no contraindications.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man comes to the outpatient clinic for intermittent episodes of palpitations and fatigue over the past 2 months. He reports that the episodes often begin suddenly and last for several hours before resolving spontaneously. He denies chest pain, syncope, or fever. His history includes hypertension and obesity. He drinks 3 to 4 alcoholic beverages most evenings. Vital signs are BP 134/78 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 14/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac examination shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no murmur. Lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding would be most consistent with this patient’s suspected arrhythmia?

answer_choices.text: Forceful apical impulse with a sustained left ventricular heave
Loud systolic murmur heard best at the apex radiating to the axilla
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound
Variable intensity of the first heart sound
Pulsus paradoxus with diminished heart sounds

questions.rationale: An irregularly irregular rhythm with episodic palpitations in an older adult is most consistent with atrial fibrillation. Because atrial contraction is absent and ventricular filling varies beat to beat, the intensity of S1 can vary on exam. This finding fits the expected hemodynamic consequences of atrial fibrillation and is a classic physical examination clue.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A forceful apical impulse with a sustained left ventricular heave is more consistent with left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic pressure overload, such as longstanding hypertension or aortic stenosis.
A loud apical systolic murmur radiating to the axilla suggests mitral regurgitation, which may coexist with atrial fibrillation but is not the best finding expected from the arrhythmia itself.
Fixed splitting of S2 is most characteristic of an atrial septal defect and is not a typical finding in atrial fibrillation.
Pulsus paradoxus with muffled heart sounds suggests pericardial tamponade or large pericardial effusion, not atrial fibrillation.

questions.teaching_point: Atrial fibrillation commonly causes an irregularly irregular pulse and variable S1 intensity due to inconsistent ventricular filling.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of intermittent tingling around his mouth and in both hands since this morning. He also reports painful cramping in his forearms after opening a jar and says his fingers seemed to curl inward when he was checking his blood pressure at home. Two weeks ago, he underwent a thyroidectomy for multinodular goiter. He has no fever, chest pain, or weakness. Vital signs are normal. On examination, his hand is held in a flexed, cramped posture that becomes more pronounced after a blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure for several minutes.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical finding is most consistent with this patient’s condition?

answer_choices.text: Facial muscle twitching when the area over the facial nerve is tapped
Resting tremor that decreases with intentional movement
Asterixis when the wrists are dorsiflexed
Unilateral ptosis with diplopia that worsens later in the day
Delayed relaxation of the deep tendon reflexes at the ankle

questions.rationale: This patient has symptomatic hypocalcemia, likely from post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism, suggested by perioral paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, and provoked hand contraction with blood pressure cuff inflation. A facial muscle twitch after tapping over the facial nerve is a classic sign of neuromuscular irritability seen with hypocalcemia.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A resting tremor that improves with movement suggests Parkinson disease and does not match the acute paresthesias and tetany of hypocalcemia.
Asterixis is a sign of metabolic encephalopathy such as hepatic or uremic disease and is not a typical physical finding of hypocalcemia.
Ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day are characteristic of myasthenia gravis, which causes fatigable weakness rather than painful carpopedal spasm.
Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes is more typical of hypothyroidism, not the neuromuscular irritability seen in hypocalcemia.

questions.teaching_point: Acute hypocalcemia causes neuromuscular irritability with perioral paresthesias, tetany, and signs such as facial twitching or carpopedal spasm.

questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD presents to a urgent care clinic with sudden right-sided chest pain and increased shortness of breath that began while he was resting at home 1 hour ago. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and uses home oxygen intermittently. Vital signs are blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, heart rate 104/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 89% on room air. On exam, he appears uncomfortable and has decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance over the right hemithorax. He is speaking in full sentences and has no tracheal deviation or jugular venous distention. An upright chest radiograph shows a moderate right-sided pneumothorax without mediastinal shift.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Administer supplemental oxygen and observe with repeat chest radiography in 4 to 6 hours
Provide supplemental oxygen and arrange immediate needle decompression
Admit for tube thoracostomy with small-bore catheter drainage
Discharge with return precautions and repeat examination in 48 hours
Perform needle aspiration as definitive outpatient treatment and discharge if symptoms improve

questions.rationale: This patient has a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax due to severe COPD. He is hemodynamically stable and does not have tension physiology, but secondary pneumothorax is less well tolerated than primary pneumothorax because of limited cardiopulmonary reserve. A moderate-sized secondary pneumothorax should be managed in the hospital with pleural drainage, such as tube thoracostomy with a small-bore catheter, rather than outpatient observation or discharge. Supplemental oxygen may be used as an adjunct, but definitive drainage and admission are the appropriate next steps.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Observation with supplemental oxygen may be reasonable for a very small, minimally symptomatic pneumothorax in a stable patient, but a moderate secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in severe COPD generally requires inpatient drainage.

Needle decompression is reserved for tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic instability or clear signs of tension physiology. This patient is stable and has no mediastinal shift or jugular venous distention.
Discharge is inappropriate because secondary spontaneous pneumothorax carries a higher risk of respiratory decompensation and usually needs hospital-based management.

Needle aspiration is more commonly considered for selected primary spontaneous pneumothoraces; in secondary spontaneous pneumothorax, definitive inpatient drainage is usually preferred, especially when the pneumothorax is moderate and the patient has COPD.

questions.teaching_point: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax in a patient with significant underlying lung disease usually requires hospital admission and pleural drainage rather than outpatient observation or discharge.

questions.vignette: A 78-year-old man follows up in clinic for hypertension. He has type 2 diabetes and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. His home blood pressure log over the past 2 weeks shows readings ranging from 148-156/78-84 mm Hg. In the office today, his blood pressure is 152/80 mm Hg on two measurements. He takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and reports no dizziness, falls, chest pain, or edema. Recent labs show creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, and estimated GFR 48 mL/min/1.73 m2, which are unchanged from baseline. He asks what should be done next to better control his blood pressure.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Switch lisinopril to losartan 100 mg daily

questions.rationale: He has persistent above-goal blood pressure despite a tolerated ACE inhibitor dose, and his kidney function and potassium are stable. The most appropriate next step is to maximize the ACE inhibitor dose before moving to additional agents. In a patient with diabetes and CKD, continuing renin-angiotensin system blockade is appropriate, and up-titration is preferred when the medication is tolerated and not yet maximized.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Spironolactone is typically reserved for resistant hypertension and carries a higher risk of hyperkalemia, especially in older adults with CKD who are already taking an ACE inhibitor.
Adding a thiazide diuretic can be appropriate later, but the first step here is to optimize the current ACE inhibitor dose because he is tolerating it and has room for titration.
Clonidine is not a preferred long-term outpatient agent for routine hypertension management in older adults because of adverse effects such as sedation, rebound hypertension, and orthostasis.
Switching from lisinopril to losartan would not improve blood pressure control meaningfully because both are renin-angiotensin system blockers; there is no indication of ACE inhibitor intolerance.

questions.teaching_point: If an older adult with CKD tolerates an ACE inhibitor but remains above goal, the next step is usually to titrate the current agent before adding higher-risk medications.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is seen in clinic for gradually worsening exertional shortness of breath and decreased exercise tolerance over the past 6 months. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. On exam, his carotid upstroke is delayed and diminished. A harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur is heard best at the right upper sternal border and radiates to the neck. Echocardiography shows a heavily calcified aortic valve with a mean gradient of 46 mm Hg and an aortic valve area of 0.8 cm2. His blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg, and he denies chest pain, syncope, or edema.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Start low-dose furosemide for symptom relief and reassess in 6 months
Initiate warfarin to reduce the risk of valve-associated thromboembolism
Begin amlodipine to lower afterload and improve cardiac output
Provide reassurance and repeat echocardiography in 1 year
Refer the patient for aortic valve replacement evaluation

questions.rationale: This patient has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis based on exertional dyspnea plus echocardiographic criteria (aortic valve area <1.0 cm2 and mean gradient >40 mm Hg). In adults with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis, the appropriate next step is referral for aortic valve replacement evaluation, usually with either surgical AVR or transcatheter AVR depending on surgical risk and anatomy. Medical therapy does not correct the fixed outflow obstruction and should not delay definitive treatment.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Diuretics may be used cautiously for congestion, but they do not address the underlying severe symptomatic valve obstruction and are not definitive management. This patient needs valve intervention evaluation, not watchful symptomatic treatment alone.

Warfarin is not indicated for native calcific aortic stenosis unless there is another reason for anticoagulation, such as atrial fibrillation or a mechanical valve. It does not improve the stenosis or prevent progression of symptoms.

Amlodipine does not treat severe aortic stenosis and vasodilation can be poorly tolerated in patients with fixed outflow obstruction. Lowering afterload does not relieve the mechanical obstruction at the valve.

Reassurance and surveillance are appropriate for mild or asymptomatic disease, not for symptomatic severe aortic stenosis. Delaying intervention in a symptomatic patient risks worsening heart failure, syncope, or sudden death.

questions.teaching_point: Symptomatic severe aortic stenosis requires prompt referral for aortic valve replacement; medications may temporarily palliate symptoms but do not replace definitive treatment.

questions.vignette: A 79-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease comes to clinic for worsening fatigue and reduced urine output over 3 days. He recently had a 3-day episode of vomiting and diarrhea that is now improving. His medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and ibuprofen twice daily for chronic knee pain. He is afebrile, blood pressure is 94/58 mm Hg, mucous membranes are dry, and orthostatic symptoms are present. Laboratory studies show creatinine increased from a baseline of 1.4 mg/dL to 2.3 mg/dL and BUN is elevated out of proportion to creatinine. Urinalysis is bland.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate outpatient management?

answer_choices.text: Order renal ultrasonography to evaluate for postrenal obstruction before making any medication changes
Continue current medications and repeat creatinine in 3 months
Begin oral prednisone for presumed acute interstitial nephritis
Start furosemide to increase urine output and correct the elevated creatinine
Stop lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and ibuprofen; encourage oral rehydration and arrange close follow-up renal function testing

questions.rationale: This patient most likely has prerenal acute kidney injury from volume depletion due to recent gastrointestinal losses, compounded by medications that reduce renal perfusion or worsen volume status (ACE inhibitor, thiazide diuretic, NSAID). The most appropriate immediate outpatient management is to stop the offending medications, restore volume with oral rehydration if he can maintain intake, and recheck kidney function promptly with close follow-up. His hypotension, dry mucous membranes, orthostatic symptoms, elevated BUN-to-creatinine ratio, and bland urinalysis support a hemodynamic, reversible process rather than intrinsic renal injury. Because he is symptomatic but not described as having severe altered mental status, pulmonary edema, or anuria, outpatient management with very close reassessment is reasonable in this stem.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Renal ultrasonography is useful when postrenal obstruction is suspected, but this presentation strongly suggests prerenal azotemia from volume depletion and nephrotoxic/hemodynamically active medications. Imaging should not delay immediate correction of the likely cause.
Waiting months is unsafe in an older patient with hypotension and rising creatinine; medication adjustment and timely reassessment are needed immediately.
Acute interstitial nephritis is not suggested by the history or bland urinalysis; corticosteroids are not indicated for uncomplicated prerenal AKI.
Loop diuretics do not treat prerenal AKI due to dehydration and may worsen renal hypoperfusion in a volume-depleted patient.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected prerenal AKI, the priority is to restore perfusion and stop nephrotoxic or hemodynamically adverse medications.

questions.vignette: A 14-year-old boy is admitted after collapsing during football practice on a hot, humid afternoon. He was confused on arrival and has remained intermittently agitated despite receiving cool IV fluids and active external cooling in the emergency department. His temperature peaked at 40.1 C (104.2 F). He has dark urine and diffuse muscle soreness. Laboratory studies show rising creatinine, elevated AST/ALT, and tea-colored urine on dipstick with few red blood cells on microscopy. The team is concerned about complications of his exertional heat illness.
questions.lead_in: Which additional laboratory study is most appropriate to monitor for a common renal complication of this condition?
questions.rationale: Exertional heat stroke can cause skeletal muscle breakdown with rhabdomyolysis, which is a major contributor to acute kidney injury in this setting. Creatine kinase is the best laboratory study to monitor for rhabdomyolysis severity and helps assess the risk of pigment-induced renal injury in a child with hyperthermia, muscle pain, dark urine, and rising creatinine.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Fractional excretion of sodium may help distinguish prerenal azotemia from intrinsic renal injury in some settings, but it does not directly monitor the muscle breakdown that commonly drives acute kidney injury after exertional heat stroke.
A 24-hour urine protein collection is used for evaluating chronic proteinuria or nephrotic-range protein loss, not for the acute evaluation of rhabdomyolysis-related kidney injury after heat stroke.
Urine eosinophils are sometimes considered in suspected acute interstitial nephritis, which is not suggested here. The presentation is more consistent with rhabdomyolysis causing pigment nephropathy.

Serum amylase is not a useful test for the expected renal complication of exertional heat stroke. Although pancreatitis can cause abdominal pain, it does not explain the dark urine, muscle soreness, and elevated creatinine in this scenario.

questions.teaching_point: In exertional heat stroke, check creatine kinase to assess for rhabdomyolysis, a key cause of acute kidney injury.

questions.vignette: A 9-year-old girl is brought to a pediatric primary care visit for fatigue and slowed school performance over the past 6 months. Her mother reports that the child has become less interested in soccer, is often constipated, and has gained 4.5 kg (10 lb) despite no major change in diet. She has also developed a hoarse voice and feels cold when classmates are comfortable. On exam, she has a dry, cool skin texture, mild periorbital puffiness, and a diffusely enlarged, nontender thyroid. Her blood pressure and heart rate are normal for age. A family member has autoimmune thyroid disease. The child has never been screened for thyroid disease and is otherwise healthy.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial evaluation for this child’s suspected hypothyroidism?

answer_choices.text: Order a thyroid ultrasound to evaluate the enlarged thyroid gland
Check antithyroid peroxidase antibodies before obtaining thyroid function tests
Reassure the family that these findings are normal in preadolescence
Start levothyroxine and repeat thyroid function tests in 6 months
Obtain a serum thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine level

questions.rationale: This child has multiple findings consistent with primary hypothyroidism, including fatigue, constipation, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, slowed school performance, hoarseness, periorbital puffiness, and diffuse goiter. The best initial evaluation is serum TSH with free T4. In primary hypothyroidism, TSH is typically elevated and free T4 is low. These studies confirm the diagnosis and help determine severity before treatment is started. Early recognition is important in children because untreated hypothyroidism can impair growth, development, and school performance.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Thyroid ultrasound is not the first test for suspected hypothyroidism with diffuse goiter. Imaging is generally reserved for a suspicious nodule, asymmetry, compressive symptoms, or concern for structural thyroid disease after biochemical evaluation.

Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies can support autoimmune thyroiditis, but they are not the initial test when hypothyroidism is suspected. Thyroid function tests should be obtained first to establish whether thyroid dysfunction is present.

These symptoms and examination findings are not normal developmental changes. Reassurance alone would miss a treatable endocrine disorder that can affect growth and neurocognitive development if left untreated.

Levothyroxine is the treatment for confirmed hypothyroidism, but thyroid function should be checked before starting therapy in a stable outpatient child. Empiric treatment without confirming the diagnosis is not appropriate here.

questions.teaching_point: In a child with symptoms and exam findings suggestive of hypothyroidism, the appropriate initial evaluation is serum TSH and free T4 before imaging, antibody testing, or treatment decisions.

questions.vignette: A 14-year-old boy is brought for follow-up of elevated blood pressure noted at three well visits over the past 6 months. He is asymptomatic. His BMI is at the 96th percentile, and he drinks several sugar-sweetened beverages daily. Blood pressure today is 144/92 mm Hg on repeated manual measurements using an appropriately sized cuff. Urinalysis is normal, serum creatinine is normal, and renal ultrasound is unremarkable. He has already completed a 3-month trial of weight loss counseling, reduced sodium intake, and increased physical activity, but his blood pressure remains in the stage 2 range on home readings and office measurements.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Order ambulatory blood pressure monitoring before treatment
Initiate antihypertensive medication therapy with a first-line agent
Reassure the family and continue lifestyle modification alone

questions.rationale: This adolescent has persistent stage 2 primary hypertension despite an adequate trial of lifestyle modification and has no evidence of secondary hypertension on initial evaluation. The next step is to start pharmacologic treatment with a first-line oral antihypertensive agent. In adolescents, acceptable first-line options include a long-acting calcium channel blocker, an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, or a thiazide diuretic, chosen based on comorbidities and contraindications. Because the vignette does not provide a condition that clearly favors one specific drug class over another, the best answer is to initiate antihypertensive medication therapy rather than continue observation or delay treatment for additional confirmation.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is helpful when the diagnosis is uncertain or white-coat hypertension is suspected. This patient already has repeated elevated manual office readings and elevated home measurements, so treatment should not be delayed for confirmation.

Hydrochlorothiazide is one acceptable first-line oral option, but it is not uniquely the best choice in this vignette. The question asks for the most appropriate next step, which is to start medication therapy; the specific class cannot be singled out from the information given.

Lifestyle modification alone is insufficient because the patient has persistent stage 2 hypertension after a reasonable trial of nonpharmacologic management. Ongoing observation without medication would leave him undertreated.

Intravenous antihypertensive therapy is reserved for hypertensive emergencies or severe symptomatic hypertension with acute end-organ injury. This asymptomatic outpatient with chronic stage 2 hypertension does not need emergent IV treatment.

questions.teaching_point: Persistent stage 2 primary hypertension in an adolescent after lifestyle modification warrants starting oral antihypertensive therapy; several drug classes are acceptable first-line options.

questions.vignette: A 13-year-old boy is admitted after 6 weeks of worsening morning headaches, nausea, and two episodes of vomiting. His parents also report declining school performance and increasing clumsiness when playing basketball. Today he had a brief generalized seizure at home. On examination, he is alert but slow to answer questions. Cranial nerves are intact, but he has mild left pronator drift and a subtle left homonymous visual field deficit. Head CT without contrast shows a heterogeneous right parietal mass with surrounding vasogenic edema and areas of necrosis; there is mild midline shift. MRI with contrast later shows an irregular ring-enhancing intra-axial lesion with central necrosis and surrounding infiltrative edema.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Glioblastoma is the most likely diagnosis. This adolescent has a rapidly progressive focal neurologic syndrome with signs of increased intracranial pressure, seizure, and a supratentorial intra-axial mass that is heterogeneous, necrotic, ring-enhancing, and associated with infiltrative edema and mass effect. In older children and adolescents, glioblastoma is an aggressive high-grade glioma that can present as a lobar mass with focal deficits and seizures. Although modern pediatric neuropathology may further classify some tumors as diffuse pediatric-type high-grade glioma, the clinical-imaging pattern here is most consistent with glioblastoma in this item.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Diffuse midline glioma arises in midline structures such as the pons, thalamus, or spinal cord, so it would be expected to produce brainstem or deep gray matter findings rather than a right parietal lobar lesion with homonymous visual field loss.

Medulloblastoma most often arises in the cerebellum and typically causes gait ataxia, truncal instability, and obstructive hydrocephalus rather than a lobar parietal mass with a focal weakness and visual field deficit.

Pilocytic astrocytoma is usually a slower-growing, well-circumscribed tumor in younger children, commonly in the posterior fossa, and classically appears cystic with a mural nodule rather than as an infiltrative necrotic ring-enhancing mass.

Ependymoma typically arises from the ventricular system, especially the fourth ventricle in children, and more often causes hydrocephalus or signs of posterior fossa involvement than a parietal intra-axial necrotic mass.

questions.teaching_point: In an older child or adolescent, a rapidly progressive supratentorial necrotic ring-enhancing mass with seizure and focal deficits is most concerning for a high-grade glioma such as glioblastoma.

questions.vignette: A 14-year-old boy is admitted for evaluation of progressive headaches over the past 8 months. His parents report that his shoes and gloves no longer fit and that he has become noticeably taller than his classmates over the past year. On examination, he has coarse facial features, frontal bossing, widened spacing between his teeth, enlarged hands and feet, and delayed pubertal development compared with peers. His blood pressure is mildly elevated.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Thin extremities with proximal muscle weakness and purple abdominal striae
Exophthalmos with a diffusely enlarged, nontender thyroid gland
Moon facies with central obesity and multiple ecchymoses
Hyperpigmentation of the skin and salt-craving behavior

questions.rationale: This adolescent has excess growth hormone starting before epiphyseal closure, causing gigantism with acromegaloid features such as accelerated linear growth, coarse facial features, and enlarged hands and feet. A pituitary somatotroph adenoma can also enlarge the sella and compress the optic chiasm, producing bitemporal hemianopsia. Headache supports a pituitary mass lesion.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Thin extremities, proximal muscle weakness, and purple striae are classic for Cushing syndrome and are not the expected findings here.
Exophthalmos with a diffuse, nontender goiter suggests Graves disease, which does not explain the overgrowth and acral enlargement.
Moon facies, central obesity, and easy bruising are features of Cushing syndrome, not growth hormone excess.
Hyperpigmentation and salt craving are associated with primary adrenal insufficiency, which would not cause accelerated growth or coarse facial features.

questions.teaching_point: In children and adolescents, excess growth hormone before epiphyseal closure causes gigantism with acromegaloid features, and pituitary mass effect can cause bitemporal hemianopsia from optic chiasm compression.

questions.vignette: A 2-month-old boy is brought to clinic for poor feeding and slow weight gain. His mother reports that he tires easily during feeds, sweats heavily, and often breathes rapidly even when he is calm. He was born at term and has had no fever or cough. On exam, he is mildly tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 56/min and has a single loud second heart sound. A harsh systolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border. His lips look slightly dusky when he cries, and his liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin. Chest radiograph from an urgent evaluation shows cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings. Echocardiography shows a single great vessel arising from the heart with a large ventricular septal defect and a common semilunar valve.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Truncus arteriosus is a conotruncal defect in which a single arterial trunk arises from the heart and supplies the systemic, coronary, and pulmonary circulations, typically with a large ventricular septal defect. Infants present in early life with a combination of mild cyanosis and congestive heart failure from pulmonary overcirculation, including tachypnea, poor feeding, failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, cardiomegaly, and increased pulmonary vascular markings. A single loud second heart sound and a systolic murmur are typical. The echocardiographic finding of a single great vessel with a common semilunar valve and VSD is most consistent with this diagnosis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A ventricular septal defect can cause tachypnea, poor feeding, hepatomegaly, and a harsh holosystolic murmur from left-to-right shunting, but it would not explain the single great vessel with a common semilunar valve or the single loud second heart sound. Mild cyanosis is also not typical unless pulmonary vascular disease develops.

Transposition of the great arteries causes parallel circulations and usually presents with profound cyanosis in the newborn period. It does not cause a single arterial trunk with a common semilunar valve, and the chest radiograph more often reflects decreased pulmonary blood flow unless there is substantial mixing.

Tetralogy of Fallot is characterized by right ventricular outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, ventricular septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy. It usually causes reduced pulmonary blood flow and more prominent cyanosis rather than pulmonary overcirculation with cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascular markings.

Patent ductus arteriosus may produce tachypnea, poor feeding, and heart failure if the shunt is large, often with a continuous murmur, but it does not produce a single great vessel arising from the heart or a common semilunar valve.

questions.teaching_point: Truncus arteriosus presents in early infancy with cyanosis and heart failure due to a single great artery overriding a VSD, producing pulmonary overcirculation and a single loud S2.

questions.vignette: A 76-year-old woman with a history of recent knee arthroplasty presents to her primary care clinic 10 days after hospital discharge. She reports new unilateral calf swelling and pleuritic chest discomfort that began yesterday. Her pulse is 108/min, respiratory rate is 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. She is hemodynamically stable and in no acute distress. The clinician is considering the pathophysiology of her likely condition.
questions.lead_in: Which mechanism most directly explains the development of this condition?

answer_choices.text: Leakage of fluid into the alveoli due to left ventricular systolic failure
Diffuse immune-mediated destruction of alveolar capillaries leading to hemorrhage
Embolization of thrombus from the deep veins to the pulmonary arterial circulation
In situ thrombosis within the coronary arteries causing myocardial ischemia
Air trapping from inflammatory narrowing of the small airways

questions.rationale: Pulmonary embolism most commonly results from a thrombus that forms in the deep veins of the legs or pelvis and then embolizes to the pulmonary arteries. This patient’s recent orthopedic surgery, unilateral leg swelling, tachycardia, and pleuritic chest pain are classic risk factors and clues for venous thromboembolism.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Pulmonary edema from left ventricular failure causes alveolar fluid accumulation and dyspnea, but it is not caused by embolic obstruction of the pulmonary arteries.
Diffuse immune-mediated alveolar capillary destruction describes a pulmonary capillaritis or vasculitic process, not the usual mechanism of pulmonary embolism.

Coronary artery thrombosis causes acute coronary syndrome, which typically presents with substernal chest pressure and may radiate to the arm or jaw rather than with unilateral calf swelling and pleuritic pain.
Air trapping from small-airway inflammation is the mechanism of obstructive airway disease such as asthma or COPD, which does not explain acute unilateral leg swelling after surgery.

questions.teaching_point: Pulmonary embolism usually occurs when a venous thrombus from the legs or pelvis embolizes to the pulmonary arterial circulation.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 18 hours after eating home-canned green beans at a family gathering. He reports progressive blurred vision, dry mouth, and trouble swallowing. On exam, he is afebrile, alert, and speaking in a quiet, nasal voice. Pupils are dilated and sluggishly reactive. Cranial nerve testing shows bilateral ptosis and reduced gag reflex. He has symmetric descending weakness in both arms and legs, and reflexes are diminished. No sensory deficits are present. His breathing is shallow, and his forced vital capacity is declining over serial measurements.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

answer_choices.text: Perform emergent endotracheal intubation and defer antitoxin therapy
Give activated charcoal and discharge if symptoms do not progress
Administer botulinum antitoxin and monitor closely with respiratory support as needed
Start pyridostigmine and arrange urgent neurology consultation
Begin high-dose intravenous ceftriaxone and admit for suspected meningitis

questions.rationale: This patient has classic foodborne botulism with cranial nerve involvement, descending symmetric weakness, autonomic findings, and progressive respiratory compromise after exposure to improperly preserved food. The most appropriate immediate treatment is prompt administration of botulinum antitoxin, which can stop progression by neutralizing circulating toxin, along with close monitoring and respiratory support because respiratory failure is a major risk.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Intubation may become necessary if respiratory failure is imminent, but antitoxin should still be given as early as possible. Deferring antitoxin would allow ongoing toxin effect and worsen neurologic progression.

Activated charcoal is not appropriate this long after ingestion and does not treat established neurotoxin-mediated paralysis. Discharge would be unsafe given the patient’s bulbar dysfunction and declining respiratory status.

Pyridostigmine is used for myasthenia gravis, which can also cause fatigable weakness and bulbar symptoms, but the exposure history, dilated pupils, dry mouth, and descending paralysis favor botulism rather than a neuromuscular junction autoimmune disorder.

Meningitis can cause altered mental status, fever, and meningeal signs; this patient is afebrile and has a flaccid descending paralysis with cranial nerve findings after a food exposure, which is much more consistent with botulism than CNS infection.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected botulism, give antitoxin immediately and provide respiratory monitoring/support; do not wait for confirmatory testing when the clinical picture is convincing.

questions.vignette: A 3-week-old term infant is brought to clinic for poor stooling and progressive abdominal distension. The infant passed meconium at 72 hours of life, then had only one small stool in the past week. He feeds slowly and has occasional nonbilious spit-ups but no fever or diarrhea. On exam, he has a distended but soft abdomen and poor weight gain. Rectal examination produces an explosive passage of stool followed by decompression of the abdomen. The mother asks what study should be done next to confirm the suspected diagnosis.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is the best next step to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Rectal suction biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test for Hirschsprung disease because it demonstrates absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal plexus, often with hypertrophied nerve trunks. This infant's delayed meconium passage, progressive abdominal distension, poor stooling, and explosive stool after rectal examination are classic for Hirschsprung disease. Contrast enema and anorectal manometry may support the diagnosis, but biopsy confirms it.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Anorectal manometry can support Hirschsprung disease by showing absence of the rectoanal inhibitory reflex, but it does not provide histologic confirmation.
An abdominal radiograph may show nonspecific bowel dilation or obstruction, but it cannot confirm Hirschsprung disease.
Serum TSH testing may be considered when evaluating constipation from hypothyroidism, but it does not confirm Hirschsprung disease and would not explain the explosive stool after rectal examination.
Contrast enema can show a transition zone with proximal dilation and a narrowed distal colon, but it is supportive rather than definitive for diagnosis.

questions.teaching_point: In an infant with delayed meconium passage, abdominal distension, and explosive stool after rectal examination, Hirschsprung disease is strongly suspected; rectal suction biopsy is the confirmatory test, while contrast enema and anorectal manometry are supportive studies.

questions.vignette: A 28-year-old man presents to urgent care with 1 day of fever, severe headache, and worsening photophobia. He says he was feeling well until last night, when he developed chills and nausea. This morning his roommate noticed he was confused and not acting right. He has no focal weakness and no history of migraine. On examination, he is febrile, ill-appearing, and has neck stiffness. You suspect acute bacterial meningitis.
questions.lead_in: Which pathophysiologic process most directly explains the patients altered mental status?

answer_choices.text: Intermittent cerebral vasospasm leading to transient focal neurologic deficits
Autoimmune destruction of acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Demyelination of CNS white matter producing slowed nerve conduction
Inflammation of the meninges causing cerebral edema, impaired cerebrospinal fluid dynamics, and increased intracranial pressure
Viral invasion of anterior horn cells causing lower motor neuron weakness

questions.rationale: Acute bacterial meningitis causes intense inflammation of the meninges and subarachnoid space. Inflammatory mediators can produce cerebral edema and disrupt cerebrospinal fluid circulation, which may increase intracranial pressure and impair cerebral function. These changes explain the patients headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, and altered mental status.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Cerebral vasospasm is classically associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage or other vascular disorders and would more likely cause sudden headache or focal neurologic deficits than a febrile meningeal syndrome.

Autoimmune acetylcholine receptor loss causes myasthenia gravis, which presents with fatigable weakness, ptosis, and diplopia rather than fever, neck stiffness, or confusion from meningeal inflammation.
Demyelination describes disorders such as multiple sclerosis, which typically cause relapsing neurologic deficits rather than acute fever, neck stiffness, and confusion.
Anterior horn cell involvement is seen in poliomyelitis and similar infections, which primarily cause flaccid weakness rather than acute meningismus and encephalopathy.

questions.teaching_point: In bacterial meningitis, meningeal inflammation can cause cerebral edema, impaired cerebrospinal fluid flow, and increased intracranial pressure, leading to altered mental status.

questions.vignette: A 27-year-old man comes to the emergency department with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began while he was watching television. He has no history of trauma. He is tall and thin, smokes cigarettes, and has mild anxiety but no prior cardiopulmonary disease. Vital signs are: temperature 36.8 C (98.2 F), heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg, respiratory rate 24/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. On examination, breath sounds are decreased over the right apex and percussion is hyperresonant on the right. The trachea is midline, and there is no jugular venous distention or hypotension.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.rationale: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is most likely because this patient has the classic risk profile of a tall, thin young adult smoker with sudden pleuritic chest pain, mild dyspnea, unilateral decreased breath sounds, and hyperresonance on exam without signs of hemodynamic instability or trauma. The midline trachea and normal blood pressure argue against tension physiology.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Community-acquired pneumonia typically presents with fever, cough, sputum production, and focal crackles or bronchial breath sounds rather than sudden onset pleuritic pain with hyperresonance.

Pulmonary embolism can cause sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, but the unilateral hyperresonance and focal decreased breath sounds are more consistent with pneumothorax than PE, and there are no strong thromboembolic risk factors provided.

A ruptured thoracic aortic aneurysm would usually present with severe tearing chest or back pain and rapid hemodynamic deterioration; the patient’s stable vitals and focal pulmonary exam findings do not fit this diagnosis.

Acute pericarditis usually causes sharp chest pain that improves when leaning forward and is associated with a pericardial friction rub or diffuse ST-segment changes, not unilateral absent breath sounds and hyperresonance.

questions.teaching_point: In a tall, thin young smoker with sudden pleuritic chest pain and unilateral decreased breath sounds with hyperresonance, primary spontaneous pneumothorax is the most likely diagnosis.

questions.vignette: A 67-year-old woman comes to clinic for worsening knee pain over the past year. The pain is dull, worse with climbing stairs and after long walks, and improves with rest. She has morning stiffness that lasts about 15 minutes. She has a body mass index of 32 kg/m2 and no history of inflammatory arthritis, trauma, or peptic ulcer disease. She has already tried weight loss, activity modification, and acetaminophen with minimal relief and asks what should be recommended next. On examination, there is bony enlargement and crepitus of the right knee without warmth or effusion.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next treatment to recommend?
questions.rationale: Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are an evidence-based treatment for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis when initial conservative measures and simple analgesics are insufficient. They provide pain relief with less systemic adverse effect risk than oral NSAIDs, making them an appropriate next outpatient option for this patient.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs are used for inflammatory arthritides such as rheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritis, which is managed with symptom-directed therapy.

Arthroscopic lavage is not recommended for uncomplicated osteoarthritis because it does not improve outcomes compared with conservative management and is not indicated without mechanical symptoms or another surgical problem.

Intra-articular corticosteroid injection can provide short-term relief for osteoarthritis flares, but topical NSAIDs are generally preferred as a next step for chronic knee osteoarthritis after acetaminophen and conservative measures.

Oral prednisone is not recommended for routine osteoarthritis management because this is a noninflammatory degenerative joint disease and systemic corticosteroids expose the patient to unnecessary adverse effects.

questions.teaching_point: For knee osteoarthritis, nonpharmacologic therapy and weight loss are foundational, and topical NSAIDs are a preferred medication option when simple analgesics are inadequate.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old man is admitted for severe unilateral right-sided headaches that began abruptly 2 hours ago. He reports that the pain is centered around his right eye and is described as excruciating, with repeated attacks lasting 30 to 60 minutes over the past week. During the episodes, he becomes restless and paces the room. He also has tearing of the right eye and nasal congestion on the same side. He has a 15-pack-year smoking history. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal, and a noncontrast head CT done in the emergency department is unrevealing. His current attack is ongoing despite oral acetaminophen taken before arrival.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this patient’s current headache episode?
questions.rationale: This patient has cluster headache, suggested by severe unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms, short recurrent attacks, and marked restlessness. The most appropriate immediate abortive therapy is high-flow oxygen delivered by nonrebreather mask, which can rapidly terminate an acute cluster attack and is especially useful in the inpatient setting.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Triptans are appropriate abortive therapy for cluster headache, but oral sumatriptan has a slower onset and is less effective for rapid relief than inhaled oxygen or a subcutaneous triptan during an acute attack.

Systemic corticosteroids can be used as transitional or bridging therapy to reduce attack frequency while preventive therapy is being established, but they are not the best immediate abortive treatment for an ongoing cluster headache attack.
Topiramate may be considered preventive therapy in selected patients with cluster headache, but it will not treat the current attack and is not an immediate intervention.
Opioids are ineffective for cluster headache and increase the risk of medication overuse and dependency; they are not recommended for acute management.

questions.teaching_point: Acute cluster headache is best aborted with high-flow oxygen or a rapid-onset triptan; oral analgesics and opioids are poor choices.

questions.vignette: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because of 4 months of intermittent headaches and occasional vomiting, usually in the morning. His parents also report that he has become clumsier when riding his bike and has started holding books closer to his face. He has no fever, neck stiffness, or recent head trauma. On examination, he is alert with normal strength and sensation, but his gait is wide-based and he sways when turning quickly. Funduscopic examination shows blurred optic disc margins bilaterally.
questions.lead_in: Which additional physical examination finding is most likely in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Distal symmetric weakness with absent ankle reflexes
Fluctuating ptosis that worsens with repeated upward gaze

questions.rationale: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a common pediatric cerebellar tumor. This child’s progressive morning headaches, vomiting, visual change from increased intracranial pressure, wide-based gait, and papilledema suggest a posterior fossa mass affecting the cerebellum. A cerebellar process commonly produces truncal ataxia and nystagmus, including downbeat nystagmus.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Distal symmetric weakness with absent ankle reflexes suggests a peripheral neuropathy such as Guillain-Barré syndrome or chronic polyneuropathy, which would not cause papilledema or morning vomiting from a brain mass.
Fluctuating ptosis that worsens with repeated upward gaze is characteristic of myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disorder, not a cerebellar mass.

Unilateral facial droop with hyperreflexia suggests an upper motor neuron lesion such as a stroke or other corticospinal tract injury, which does not fit this slowly progressive posterior fossa presentation.
A resting tremor with cogwheel rigidity is typical of parkinsonism, which is not expected in a young child and does not explain the signs of increased intracranial pressure.

questions.teaching_point: Pilocytic astrocytoma in children often presents with signs of posterior fossa involvement, including ataxia, nystagmus, headache, vomiting, and papilledema from obstructive hydrocephalus.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man with hypertension presents to his primary care clinic with 2 days of sharp, central chest discomfort that worsens when he lies flat and improves when he sits up and leans forward. He had an upper respiratory illness 1 week ago. His temperature is 37.8 C, blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg, and pulse is 96/min. Cardiac examination reveals a faint scratchy sound heard best at the left lower sternal border when he leans forward. ECG shows diffuse concave ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depressions in multiple leads. He asks why the pain is not like the pressure he had during a prior episode of stable angina.
questions.lead_in: Which underlying mechanism best explains the ECG findings in this patient?

answer_choices.text: Fibrotic thickening of the pericardium causing impaired ventricular filling and fixed cardiac output
Inflammation of the myocardium causing myocyte injury and regional conduction abnormalities
Transient coronary artery vasospasm causing episodic transmural ischemia and ST-segment elevation
Inflammation of the pericardium and adjacent epicardium causing diffuse injury currents on ECG
Incomplete relaxation of the left ventricle leading to exertional subendocardial ischemia

questions.rationale:
This patient has acute pericarditis, likely post-viral. The key ECG findings are diffuse, concave ST-segment elevations with PR-segment depressions, which result from inflammation of the pericardium and adjacent epicardium. Because the inflammation is diffuse rather than confined to a single coronary territory, it produces a generalized injury current across the epicardial surface. The positional chest pain and pericardial friction rub support the diagnosis, but the question asks for the mechanism behind the ECG changes.

Fibrotic thickening of the pericardium describes constrictive pericarditis, a chronic condition that impairs diastolic filling rather than causing acute diffuse ST elevation. Myocardial inflammation causes myocarditis, which more often presents with myocardial injury, arrhythmias, or heart failure and does not classically cause PR depression. Coronary vasospasm can cause transient ST elevation from focal ischemia, but it is not associated with a pericardial rub or the diffuse ECG pattern seen here. Incomplete relaxation of the left ventricle causing exertional subendocardial ischemia describes stable angina physiology, which causes exertional pressure-like chest pain rather than the ECG pattern of acute pericarditis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Fibrotic pericardial thickening causes constrictive pericarditis, which is a chronic disorder leading to impaired diastolic filling and signs of right-sided congestion, not diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression.

Myocarditis involves inflammation of the myocardium, leading to myocyte injury and possible arrhythmias or heart failure. It does not classically produce the diffuse ST-segment elevations and PR depressions typical of pericarditis.
Coronary vasospasm can cause episodic chest pain with transient ST-segment elevation, but it would not explain a pericardial friction rub, positional pain, or the diffuse inflammatory ECG pattern.

Impaired left ventricular relaxation with exertional subendocardial ischemia describes stable angina or diastolic dysfunction physiology, which causes exertional pressure-like discomfort rather than the positional pain and diffuse ECG changes seen here.

questions.teaching_point: Acute pericarditis causes diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR depression because inflammation of the pericardium and epicardium creates a generalized injury current on ECG.

questions.vignette: A 24-year-old woman is scheduled for urgent laparoscopic appendectomy after 2 days of worsening right lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. On pre-op evaluation, she appears cachectic and guarded about her eating habits. Her BMI is 15.8 kg/m2, and she reports 8 kg of weight loss over 4 months. She exercises for 2 hours daily and becomes distressed when asked about food intake. She denies vomiting or laxative use. Vitals are blood pressure 88/54 mm Hg, heart rate 42/min, and temperature 36.1 C (97.0 F). Exam shows dry mucous membranes and lanugo on the forearms. Which additional diagnostic study is most appropriate before anesthesia is administered?
questions.lead_in: Which additional diagnostic study is most appropriate before anesthesia is administered?
questions.rationale: This patient has features strongly suggestive of anorexia nervosa with severe malnutrition and physiologic instability, including bradycardia, hypotension, and significant low body weight. Before anesthesia, the most important additional study is a 12-lead ECG to assess for conduction abnormalities and QT prolongation, which increase perioperative arrhythmia risk in patients with anorexia nervosa and electrolyte disturbances. In the perioperative setting, identifying occult cardiac risk is immediately relevant to safe anesthesia planning.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Brain MRI could be considered if there were focal neurologic deficits, headaches, or concern for a central cause of weight loss, but those features are not present and it would not be the most appropriate pre-anesthesia study.

Upper endoscopy may be appropriate if she had symptoms suggesting an esophageal or gastric source of weight loss, but the presentation already supports anorexia nervosa and the urgent priority is cardiac risk assessment before anesthesia.

A serum cortisol level may be useful when adrenal insufficiency is suspected, but her history and exam are more consistent with restrictive eating and malnutrition, and cortisol testing would not address the immediate perioperative cardiac risk.

An arterial blood gas can be useful in critically ill patients with respiratory failure or severe acid-base disturbance, but there is no evidence of ventilatory compromise here; ECG evaluation is a more targeted and important preoperative study.

questions.teaching_point: In medically unstable patients with suspected anorexia nervosa, perioperative evaluation should prioritize cardiac assessment, especially ECG screening for bradyarrhythmias and QT prolongation.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man is evaluated in clinic for 2 months of progressively worsening headaches and new difficulty finding words. His wife says he has become more forgetful and had a brief episode last week in which his right hand and face jerked rhythmically for about 1 minute, followed by several minutes of confusion. He has also had two episodes of vomiting in the morning. He has no fever, neck stiffness, or recent trauma. Neurologic examination shows mild right arm weakness and slowed speech. MRI of the brain with gadolinium reveals a heterogeneously enhancing left frontal lobe mass with central necrosis and surrounding vasogenic edema.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.rationale: Glioblastoma is the most likely diagnosis because the patient has a rapidly progressive focal neurologic syndrome with headache, new-onset seizure, cognitive/behavioral change, and MRI showing a heterogeneously enhancing mass with central necrosis and surrounding edema. In adults, this aggressive infiltrating astrocytic tumor commonly presents with signs of increased intracranial pressure and focal deficits.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Meningiomas are usually slow-growing extra-axial masses with more indolent symptoms; they can cause focal deficits or seizures, but central necrosis and the rapid progression described here are less typical.

Primary CNS lymphoma can present with focal deficits and enhancing brain lesions, but it is more strongly associated with immunosuppression and often shows deep periventricular involvement rather than a necrotic frontal lobe mass in an immunocompetent adult.

Oligodendrogliomas can cause seizures and frontal lobe symptoms, but they are typically slower growing and classically have calcifications on imaging rather than an aggressive heterogeneously enhancing necrotic lesion.

A brain abscess can produce headache, seizures, and ring-enhancing lesions, but fever, systemic infectious symptoms, or an obvious source of infection are usually present; the MRI description and subacute progressive course are more consistent with a high-grade glioma.

questions.teaching_point: In an adult with progressive focal deficits, seizures, and a heterogeneously enhancing necrotic brain mass with edema, glioblastoma is the leading diagnosis.

questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic because of 2 days of fever, chills, and right-sided flank pain. She also reports urinary frequency and burning with urination. She has no vaginal discharge or pelvic pain. Temperature is 38.6 C (101.5 F), heart rate is 104/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. Examination shows right costovertebral angle tenderness. A point-of-care urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrites. She is able to drink fluids, is not pregnant, and has no history of kidney stones or urinary tract abnormalities.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study should be obtained now, without delaying treatment?

answer_choices.text: Noncontrast helical CT of the abdomen and pelvis

questions.rationale: Urine culture and sensitivity should be obtained before antibiotics, but treatment of suspected acute pyelonephritis should not be delayed while waiting for results. The diagnosis is supported clinically by fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, urinary symptoms, and a positive urine dipstick. A urine culture identifies the causative organism and guides antibiotic selection, which is especially important in pyelonephritis because resistant pathogens are more common than in uncomplicated cystitis.

distractor_rationales.explanation: A complete blood count may show leukocytosis and help assess illness severity, but it is not the key diagnostic study for confirming the suspected upper urinary tract infection or guiding antibiotic choice.

Renal ultrasonography is useful when obstruction, hydronephrosis, pregnancy, or a structural abnormality is suspected, but it is not the best routine study for an otherwise stable outpatient with straightforward pyelonephritis.

Noncontrast CT is preferred when nephrolithiasis is suspected or when complications such as obstruction, abscess, or emphysematous infection are concerns; this patient has no stone history, no severe illness, and no findings that make immediate CT the best next step.

A basic metabolic panel can assess kidney function and electrolyte status, but it does not confirm pyelonephritis and is not the most important study to obtain before starting empiric outpatient therapy in this stable patient.

questions.teaching_point: Acute pyelonephritis is usually a clinical diagnosis; obtain a urine culture before antibiotics when possible, but do not delay treatment in a stable patient, and reserve imaging for suspected obstruction, pregnancy, severe illness, or treatment failure.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is admitted for severe right-sided headache attacks that began 2 days ago. Each episode lasts about 45 minutes, occurs several times a day, and is associated with tearing of the right eye, nasal congestion, and restlessness. He paces the room during attacks and says the pain is worst around the right eye. He has a history of hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has no focal neurologic deficits, fever, neck stiffness, or visual loss. The admitting team suspects cluster headache and wants to start an acute treatment that is effective during an attack and safe to use with his current conditions.
questions.lead_in: Which treatment is the most appropriate initial therapy for aborting his headache attacks while he is hospitalized?
questions.rationale: High-flow 100% oxygen via a nonrebreather mask is a first-line abortive treatment for cluster headache and is appropriate for an inpatient setting because it can be started immediately during an attack. Cluster headache attacks are brief, severe, unilateral, and associated with autonomic symptoms; treatment should rapidly terminate the active episode. In this patient, oxygen is the best initial abortive option because it is effective and avoids the cardiovascular concerns that may limit triptan use in some older adults with comorbid disease.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Oral prednisone can be used as a short-term transitional therapy in cluster headache, but it is not the best immediate abortive treatment for an active attack.
Intravenous morphine is not recommended for cluster headache because it does not reliably abort attacks and exposes the patient to unnecessary adverse effects.

Subcutaneous sumatriptan can abort cluster headache attacks, but it is less suitable here because triptans can be limited by vascular risk and other contraindications in older adults with hypertension or possible cardiovascular disease.
Oral propranolol is a migraine prophylactic agent, not an acute cluster headache treatment, and it would not abort the current attacks.

questions.teaching_point: Cluster headache attacks are best aborted with high-flow oxygen or a triptan; in patients where triptans are less desirable, high-flow oxygen is the preferred first-line inpatient abortive therapy.

questions.vignette: A 72-year-old man is brought to his primary care clinic by his daughter because of 3 months of worsening headaches and subtle personality changes. He has also become forgetful at work and recently got lost driving to a familiar grocery store. Over the past 2 weeks, he has had two episodes of brief left arm twitching followed by confusion. He has a history of hypertension and former tobacco use. Neurologic examination shows mild left pronator drift and slowed left-hand rapid alternating movements. Funduscopic examination reveals no papilledema. A noncontrast head CT obtained after the seizure-like episode shows a right frontal lobe mass with surrounding vasogenic edema and areas of central necrosis.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer disease

questions.rationale: Glioblastoma multiforme is the most likely diagnosis because this older adult has a rapidly progressive focal neurologic syndrome with headaches, personality/cognitive changes, focal motor deficits, and new focal seizures. Imaging shows a mass with surrounding vasogenic edema and central necrosis, which is classic for an aggressive infiltrating primary brain tumor such as glioblastoma.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Meningiomas can cause slowly progressive neurologic symptoms in older adults, but they are typically extra-axial, well circumscribed, and not associated with central necrosis on imaging.

Primary CNS lymphoma can present with neurologic deficits and cognitive changes, but it is more strongly associated with immunosuppression and usually presents with enhancing lesions rather than a necrotic frontal lobe mass in this context.
Subdural hematoma can cause confusion, headache, and focal deficits in older adults, especially after trauma, but it would not typically present as an intraparenchymal necrotic mass on CT.
Alzheimer disease and mild cognitive impairment cause gradually progressive memory loss, but they do not explain focal neurologic deficits, new seizures, or a mass lesion with edema and necrosis.

questions.teaching_point: In an older adult, progressive focal deficits, seizures, and a necrotic mass with vasogenic edema strongly suggest glioblastoma.

questions.vignette: A 58-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of 2 days of tingling around his mouth and in both hands, muscle cramps, and intermittent carpopedal spasms. He recently underwent thyroid surgery and has been taking only acetaminophen at home. He appears anxious and is breathing rapidly. Examination shows bilateral hand flexion at the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints when a blood pressure cuff is inflated on his upper arm. Heart rate is 104/min, blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg, and mental status is intact.
questions.lead_in: Which finding is most consistent with this patient's condition?

answer_choices.text: Serum phosphate is elevated and parathyroid hormone is elevated despite low calcium
Serum phosphate is elevated and parathyroid hormone is low after recent neck surgery
Muscle weakness improves with repeated activity and ptosis worsens later in the day
Deep tendon reflexes are diminished and the patient reports constipation and polyuria
Serum magnesium is low after chronic diarrhea and proton pump inhibitor use

questions.rationale:
This patient has symptomatic hypocalcemia due to postsurgical hypoparathyroidism after thyroid surgery. Injury or removal of the parathyroid glands leads to low parathyroid hormone, which decreases serum calcium and increases serum phosphate. The perioral and distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, and positive Trousseau sign are classic manifestations of hypocalcemia.

A low magnesium state can also cause hypocalcemia, but the history in this case strongly points to postoperative hypoparathyroidism. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, not tetany. Hypercalcemia causes decreased deep tendon reflexes, constipation, and polyuria. Elevated phosphate with elevated parathyroid hormone despite hypocalcemia suggests pseudohypoparathyroidism, which would not fit the recent thyroid surgery in this stem.

distractor_rationales.explanation: This pattern suggests pseudohypoparathyroidism, in which parathyroid hormone is elevated but ineffective. Although it can produce hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, it is not the best fit for this postoperative patient.

Fatigable weakness that improves with repeated activity and ptosis that worsens later in the day are characteristic of myasthenia gravis, which does not cause carpopedal spasm or a positive Trousseau sign.
Diminished deep tendon reflexes with constipation and polyuria are more consistent with hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia.

Hypomagnesemia can cause neuromuscular irritability and secondary hypocalcemia, but the recent thyroid surgery makes postsurgical hypoparathyroidism the more likely cause here. Chronic diarrhea and proton pump inhibitor use are plausible risk factors for low magnesium, but they are not supported by the stem.

questions.teaching_point: After thyroid or parathyroid surgery, new perioral paresthesias, tetany, and a positive Trousseau sign should prompt concern for hypocalcemia due to hypoparathyroidism, typically with low PTH and hyperphosphatemia.

questions.vignette: A 42-year-old man is admitted for 10 days of progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough. He has HIV and stopped taking antiretroviral therapy several months ago. He reports fatigue and low-grade fevers but no sputum production or pleuritic chest pain. On exam, he is tachypneic with an oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. Lung auscultation is clear. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse interstitial infiltrates. The clinician suspects Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and wants the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis while minimizing risk to the patient.
questions.lead_in: Which diagnostic study is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage specimen with silver stain or direct immunofluorescence for Pneumocystis organisms

questions.rationale: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is suspected in an immunocompromised patient with subacute dyspnea, nonproductive cough, hypoxemia, and diffuse interstitial infiltrates. The diagnosis is confirmed by identifying the organism in a respiratory specimen. Induced sputum is a noninvasive initial approach, and bronchoalveolar lavage has higher diagnostic yield if needed; special staining or direct immunofluorescence is used to detect Pneumocystis organisms. This provides confirmation while avoiding the unnecessary invasiveness of tissue biopsy.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Transbronchial lung biopsy can demonstrate organisms or pathology, but it is more invasive than induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage and is not the preferred confirmatory test in this setting.
Serum beta-D-glucan can support the diagnosis of Pneumocystis infection, but it is nonspecific and does not definitively confirm the organism.
Arterial blood gas measurement assesses the severity of hypoxemia and gas exchange impairment, but it does not establish the diagnosis.
High-resolution chest computed tomography can show findings compatible with Pneumocystis pneumonia, but imaging alone is not confirmatory.

questions.teaching_point: In suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia, confirm the diagnosis with induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage using special staining or immunofluorescence; imaging and serum markers may support suspicion but are not definitive.

questions.vignette: A 74-year-old man is hospitalized for community-acquired pneumonia. On hospital day 2, nurses report that he has been increasingly disoriented and restless since last night. He has been trying to pull out his IV and repeatedly asks where he is, but earlier this morning he was able to answer questions appropriately. His wife says he was fully independent and cognitively intact before admission. He has been febrile, has slept poorly, and received oxycodone for pleuritic pain. On examination, he is inattentive, fluctuates between agitation and drowsiness, and misidentifies the current month and location. His speech is disorganized, but there is no focal neurologic deficit.
questions.lead_in: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

answer_choices.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features

questions.rationale: Delirium is the most likely diagnosis because the patient has an acute change in mental status during hospitalization, impaired attention, fluctuating course, disorganized thinking, and altered level of consciousness. Common precipitants include infection, hypoxia, sleep deprivation, and medications such as opioids.

distractor_rationales.explanation: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features can cause low mood, slowed thinking, and sometimes delusions, but it does not typically produce acute fluctuating inattention and altered awareness.

Catatonia is characterized by prominent psychomotor abnormalities such as mutism, stupor, posturing, or waxy flexibility, which are not described here; the key findings are fluctuating attention and awareness.
Dementia with Lewy bodies causes chronic progressive cognitive decline and visual hallucinations, not an abrupt fluctuating inattention developing over hours in the setting of acute illness.
A transient ischemic attack can cause abrupt neurologic symptoms, but it would usually produce focal deficits rather than a global fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition.

questions.teaching_point: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and awareness, usually triggered by an underlying medical illness, medication, or environmental stressor in hospitalized adults.

questions.vignette: A 62-year-old woman comes to an outpatient clinic for worsening right knee pain over the past year. The pain is worse after long walks and when climbing stairs, and it improves with rest. She denies fever, recent injury, prolonged morning stiffness, or pain in other joints. Exam shows bony enlargement and mild crepitus of the right knee without warmth or erythema. Her BMI is 31 kg/m2. She has a history of hypertension and takes lisinopril. She has tried intermittent acetaminophen with only minimal relief and asks what else can help.
questions.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

answer_choices.text: Recommend a structured exercise and weight-loss program with topical NSAID therapy
Refer urgently for arthrocentesis and intra-articular antibiotics
Initiate hydroxychloroquine to slow joint damage
Begin allopurinol for long-term urate lowering

questions.rationale: This patient has typical knee osteoarthritis with activity-related pain, brief or absent morning stiffness, crepitus, and bony enlargement.
